### Dedication

To the silenced, the disappeared, the punished for truth: this is for
you, yours. Up yours, not. This is against the criminals, the abusers,
all who harass and loathe our lives. To my love and her father, denied
justice, and to all whose lives were shattered by systems built to
protect power, not live. This ongoing work stands as witness. Justice is
not optional, is owed. To my love, for our life. Thanks.

*^*†*^^*\ *^*To the fallen, loving ones, never wishing to do harm. To us
remaining, in living loving memory, taking this action forward. **

violence, and the ethics of medication management in contemporary
Spain - A bio-cultural and trans-disciplinary action research toward

original academic work conducted independently by the author. All
sources consulted or referenced are duly acknowledged, and any ideas,
texts, or materials not my own have been properly cited in accordance
with scientific and academic standards. This work has not been
submitted, in whole or in part, for any other degree or academic
recognition at this or any other institution. The empirical research,
analytical development, and writing process adhered to the ethical
principles governing scientific research, including those concerning
human subjects, consent, confidentiality, and integrity. The content
reflects the intellectual trajectory and field-based findings developed
during the researcher's doctoral professor in training work within the
doctoral programme at Universitat Rovira i Virgili, aligning with the
institutional and disciplinary requirements therein and open science
best and bettering practices.

****

****Declaration of intent: ****This dissertation is not a collection of
opinions, better beliefs, or speculative remedies. It is a scientific
document grounded in the demand for best practices and continual
improvement in mental health care. It argues that healing must be
demonstrable, when a problem is present, it must resolve through
intervention without causing further harm. The work emerges from direct
experience of prolonged institutional and interpersonal violence,
including coercion, forced treatment, and systemic neglect. It reflects
on a reality where cruelty is tolerated, pathology imposed, and
suffering weaponized. What is presented here is the product of survival
and empirical observation, a structured response to abuses normalized
under the guise of care. It is submitted with a clear aim: to support a
shift toward evidence-based, rights-respecting, and humane systems of
health, free of coercion and anchored in justice.****

### Aknowledgements and support remarks: 

\
I thank my love, Herti Noviyanti.

The rest of this section remains under preparation and will be finalized
following the external review process, scheduled for completion at the
end of summer. It will include a carefully verified and ethically
composed acknowledgment of the many individuals whose contributions made
this dissertation possible under conditions of extreme adversity,
including documented torture, prolonged violence, and institutional
betrayal. These abuses nearly resulted in the loss of life and have
caused enduring harm to the researcher and their close ones. They must
be recognized clearly, not diluted nor abstracted, as acts of cruelty
that directly opposed the values this work seeks to defend. Throughout
five years of persistent research, dialogue, and resistance, hundreds of
persons contributed to this journey in multiple capacities. Colleagues,
coauthors, field informants, teachers, professors, professionals,
friends, allies, and fellow survivors all played indispensable roles.
Parents and caregivers who stand for the dignity of children and the
value of health and peaceful coexistence are likewise part of this
network of care and shared responsibility. Their presence and support
helped sustain not only the development of this thesis, but also the
possibility of continuing to live, think, and build responsibly despite
systematic attempts to silence or destroy.

The full list of acknowledgments will be made available through the
dissertation's online repository and the open science laboratory and
fieldwork notebook that accompany this work. This digital space will
serve not only to credit contributions but also to reconnect with all
participants engaged during the action-research process. It will open a
space for ongoing collaboration, including follow-up interviews and
joint reflection through the dissemination and engagement platform of
the EU BEACON One Health Education COST Action, which now continues and
expands the mission of this thesis. This dissertation is not only an
individual scholarly achievement but a collective act of survival and
intellectual resistance. It is a commitment to justice, the preservation
of truth, and the promotion of systems capable of fostering health,
equity, and mutual recognition. Final expressions of gratitude will be
included with the explicit consent of each individual, ensuring their
acknowledgment is respectful, accurate, and aligned with the shared
ethical principles of this work.

### **Readers guide to facilitate lecture**

****

This doctoral dissertation is structured as a trans-disciplinary
ethnography of psychiatric coercion and institutional betrayal, grounded
in bio-cultural theory and action-research. It reflects a five-year
investigation into systemic violence within mental health systems,
primarily in Spain, with comparative reflections from international
fieldwork and global research networks. The thesis integrates narrative,
legal, clinical, and methodological registers, Yet, its primary strength
lies in the empirical synthesis of lived experience, field observations,
and documented testimonies.. The dissertation examines processes of
decision-making and the autonomous management of medication, as well as
their perception within Spanish mental health contexts. From this
starting point, the research delves into the widespread realities of
overmedication and coercive care, phenomena that emerge as structural
features rather than isolated abuses. The testimonies and lived
experiences gathered throughout this research emerge from an engaged and
participatory fieldwork process in which the researcher contributed
actively to community networks, supported the translation and
dissemination of critical materials into Spanish, and facilitated spaces
of mutual learning and advocacy. Rather than occupying a distant
observational role, the researcher collaborated alongside affected
individuals and collectives, bearing witness to the cumulative harms
produced within mental health systems. These iatrogenic harms extend
beyond pharmacological interventions to include forced hospitalizations,
isolation, and the systematic erosion of autonomy, as well as the
persistent marginalization, silencing, and social exclusion that follow
people beyond institutional settings and deepen their suffering. The
witnessing of others\' pain, such as observing peers subjected to
restraint, sedation, or neglect, creates a collective and relational
trauma that reinforces an atmosphere of fear, hopelessness, and
abandonment. These intersecting forms of violence contribute not only to
individual suffering but also to a broader social death, in which
systems intended to provide care perpetuate cycles of harm and
exclusion.

The work is split in the following chapters:

****1 - Introduction: violence, coercion, and structural frames.
****Introduces the thematic and analytical premises of the dissertation,
focusing on the structural character of psychiatric coercion, the
erosion of autonomy, and epistemic exclusion. The chapter frames the
research within the broader urgency of health systems reform grounded in
human rights, scientific ethics, and justice.

****2 - Methodological framework: action research and positionality.
****Outlines the bio-cultural and action-research design underpinning
the study. It details the methodological tools, surveys, testimonies,
ethnography, while positioning the author as a survivor-researcher and
reflecting on ethical, epistemological, and structural implications of
situated knowledge.

****3 - Survey findings: patterns, perceptions, and psychiatric
practice. ****Presents the results of national and transnational surveys
with professionals, users, and stakeholders. Findings highlight
prevailing perceptions of coercion, clinical norms, trust dynamics, and
systemic dysfunctions within psychiatric practice.

****4 - Fieldwork and testimony: lived structures of betrayal.
****Documents extended participant observation and in-depth testimonies
across institutional, professional, and familial settings. This chapter
brings to light trajectories of psychiatric violence, complicity,
silencing, and the emergence of resistance and situated recovery.

****5 - Analytical synthesis: institutional logics and resistance.
****Integrates findings across all empirical sources to examine the
underlying institutional and discursive structures sustaining coercion.
It interrogates the medical legitimization of harm, the erasure of
embodied knowledge, and the spaces of refusal and counter-power.

****6 - Legal and ethical dimensions: norms, violations, and
accountability. ****Provides an introductory analysis of relevant legal
and normative frameworks, highlighting their role in enabling or failing
to prevent psychiatric violence. This chapter serves as an ethical
reference point, grounded in constitutional and international human
rights principles.

****7 - Work ongoing and next steps: one health, pedagogy, and
rights-based systems. ****Proposes concrete strategies for
implementation through shared decision-making, collaborative medication
management, open science, and transformative pedagogy. The chapter
articulates an inclusive roadmap grounded in dignity, justice, planetary
health, and epistemic repair.

****8 - Final conclusions: scientific contributions and systemic
redesign. ****Synthesizes the scientific, ethical, and political
contributions of the dissertation. It reaffirms the responsibility of
knowledge production to dismantle systems of abuse and calls for the
urgent reconfiguration of psychiatric services as part of a broader
structural transformation.

****Annex A**** details the instruments developed and applied in the
participatory action-research process. It documents the rationale,
collaborative design, experiential focus, and integration strategies
used to construct and validate the surveys within a rights-based and
survivor-informed research framework.

****Annex B**** introduces the ethical foundations of qualitative
psychological research. It explores the methodological implications of
working under conditions of structural vulnerability and epistemic
asymmetry, with emphasis on positionality, harm reduction, informed
consent, and research integrity.

****Annex C**** reproduces the peer-reviewed article published in
**Frontiers in Psychology** on the implementation of open dialogue in
Spain. It highlights institutional barriers, ethical tensions, and the
transformative potential of dialogical practices within a predominantly
coercive system.

****Annex D**** contains the manuscript analysing xenophobia as an
aggressive structure that intersects with psychiatric misdiagnosis and
racialised harm. It contextualises epistemic exclusion, somatic impact,
and structural discrimination within broader patterns of
institutionalised violence.

****Annex E**** presents a trans-disciplinary analysis of the nocebo
effect and the giving up given up syndrome, drawing on transcultural
psychiatry and embodied biology. It frames chronic psychosomatic
suffering as a product of sociomedical breakdown, proposing more humane
explanatory models.

****Annex F**** offers a book chapter published by **Nature--Springer**
on better ways to coercion. It discusses dialogical ethics, service user
leadership, therapeutic alliances, and systemic reform through
evidence-based, rights-informed, and person-centred approaches.

****Annex G**** documents the presentation delivered at the 2023
international conference on political abuses of psychiatry. It
synthesises expert testimony and comparative case analysis, addressing
institutional repression, misuse of forensic psychiatry, and systemic
violations.

****Annex H**** translates the core findings of this dissertation into a
structured policy summary. It proposes a roadmap for reform based on
legal, clinical, and scientific evidence, aligned with constitutional
protections and international human rights norms.

****Annex I**** contains the media dissemination kit prepared to ensure
broad public visibility of the dissertation's findings. It includes
visual materials, press strategy, and communication tools for knowledge
translation and open access outreach.

****Annex K**** outlines the Horizon Europe proposals developed as
direct extensions of this research. It describes the implementation
logic, collaborative alliances, and policy relevance of the one
health-based interventions submitted for European funding.

****Annex J**** presents additional tables, on the historical, cultural
and biomedical context of the thesis

\
****Readers are advised to approach the present work as both a formal
scientific contribution and a testimony-driven intervention aimed at
transforming harmful institutional practices. The language employed is
at times severe, a deliberate choice to reflect the gravity and
persistence of the violations documented. While not every chapter
expands on full legal or computational developments, the thesis
maintains methodological integrity and conceptual coherence in service
of its emancipatory objectives. This dissertation emerges from
conditions of extreme institutional violence, sustained interpersonal
abuse, and systemic neglect, directly experienced by the author and
corroborated through preventable tragedies that remain ongoing within
contemporary psychiatric regimes. It offers a scientific ethnography of
coercion, betrayal, and structural injustice in mental health systems,
taking Spain as its principal site of inquiry, with comparative insights
from international contexts. Guided by a bio-cultural and action
research methodology, the study interrogates the entanglement of forced
pharmacological intervention, diagnostic arbitrariness, and systemic
disempowerment. It documents how psychiatric and bureaucratic
mechanisms, often cloaked in clinical or juridical language, perpetuate
exclusion, inflict iatrogenic harm, and erode relational and existential
continuity. ****

### ****The empirical corpus includes mixed methods surveys, verified clinical and legal documentation, and extensive ethnographic fieldwork, all presented with methodological precision. A clear distinction is maintained between analytical results and reflexive testimony. While the author\'s embedded positionality is methodologically activated in specific chapters, the core findings retain their evidentiary grounding. This dual structure, blending systematic inquiry with situated critique, ensures thematic coherence and transparency throughout. More than a conventional academic investigation, this dissertation constitutes a deliberate ethical and political intervention. It outlines a viable path toward institutional transformation anchored in non negotiable human dignity, relational justice, and structural accountability. Situated within the broader framework of one health and aligned with global human rights principles, it offers a robust foundation for urgently needed reform in psychiatric, legal, and educational domains. ****

### ****To support maximal accessibility, the online version of this dissertation is being continuously updated and improved. It includes translations, language adaptation modules, and accessibility features for cognitive, sensory, and motor diversity. The repository is also set to host all relevant used open source tools, as well as version controlled instruments, coding frameworks, and analytic resources, including open courseware, reality check lists, research, medical and administrative protocols, and other resources to further facilitate the implementation and constant improvement. That living archive, not included in this file, is designed to serve diverse publics and collaborative networks committed to justice, healing, and systemic change. ****

### ****Both this guide and the map, point to the future.****

### ** Social Impact of the Thesis**

****

This dissertation generates direct and indirect contributions to public
health, clinical practice, legal governance, and the design of equitable
social systems. It documents and analyzes how coercive psychiatric
practices, particularly the routinization of non-consensual medication
and diagnostic overreach, compromise individual health outcomes, reduce
professional accountability, and undermine the structural integrity of
mental health systems. These practices not only violate ethical
standards and clinical guidelines but also produce chronic harm that
extends beyond the individual to families, communities, and
institutions. The research demonstrates that coercion and sustained
overmedicalization generate long-term physiological, psychological,
relational, and legal sequelae. These include medication-induced
comorbidities, iatrogenic disability, weakened cognitive and affective
capacities, deterioration of trust in health services, and the social
deactivation of entire groups through administrative incapacitation and
symbolic exclusion. The dissertation offers new evidence to support
systemic reforms aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development
Goals, specifically those related to ensuring healthy lives and
promoting well-being for all at all ages (table 1), achieving gender
equality, reducing inequality within and among countries, promoting
inclusive and equitable quality education (table 2), and building
peaceful and just institutions that provide access to justice and
protect fundamental rights (table 3).

### ****Table 1. Biological dimension: somatic health, medication practices, and physiological outcomes****

  ------------ ---------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ****2****    Zero Hunger                              Emphasizes the metabolic, nutritional, and somatic effects of psychotropic medication, especially in the context of neglecting dietary needs.
  ****3****    Good Health and Well-being               Central to the thesis. Promotes rights-based and clinically effective care to reduce iatrogenic harm and optimize physiological health outcomes.
  ****6****    Clean Water and Sanitation               Addresses environmental health risks linked to pharmaceutical waste from chronic overprescription in psychiatric systems.
  ****12****   Responsible Consumption and Production   Advocates for rational pharmacological use, deprescription, and evaluation of medication-related harm within psychiatric services.

This table presents the SDGs that intersect with the biological aspects
of psychiatric care, including the physiological effects of psychotropic
medication, metabolic health, environmental contamination through
pharmaceutical waste, and the biological implications of overmedication
and poor nutritional integration in mental health systems.\

The findings show that psychiatric coercion ought to be understood as a
generator of medically and socially quantifiable harm. It contributes to
the onset and exacerbation of somatic illness, increases risk factors
for suicide, and contributes to the erosion of the basic conditions for
health, including relational stability, legal protection, and the
preservation of bodily autonomy. These harms are often concentrated
among persons already exposed to cumulative disadvantage. Women, minors,
trauma survivors, people living in poverty, and racialized or migrant
populations are disproportionately subjected to forced treatment,
pathologization, and institutional neglect (table 2). These practices
conceal rather than address the material and relational determinants of
distress. Instead of receiving protection, support, or access to social
services, individuals are funneled into psychiatric systems where their
experience is reframed as disorder, and their legal and civic standing
is progressively eroded. The consequences include loss of custody of
children, deterioration of physical health due to polypharmacy,
breakdown of social networks, and persistent exclusion from employment,
education, and housing systems. The dissertation identifies these
mechanisms as producing a measurable form of social death, characterized
by administrative invisibilization, narrative erasure, and the loss of
control over one's own medical and legal trajectory.

****Table 2. Psychological dimension: mental autonomy, identity,
recovery, and professional knowledge****

  ----------- --------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ****3****   Good Health and Well-being        Prioritizes recovery-oriented models that preserve narrative identity, legal agency, and emotional regulation.
  ****4****   Quality Education                 Supports trauma-informed psychiatric education, patient literacy, and reflexive professional practice.
  ****5****   Gender Equality                   Addresses the psychological consequences of gender-based violence and the need for gender-sensitive diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.
  ****8****   Decent Work and Economic Growth   Focuses on restoring occupational agency and reducing psychiatric exclusion from the labor force through empowerment and reintegration.
  ----------- --------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This table identifies SDGs relevant to the psychological domain,
focusing on autonomy, identity, trauma recovery, educational access for
both professionals and patients, and the restoration of personal agency
through ethically informed psychiatric practice.\

In addition to its clinical and legal dimensions, the dissertation
foregrounds the necessity of social interventions as prerequisites for
mental health. Safe housing, adequate nutrition, economic security, and
relational continuity are presented not as ancillary concerns but as
central components of psychiatric care. Mental health cannot be
separated from the conditions that sustain life. In this sense, the
thesis contributes to the articulation of a medical paradigm that is
structurally competent, ecologically integrated, and sensitive to the
distribution of power and resources. It argues that the prevention of
psychiatric crisis, chronicity, and suicide depends not only on
pharmacological management but on the deployment of cross-sectoral
public policies that address structural deprivation. The research
supports the construction of care systems that prioritize early
protection of children, sustained support for caregivers, and the
prevention of domestic and institutional violence. It emphasizes that
without the protection of infancy, and without the capacity of
institutions to detect and respond to violence and neglect at early
stages, the escalation of suffering into diagnosable illness becomes
normalized. This constitutes not only a failure of psychiatry but a
failure of medicine and governance more broadly.

The action-research framework applied in this thesis demonstrates that
better models of care; based on shared decision-making, gradual and safe
deprescription, ethical evaluation of practices, and the reintegration
of users as agents of knowledge; can reduce harm, prevent institutional
dependency, and increase long-term quality of life for patients and
families. These models improve clinical outcomes, reduce the burden on
emergency and inpatient services, and contribute to the rational
allocation of medical and social resources. They promote sustainable
care practices that integrate biological, psychological, legal, and
cultural dimensions of health, in line with the principles of a health
system oriented toward prevention, continuity of care, and intersectoral
cooperation. The findings show that the implementation of dialogical
frameworks, supported by legal safeguards and institutional
transparency, can create conditions where mental health care is not a
site of control and containment but one of recovery, participation, and
sustained well-being.

****Table 3. Social dimension: legal structures, institutional design,
inequality, and relational inclusion****

  ------------ ----------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ****1****    No Poverty                                Demonstrates how deprivation is reframed as illness, and how economic supports are essential to reducing coercion and exclusion.
  ****9****    Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure   Supports ethical infrastructure for mental health governance, including open-source tools for monitoring coercion.
  ****10****   Reduced Inequalities                      Documents how coercion disproportionately targets marginalized groups, and proposes structural reforms for equitable access and treatment.
  ****11****   Sustainable Cities and Communities        Advocates for integrated community mental health services that include housing, networks of care, and civic participation.
  ****16****   Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions    Central to the thesis. Promotes legal safeguards, institutional accountability, and protection from psychiatric abuse.
  ****17****   Partnerships for the Goals                Emphasizes trans-disciplinary and user-survivor collaboration in service design, implementation, and governance.
  ------------ ----------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This table outlines SDGs that relate to the social structures shaping
psychiatric experiences, including legal accountability, anti-poverty
measures, reduction of systemic inequality, infrastructure development
for equitable care, and the creation of participatory institutions
capable of protecting human rights and social inclusion.\

The social impact of this dissertation (table 3) lies in its capacity to
inform structural reform across medical, legal, and policy systems. It
provides empirical and conceptual tools for institutional learning,
redefines psychiatric responsibility, and advances a clinical and
ethical framework in which health is understood as a relational and
collective condition. It analyses the layered determinants of
preventable deterioration and premature death, including
substance-related mortality, iatrogenic illness, and loss of function.
Rejecting reductionist models that isolate suffering from its structural
context, it builds an integrated analytic grounded in medical
anthropology, cognitive science, and legal reasoning. It distinguishes
immediate drivers such as deprivation, coercive care, and environmental
harm from deeper failures in governance, legitimacy, and epistemic
recognition. Drawing on ethnographic and surveys data, this dissertation
formulates a translational framework for the identification and
correction of systemic dysfunction from bleeding edge knowledge and
expert testimonies, from lived and professional accounts. This framework
underpins the EU BEACON One Health Education initiative on infancy
education for a sustainable future through new technologies, offering an
applied model for interdisciplinary coordination, rights-based reform,
and the restoration of health as a structural and ethical global
imperative.

### Researcher short biography

The author of this dissertation (it/those, showing the dehumanization
and betrayal suffered at the hands or severe abusers, who regarded its
life as worse than garbage and a nuisance to beat and throw away) is a
university professor and physician-scientist in training, currently
undertaking doctoral research at the Medical Anthropology Research
Center of Universitat Rovira i Virgili, Spain. Its academic formation
spans neuroscience, biological and evolutionary anthropology,
psychiatric genetics, and dialogical approaches to mental health. It
holds postgraduate degrees in collective mental health and human
diversity and is the recipient of a highly competitive excellence grant
awarded by the Spanish Ministry of Universities for university
professors in training. Its research integrates biomedical, legal, and
ethnographic perspectives to address core tensions between coercion,
autonomy, and recovery in psychiatric care. Before initiating this
doctoral project, as undergraduate neurosciences and smart systems
student, it acquired direct exposure to the biomedical system as a
participant in two phase 0 clinical trials to earn a living and fund its
studies, including inpatient follow-up, aiming to understand the
infrastructure and epistemology of human pharmacological testing from
within.

Its career trajectory combines advanced scientific training with early
and sustained engagement in international legal research, including work
at the Stanford Center for Legal Informatics (CodeX) as contractor, the
Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies in Geneva,
and the University of Arizona College of Law. Its previous research
focused on cognitive bias, decision-making under uncertainty, and the
sociopolitical dynamics of arbitration systems. More recently, it
contributed to psychiatric genomics research at FIDMAG Hermanas
Hospitalarias, investigating the neurobiological substrates of diagnoses
such as schizophrenia at master level. Rooted in a family history of
transgenerational trauma and informed by personal and academic proximity
to structural violence, his approach to psychiatry is critical yet
grounded, oriented not toward denunciation but toward scientific clarity
and systemic improvement. Its work unfolds across clinical, legal, and
community settings, involving direct observation, stakeholder
interviews, and participation in European and international networks
focused on mental health and human rights. The dissertation is both a
contribution to academic knowledge and a call for institutional
responsibility, aligning medical care with the principles of justice,
dignity, and recovery.

The researcher was born into a culturally asymmetrical and economically
stratified kinship system, with opposing configurations of power,
ethics, and social function across parental lineages. The maternal line,
predominantly Catalan, was structurally embedded in an upper-class
inheritance system, marked by sustained access to property, symbolic
capital, and social status not earned through labor but through
intergenerational transfer. Within this setting, superiority was
culturally and socially internalized, producing patterns of authority
and entitlement reinforced by regional identity. This lineage displayed
recurrent behavioral control strategies, including infantilization,
boundary manipulation, and strategic dependence induction, normalized
within the domestic sphere. The institution of marriage, under
historical Spanish civil law, enabled legal and economic control by the
husband, whose post-marital behavior transitioned from performative
romance to dominance. These conditions were legally sanctioned under a
patriarchal civil code in force until reforms introduced progressively
during the late 1970s and early 1980s, which had previously conferred
disproportionate authority to male heads of household over spousal and
child-related decisions.

In contrast, the paternal line functioned within a structurally distinct
paradigm. While subject to relative economic constraint, it preserved
relational ethics grounded in reciprocity and caregiving. Despite the
pressures of traditional gender roles, the paternal grandparents
sustained a marital dynamic characterized by mutual support and
resilience. While socially less privileged, it maintained relational
coherence, labor-based dignity, and pedagogical care practices. The
younger son, an engineer by training, demonstrated cognitive and
emotional integrity prior to external intervention, following a healthy
lifestyle as well as rich social life. Subsequent psychiatric labeling
and institutional involvement precipitated rapid deterioration, with no
recovery trajectory observed, consistent with existing literature on
iatrogenic harm under coercive psychiatric regimes. The grandparents,
despite age-related vulnerability, modeled ethical restraint and
caregiving integrity.

The behavioral patterns in the maternal lineage were typified by
psychological destabilization strategies, covert dependency induction,
and systemic displacement of responsibility. The most cognitively
divergent and ethically consistent member, a nurse who had qualified for
medical studies, was pathologized through the instrumental use of
psychiatric diagnosis. Her case exemplifies the conflation of dissent
with disorder, and the use of institutional labeling to neutralize
functional difference within authoritarian family systems. The
differential outcomes between lineages are not incidental but
structurally conditioned by the distribution of power, recognition, and
control over narrative legitimacy.

****The researcher's early exposure to this bifurcated kinship
configuration, including forced exit from the household before legal
majority and subsequent international mobility through early marriage
and expatriation, produced the necessary preconditions for a multiscalar
analytical orientation. Longitudinal immersion in socioculturally
distinct contexts, including Chile, United Kingdom, France, China,
Sweden, and multiple regions of Spain, expanded the observational
repertoire and enabled comparative systems analysis of familial
governance, psychiatric institutionalism, and the legal-medical
interface. The anthropologist, as a scientific instrument, is not
separate from the field but part of its relational matrix. Ethnographic
knowledge production is grounded in situated perception, and depends on
the capacity to register and interpret patterns of interaction, meaning,
and harm across multiple sensory, cognitive, and affective registers.
Anthropology, more than any other discipline, requires the total
engagement of the researcher's embodied faculties. Observation is not
visual alone, but haptic, auditory, contextual, and juridically attuned.
The instrument ought to be trained and calibrated, not only through
academic preparation, but through experiential exposure to the
mechanisms under analysis. In this case, the instrument was subject to
torture all along, and still is. This dissertation exemplifies work
under such distress. The researcher functions simultaneously as
observer, survivor, and systems analyst. The knowledge generated is not
merely empirical but operational, designed for application in legal,
clinical, and policy domains. The research methodology reflects full
embodiment, and the conclusions produced are not extrapolations from
distance, but derivations from proximity, triangulated through legal
doctrine, institutional mapping, and ethnographic evidence. In
anthropological science, the integrity of the instrument determines the
validity of the result. This principle is upheld in the present
work.****

# **Abstracts in all official languages in Spain, and other most relevant**

**Abstract:** This thesis argues that the Spanish psychiatric system,
supported by legal and administrative structures, systematically
violates the autonomy and dignity of individuals through coercive and
non-consensual practices masquerading as care. Diagnoses are imposed
without empirical rigor, treatments are administered without valid
consent, and discomfort is decontextualized and medicalized, producing
structural iatrogenic damage that prevents recovery. At the root is the
lack of implementation of shared decision-making and respect for the
right to self-determination. Anchored in participatory action research
from a bio-cultural analysis perspective, this work integrates
ethnographic, legal, and analytical evidence to document these
mechanisms and propose grounded better ways focused on human rights,
prevention, and collaborative care. The findings corroborate the
existing medical consensus that ethical and effective health care, which
also includes mental health in the most serious cases, ought to be
rights-based, non-coercive, recovery-oriented, personalized, and based
on trust and shared responsibility, not submission.

**Ringkasan:** Ini adalah argumen bahwa sistem psikologi Spanyol, yang
berfungsi untuk membangun struktur hukum dan administrasi, melanggar
sistem otonomi dan martabat individu melalui praktik pemaksaan dan tidak
ada konsensus dari para mascarad tentang perhatian mereka. Diagnostik
tersebut diterapkan secara empiris, sistem administrasinya memiliki
persetujuan yang valid dan bersifat dekontekstualisasi dan medis,
menghasilkan struktur iatrogenik yang menghambat pemulihan. Hal ini
merupakan tugas pelaksanaan tekanan keputusan bersama dan menghormati
hak penentuan otomatis. Memasukkan penyelidikan-tindakan partisipatif
dari analisis penting biokultural, meminta tiga bukti integrasi
etnograf, hukum, dan analitis untuk mekanisme dokumenter dan mengusulkan
alternatif-alternatif yang dilakukan di pusat-pusat manusia, pencegahan
dan kolaborasi. Masalah-masalah tersebut menguatkan konsensus medis yang
ada bahwa perawatan sanitasi yang efektif dan efektif, yang juga
termasuk memberi salam mental pada kasus-kasus yang lebih besar, telah
menjadi sangat lemah, tidak ada paksaan, berorientasi pada pemulihan,
personalisasi dan berdasarkan kepercayaan, dan tanggung jawab bersama,
tidak dalam penyerahan.

**Résumé **: Cet argument affirme que le système psychiatrique espagnol,
soutenu par les structures juridiques et administratives, viole
systématiquement l\'autonomie et la dignité des individus dans le cadre
de pratiques coercitives et aucun consensus ne s\'éloigne de
l\'attention. Les diagnostics imposent une rigueur empirique, les
traités sont administrés avec un consentement valide et le problème est
décontextuel et médical, produisant une structure iatrogènique qui
empêche la récupération. Dans l\'affaire, il y a la manque de mise en
œuvre de la pression des décisions partagée et le respect du droit à
l\'autodétermination. Ancorat en la investigació-acció participativa
d\'un vessant d\'anàlisis bio-cultural, ce treball intégra des preuves
ethnogràfiques, juridiques et analytiques pour documenter ces mécanismes
et proposer des better ways fondées sur les principes centraux chez les
humains, la prévention et l\'attention collaborative. Les troballes
corroborent les consensus médicaux existants selon lesquels l\'attention
sanitaire est efficace et efficace, qui inclut également le salut mental
dans les cas les plus graves, qui ont été fondés sur des droits, non
coercitifs, orientés vers la récupération, personnalisés et fondés sur
la confiance et la responsabilité partagée, non dans la soumission.

**Laburpena:** Espainiako sistema psikiatrikoaren argudioa, egitura
juridikoen eta administratiboen babesa, autonomiaren sistema urratzea
eta pertsonen duintasunari buruzko koerzitiboen praktikaren bidez eta
arretarako adostasunik ez duten emmascaratzeen bidez. Zentzumen
zorroztasun enpirikoa inposatzen dute diagnostikoek, tratamenduak
zentzumenaren adostasuna administratzen dute, malestarren
deskontextualizazioa eta medikuntzaren ondorioz, errekuperazioa
eragozten duten egitura iatrogeniko bat ekoizten dute. A l\'arrel hi ha
la manca d\'implementació de la presa de decisions compartida i el
respect pel dret a l\'autodeterminació. Ancorat en la

analítiques per dokumentatzeko mekanismoak eta proposar better ways
fonamentades centrades en els derechos humans, la prevenció i l\'atenció
col·laborativa. Les troballes corroboren el consens medical existent que
l\'atenció sanitària ètica i eficaç, hori ere barne hartzen du la salut
mental en los casos más greus, no ha de ser fundada en derechos, no
coercitiva, orientada a la recuperación, personalizada y basada en la
confianza y la responsabilidad compartida, no en la submisión.

**Resumo:** Tesí argumenta que o sistema psiquiàtric espanyol, sostingut
por estruturas legais e administrativas, viola sistemàticament
l\'autonomia e a dignitat dos individus a través de prácticas
coercitives e non consensuades emmascarades com a atenció. Os
diagnòstics imponse o rigor empírico do sentido, os tratamentos
s\'administren o consentimento do sentido vàlid e o malestar é

estructural que impediu a recuperación. A l\'arrel hi ha la manca
d\'implementació da presa de decisions compartida i el respecte pel dret
a l\'autodeterminació. Ancora na investigación-acción participativa des
d'una vessant d'anàlisis bio-cultural, este traballo integra evidències

consensos médicos existentes que a atención sanitària ètica e eficaç,
que tamén inclúe o salut mental nos casos máis greus, ha de ser basado
en dereitos, non coercitiva, orientada á recuperación, personalizada i
basada na confianza e na responsabilidade compartida, non na submisión.

**Resum:** Aquesta tesi argumenta que el sistema psiquiàtric espanyol,
sostingut per estructures legals i administratives, viola
sistemàticament l\'autonomia i la dignitat dels individus a través de
pràctiques coercitives i no consensuades emmascarades com a atenció. Els
diagnòstics s\'imposen sense rigor empíric, els tractaments
s\'administren sense consentiment vàlid i el malestar es
descontextualitza i es medicalitza, produint un dany iatrogènic
estructural que impedeix la recuperació. A l\'arrel hi ha la manca
d\'implementació de la presa de decisions compartida i el respecte pel

integra evidències etnogràfiques, legals i analítiques per documentar
aquests mecanismes i proposar better ways fonamentades centrades en els
drets humans, la prevenció i l\'atenció col·laborativa. Les troballes
corroboren el consens mèdic existent que l\'atenció sanitària ètica i
eficaç, que també inclou la salut mental en els casos més greus, ha de
ser basada en drets, no coercitiva, orientada a la recuperació,

no en la submissió.

**Resumen:** Aquesta tesi argumenta que el sistema psiquiátrico español,
sustentado por estructuras legales y administrativas, viola el sistema
de autonomía y la dignidad de los individuos a través de prácticas
coercitivas y no consensuadas emmascarades com a atención. Los
diagnósticos se imponen con sentido de rigor empírico, los tratamientos
se administran con sentido consentimiento válido y el malestar es
descontextualización y es medicalización, produciendo una iatrogénesis
estructural que impide la recuperación. A l\'arrel hi ha la manca
d\'implementació de la presa de decisiones compartida i el respecte pel
dret a l\'autodeterminació. Ancorat en la investigació-acció
participativa des d'una vessant d'análisis bio-cultural, aquest treball
integra evidències etnogràfiques, legals i analítiques per documentar
aquests mecanismes y proponer alternativas fonamentadas centrades en los
derechos humanos, la prevención y la atención colaborativa. Les
troballes corroboren el consenso médico existente que la atención
sanitaria ética y eficaz, que también incluye la salud mental en los
casos más graves, ha de ser basada en derechos, no coercitiva, orientada
a la recuperación, personalizada y basada en la confianza y la
responsabilidad compartida, no en la sumisión.

# **                                         Chapter 1. General framework and delimitation of the research**

**Summary: **This chapter establishes the foundational premises of the
dissertation by articulating the structural urgency and scientific
rationale for investigating psychiatric violence, institutional
betrayal, and systemic repression within contemporary mental health
frameworks, particularly in the Spanish context. Through a bio-cultural
and action-research perspective, the chapter situates the inquiry at the
intersection of medical anthropology, legal analysis, and lived
experience, drawing on a wide empirical base including fieldwork, policy
analysis, and professional testimony. It sets forth the critical claim
that coercion in psychiatry is not an exceptional measure but a
normalized, routinized mechanism of social control embedded in the logic
and everyday operation of clinical institutions. This chapter exposes
the failure of dominant psychiatric paradigms to address the roots of
distress, emphasizing how the structural causes of suffering; such as
poverty, abuse, gendered violence, and institutional betrayal, are
routinely depoliticized and converted into individual pathologies. This
chapter further outlines how institutional discourse and practice
reconfigure adaptive or protest behaviours into markers of disorder,
legitimizing forced treatments that often produce iatrogenic harm and
psychological disablement. By examining the erosion of autonomy, the
silencing of narrative agency, and the moral disengagement inherent in
coercive systems, it calls attention to the systematic reproduction of
suffering under the guise of care. It also presents the current
configuration of mental health services in Spain, in the European Union,
and comparable systems, violates fundamental rights, degrades the
clinical relationship, and undermines democratic and constitutional
protections. It underscores that such violence is not simply medical but
deeply political and epistemic, supported by bureaucratic inertia, legal
ambiguity, and a culture of professional impunity. By framing mental
health as a matter of public ethics, structural justice, and ecological
responsibility, this chapter lays the groundwork for the dissertation's
integrated methodological and theoretical architecture and announces the
urgency of a rights-based, trauma informed, non-harmful, society-wide,
gendered, transcutlural and recovery oriented one health approach to a
most human mental health reform. This chapter delineates the core
hypotheses and ethical orientation of the study, emphasizing that
transformation ought to be grounded in non-coercive, dialogical, and
structurally aware practices.

**1. Thesis, aim and objectives**

****Thesis: ****This dissertation investigates how psychiatric systems
can transition from coercive and overmedicalized practices toward
evidence-based models of recovery-oriented care, grounded in patient
autonomy, shared decision-making and culturally situated best practices.

This dissertation investigates how psychiatric systems can transition
from coercive and overmedicalized practices toward evidence-based,
recovery-oriented models of care grounded in patient autonomy, shared
decision-making, and culturally contextualized clinical reasoning. The
thesis posits that coercive and pharmacologically dominant interventions
in contemporary psychiatry are not exceptional nor residual but are
instead structurally maintained by institutional norms, juridical
indeterminacy, and administrative fragmentation. These practices remain
embedded across clinical, familial, and bureaucratic domains, producing
a continuum of control that obstructs recovery, suppresses agency, and
perpetuates social and physiological harm. Coercion, conceptualized
herein as the systematic exclusion of the individual from decisions
concerning their own treatment, functions as a legitimized institutional
response to psychosocial distress, often replacing substantive care with
enforced compliance. The research argues that such practices reflect not
the failure of isolated actors but the normalization of technocratic
logic under conditions of risk aversion, diagnostic reductionism, and
epistemic asymmetry ****(Torrents & Björkdahl, 2024)****.

The thesis advances the proposition that a sustainable transformation of
psychiatric care requires not only technical amendments to protocols or
enhanced practitioner training but a systemic reconfiguration toward
dialogically informed, procedurally accountable, and structurally
responsive forms of care. Dialogical practice, in this context, is not
reduced to a specific branded methodology but conceptualized as a
foundational epistemological principle grounded in mutual recognition,
institutional reflexivity, and reciprocal legitimization of knowledge
claims. The empirical validation of this proposition is carried out
through a mixed-methods framework incorporating legal analysis, clinical
ethnography, and embedded participant observation across multiple
psychiatric and policy environments (****Mead & Filson, 2017; Carr,
1988****). The findings elucidate how normative frameworks often coexist
with violations in practice, and how professionals themselves operate
under constraints that undermine ethical care. The thesis does not
merely critique, but delineates institutional pathways toward coherent,
lawful, and recovery-promoting systems of mental health governance
(****Riker, 2017****).

This dissertation is guided by the central research question: ****How do
coercive psychiatric practices, overmedication, and institutional
neglect persist within the Spanish mental health system despite legal
safeguards, clinical ethics, and international human rights
standards?**** Conversely, it also asks: ****What systemic, clinical,
and epistemological conditions enable the emergence and consolidation of
participatory, trauma-informed, and biologically grounded psychiatric
care that respects autonomy, protects rights, and improves outcomes?****

****Aim:** **To contribute to the development and implementation of
clinical, legal and institutional frameworks that promote self-managed
and participatory mental health care, based on action-research embedded
in real-world settings and oriented toward continuous system
improvement.

The aim of a thesis refers to its principal purpose or intended
contribution. It articulates what the research seeks to achieve at a
systemic or conceptual level, distinguishing it from the thesis itself,
which presents a central proposition to be argued and demonstrated.
While the thesis posits a testable claim grounded in empirical and
theoretical evidence, the aim defines the overarching orientation of the
work, including its intended impact on policy, practice, or scientific
understanding. In action-research frameworks, such as the one adopted
here, the aim also encompasses applied objectives and transformative
intentions embedded within real-world systems.

The aim of this dissertation is to support the emergence and
implementation of psychiatric systems that are capable of real-time
correction, structural accountability, and the preservation of both
bodily and legal integrity. It seeks to foster a paradigmatic transition
away from a unidimensional reliance on psychopharmacological control
toward an integrative model of care rooted in interdisciplinary evidence
and therapeutic reciprocity. This model is predicated on the
understanding that mental health cannot be reduced to neurochemical
imbalance or behavioral deviation but ought to be interpreted through
the interaction of biological regulation, experiential development, and
sociopolitical context. The research integrates contributions from
translational neuroscience, physiological psychiatry,
psychoneuroimmunology, psychoneuroendocrinology, developmental
psychopathology, trauma-informed frameworks, nutritional psychiatry,
psychosocial epidemiology, and ecological public health. These
disciplines provide converging evidence on how trauma, inflammation,
metabolic dysregulation, and environmental precarity shape both the
emergence and chronicity of psychiatric conditions (****Gooding et al.,
2022****).

In parallel, the dissertation draws from cultural psychology,
phenomenological psychiatry, narrative theory, and medical anthropology
to situate clinical phenomena within relational, cultural, and
historical matrices. Theories of embodied cognition, the extended mind,
and relational consciousness are employed not as speculative frameworks
but as scientifically corroborated perspectives on the distributed and
socially mediated nature of mental processes. This conceptual
orientation is operationalized through the design of participatory
feedback mechanisms, patient-led evaluative structures, and embedded
data infrastructures, allowing clinical systems to recalibrate based on
experiential, physiological, and ethical inputs. The aim is not to
displace psychiatry but to realign it with a broader horizon of
empirical coherence, patient protection, and epistemic humility. The
dissertation intervenes at the intersection of clinical decision-making,
institutional design, and legal structure, offering pragmatic models of
regulation and care grounded in ongoing verification, transparent
governance, and open science standards (****Suess Schwend et al.,
2016****).

The integration of these disciplines and methodologies informs a
comprehensive framework through which psychiatric governance can become
both scientifically valid and socially just. The objectives derived from
this aim are elaborated across biological, psychological, and social
domains of intervention and correspond to the structure of this
dissertation. These objectives are detailed below and implemented
through rigorous multi-sited fieldwork, participatory action research,
and critical legal-ethical analysis:

The biological dimension of this dissertation, table 1, integrates an
exploration into the full potential of current best practices, a human
approach to rapport, trust and both shared decisions and responsibility,
and new technologies to support precision, accountability, and
continuous improvement in clinical practice. The thesis maintains that
health ought to be understood not as the management of isolated symptoms
but as the result of dynamic interactions between biological integrity,
contextual conditions, and institutional responsibility. In Spain,
persistent overreliance on pharmacological protocols has entrenched a
medical model that neglects both systemic harms and the possibility of
recovery. This work challenges such structural inertia by introducing
open data frameworks, biosignal-informed monitoring, and interoperable
documentation systems that empower patients and clinicians to
co-evaluate treatment effects in real time. By embedding positive
feedback loops within participatory action research cycles and adopting
open science standards, the synthesis model reorients health systems
toward adaptive learning and biomedical accountability. Legal safeguards
and regulatory mechanisms are proposed to ensure transparency, protect
patient data, and prevent the misuse of diagnostic categories and
therapeutic interventions that might otherwise reinforce chronicity and
systemic exclusion.

At the psychological level, table 2, new technologies are mobilized not
for surveillance or standardization, but for restoring agency, memory,
and personhood within therapeutic processes. This thesis defends the
centrality of narrative, self-determination, and cognitive restoration
as key pillars of healing. The antithesis it opposes is a clinical
culture that too often ignores subjective complexity, forces diagnostic
imposition, and strips the individual of interpretive power. To counter
this, the research deploys digital storytelling tools, reflexive
platforms for therapeutic alliance assessment, and decision-support
systems aligned with trauma-informed and rights-based frameworks.
Feedback loops are built into the structure of care itself, allowing for
regular recalibration and person-centered learning. These systems are
designed not only for individual care but for structural change: civil
society engagement, patient-led data interpretation, and continuous
education of professionals are embedded as core functions. Legal
analysis further identifies procedural loopholes and proposes
enforceable guarantees to protect against identity erasure and epistemic
harm, reasserting the right to evolve beyond labels and to recover fully
(****Tomé, 2014****).

At the social level, table 6, the dissertation advances a synthesis
where institutional reform is sustained by real-time coordination, civic
participation, and full data transparency. Through the EU BEACON One
Health Education initiative, the research supports an architecture for
systems integration that enables ongoing structural correction and legal
enforceability. Participatory digital infrastructures allow for
multilevel input ,from families, professionals, users, and civil society
,creating scalable mechanisms for identifying harmful practices,
highlighting best models, and ensuring policy coherence. Open science is
not an add-on but a foundational principle: all data is anonymized,
encrypted, and made accessible for democratic oversight, with clear
limits set to prevent institutional capture or reappropriation. Feedback
mechanisms are calibrated to track not only health outcomes but
institutional behavior, closing gaps in enforcement and reducing
impunity. The model refuses the assumption of chronicity as an
inevitable outcome, insisting instead on a forward-facing ethics of
possibility, resilience, and structural repair. In this vision, health
is not a static state nor a managed deficit, but a relational, social,
and dynamic capacity that ought to be protected and continuously renewed
****(Baum et al., 2006)****.
