\
This dissertation defends a thesis that is both scientifically grounded
and ethically imperative: that recovery in mental health is not only
possible but ought to be structurally enabled, institutionally
supported, and epistemically protected. Against entrenched systems that
perpetuate coercion, chronicity, and epistemic injustice under the guise
of care, the research offers a multidimensional synthesis grounded in
the best available evidence and the lived realities of those most
affected. By integrating translational neuroscience, dialogical and
developmental models, legal safeguards, and participatory technologies,
the dissertation articulates a coherent and actionable framework for
system-wide transformation. Its implementation through the EU BEACON One
Health Education action, founded by the researcher during this thesis
participatory action-research fieldwork, exemplifies how research can
inform practice and policy without compromise, ensuring transparency,
accountability, and democratic engagement at all levels. Health, in this
model, is not a managerial abstraction but a dynamic, relational
achievement sustained by procedural integrity, educational investment,
and shared commitment to human dignity. The research does not merely
critique existing systems; it operationalizes their reconfiguration,
affirming that recovery is not to be the exception, but the ethical and
structural baseline from which all psychiatric care ought to begin
****(Ochocka et al., 2002; Speers & Lathlean, 2015)****.

##  **1.1. Brief historical-structural background: care, coercion and governance in Spain**

\
The governance of mental distress in the Iberian Peninsula has
historically functioned as an apparatus of normative regulation,
entwined with broader regimes of religious, political, and social
control. From the late medieval period through the early modern era,
deviation from established moral and epistemic orders was not merely
tolerated or interpreted but actively repressed through institutional
mechanisms that conflated spiritual error, cognitive dissonance, and
behavioral irregularity. Early Christian and Islamic traditions, though
distinct in theological framing, both contributed to a moralisation of
suffering in which distress was interpreted as either a sign of divine
punishment or a rupture of spiritual integrity. Institutional responses
were structured accordingly. Monastic, charitable, and later
inquisitorial systems deployed rituals of purification, prayer, fasting,
confinement, and exorcism, often without any distinction between
psychological, somatic, and moral phenomena. The individual in distress
was not treated as a bearer of epistemically valid experience but rather
as a symptom of disorder within the social or cosmological order. These
dynamics laid the foundation for a mode of care that operated less
through therapeutic recognition than through sacrificial containment,
where the boundary between cure and exclusion was systematically erased
****(Van Bilsen, 2016; Asad et al., 2024; Alotaibi, 2025)****.

By the eighteenth century, the rise of Enlightenment rationalism and
biomedical empiricism signalled a partial shift in explanatory
frameworks. However, the consolidation of psychiatric knowledge as an
institutional field did not dismantle the punitive architecture of
earlier systems but rather rearticulated it through secularised
classifications and clinical authority. The emergence of asylums across
Europe, including Spain, institutionalised this transition. Framed under
the ideology of moral treatment, these facilities combined therapeutic
rhetoric with disciplinary spatial design, reinforcing the separation
between the so-called sane and the insane. In the Spanish context, the
provincialisation of mental hospitals entrenched a custodial model in
which legal, familial, and professional prerogatives converged to
authorise prolonged confinement. Diagnostic categories lacked
standardisation and were frequently employed to justify social
exclusion, often under the pretext of managing risk or incapacity.
Treatment was oriented not toward understanding or recovery, but toward
submission, surveillance, and pharmacological restraint. The
architectural continuity with earlier religious institutions was
paralleled by administrative logics that prioritised order over care and
compliance over cure. The structural function of psychiatry thus
replicated earlier theological models of containment, though now under
the legitimation of scientific modernity (Locke, 1690/1975; Battie,
1751/1975; Tuke, 1796/1975; Pinel & Esquirol, 1838/1994).

Throughout the nineteenth century, Spanish psychiatry underwent
professional consolidation, drawing on French and German nosological
systems to reinforce the authority of the clinical gaze. Diagnostic
taxonomies such as melancholia, mania, and moral insanity became
embedded in medico-legal discourse and served as instruments for
managing deviance in both public and private spheres. These
classifications did not emerge from dialogical engagement with the
affected but from an epistemology of expertise that located the power to
define pathology in the professional observer. This process was deeply
gendered. The pathologisation of female agency through categories such
as hysteria served to institutionalise patriarchal control, while the
disproportionate confinement of women for behaviours deemed
transgressive ,whether sexual, emotional, or spiritual ,revealed
psychiatry's complicity in enforcing normative femininity. Psychiatric
institutions thus became not spaces of healing but mechanisms of
biopolitical triage, where the lines between illness, illegitimacy, and
nonconformity were collapsed under medical rationality. In this
configuration, care was not emancipatory but regulatory, and recovery
was subordinated to institutional interests in containment, control, and
social reproduction (Rodríguez‑Morini, 2002).

In the early twentieth century, Spanish psychiatry was increasingly
shaped by eugenic and nationalist doctrines that conflated public health
with moral hygiene. During the 1920s and 1930s, institutional policies
adopted segregationist and sterilization-oriented frameworks aimed at
excluding individuals perceived as degenerative. These tendencies
intensified under Francoist rule, where psychiatric institutions became
integral to the apparatus of state repression. Rather than spaces for
clinical care, they functioned as instruments of political and social
control. Those who diverged from national-Catholic ideals ,whether due
to political dissent, sexual orientation, or trauma-related responses
,were subjected to coercive hospitalization, invasive treatments, and
indefinite confinement. Psychiatric diagnoses operated as tools to
delegitimize non-conforming identities, framing distress as pathology
and dissent as illness. Clinical practices merged with authoritarian
legal logics, erasing procedural safeguards. Medical records were
inaccessible, appeals nonviable, and treatments designed to ensure
submission rather than healing. This convergence established a legacy of
medical impunity and epistemic opacity that continues to influence
institutional norms in contemporary Spain (Espinosa & Comelles, 1966;
Tusell, 2010; Alonso‑Tejada & López‑Morales, 2015).

Following the democratic transition, legislative reforms in the 1980s
and 1990s aimed to replace institutional confinement with
community-based care and uphold human rights in mental health treatment.
Nevertheless, implementation remained partial and under-resourced.
Asylums were closed without establishing robust better ways, and many
psychiatric functions were subsumed within general hospitals or
delegated to private entities. The underlying paradigm of control
remained intact. Professional hierarchies were preserved, diagnostic
taxonomies remained unchallenged, and intervention practices continued
to prioritize pharmacological sedation over dialogical engagement.
Community psychiatry, while rhetorically endorsed, failed to deliver
integrated or participatory care. Pharmaceutical interventions,
particularly long-acting antipsychotics, gained prominence as first-line
responses to non-compliance, effectively substituting behavioral
management for therapeutic understanding. Adherence became the central
metric of clinical success, regardless of patient outcomes or informed
consent. These developments were not driven by evidence-based consensus,
but by the institutional convenience of symptom suppression over
structural change (García Espino & Lara Ladislao, 1998; Pérez‑Fernández
& Peñaranda‑Ortega, 2015; Bobes, Vázquez‑Barquero, & Salvador‑Carulla,
2010).

In the twenty-first century, the consolidation of austerity measures,
industry lobbying, and professional self-preservation further entrenched
pharmacological coercion as normative psychiatric practice. Involuntary
treatment was increasingly authorized through expedited judicial
processes with minimal scrutiny. The threshold for declaring incapacity
remained low, enabling the systematic erosion of legal agency for those
in distress. Psychiatric interventions were framed as protective, yet
often functioned to suppress dissenting experience rather than address
underlying causes. The language of rights was retained in policy, but
its practical application was undermined by the conflation of
non-compliance with pathology. Relatives, facing inadequate support and
misinformed about better ways, frequently acquiesced to coercive
protocols. Institutional responses privileged sedation over sustained
engagement. This continuity reveals a persistent carceral logic in
Spanish psychiatry, reframed but not dismantled. The enduring suspicion
toward user agency, the marginalisation of narrative understanding, and
the systemic resistance to power-sharing confirm that coercive
pharmacology is not a scientific inevitability but a culturally and
politically embedded legacy that demands structural redress
(Ortiz‑Gómez, 2002; Portilla, 2006).

Better approaches are and were framed as luxuries or ideological
experiments, rather than as scientifically grounded responses to
suffering. The language of rights remained in official documents but was
emptied of its practical force. Patients were denied meaningful
participation in care decisions, and refusal was interpreted not as a
statement but as a symptom. Relatives, under pressure and
misinformation, often supported coercive measures, hoping for stability
at any cost. Institutions responded with sedation, not support. The
shift from asylum to community did not dismantle the carceral function
of psychiatry. It redistributed it across new spaces and vocabularies.

These trajectories cannot be explained as neutral progressions in
medical science. They are deeply rooted in cultural traditions of
submission, obedience, and exclusion. Spain's long history of
centralized power, religious moralism, and gendered violence shaped the
reception and function of psychiatric interventions. Those deemed mad
were never fully citizens. They were subjects of care only insofar as
care enforced social order. Healing was rarely the objective. The true
goal was containment, pacification, and moral correction. This history
explains the persistence of coercive pharmacology in Spain today,
despite international recommendations advocating for shared
decision-making and recovery-oriented practices. It also reveals the
institutional reluctance to implement better ways that require
power-sharing, narrative humility, and structural investment.

The transition from confinement to overmedication ought to therefore be
seen not as reform but as adaptation. Psychiatric governance in Spain
has replaced the visible bars of the asylum with the invisible chains of
chemical control. Individuals are no longer locked away but remain
captive to institutions that monitor their compliance and dictate their
pharmacological regimen. Resistance is recoded as illness, insight as
submission, and mutism as progress. The cultural scripts that once
justified religious exorcism, moral internment, and fascist segregation
now inform clinical discourse dressed in evidence-based language but
grounded in disciplinary logic. As a result, mental health care in Spain
continues to function less as a system of healing and more as a regime
of managed normalization. This trajectory is not limited to those who
fit clinical criteria. Historically, Spain's coercive psychiatric
apparatus has targeted the poor, the racialized, the gender
nonconforming, and the socially undesirable. In the nineteenth and
twentieth centuries, asylums and mental hospitals served as containers
for surplus populations. Paupers, vagabonds, unmarried mothers,
rebellious wives, political enemies, and migrants were expelled from the
productive economy and denied full civic inclusion. Confinement was
framed as care but functioned as exclusion. Diagnosis became a tool of
administrative convenience. Poverty was pathologized. Deviance was
medicalized. The responsibility of the state was transferred into the
body of the subject (Wallace Mandell, 1962/2025; Rosenhan, 1973;
Foucault, 1961/2006).

This targeting intensified under Francoist rule, particularly against
those on the losing side of the war. The psychiatric apparatus was
mobilized to eliminate ideological dissent and deviant identity.
Homosexuality was pathologized, gender nonconformity punished, and
political resistance silenced through medical certification of
unfitness. Those who could not be integrated into the national Catholic
project were not only criminalized but psychiatrized. They were removed
from visibility, subjected to forced treatment, or simply disappeared.
This amounted to a slow form of biopolitical genocide, a state-driven
erasure of the undesirable through confinement, chemical pacification,
and epistemic annihilation. Psychiatry was not a healing discipline but
a technology of control. The residues of this function persist today.
Spain's mental health system continues to disproportionately affect
those on the margins. Migrants, racialized youth, Roma individuals,
transgender persons, and survivors of abuse are overrepresented in
coercive interventions and underrepresented in participatory care.
Universal health coverage coexists with institutional exclusion. The
language may have softened but the logic remains. Psychiatry no longer
speaks of sin or degeneration but of adherence and insight. Yet, the
outcome is the same, the production of order through the containment of
difference (Campos & Novella, 2017; Huertas, 2017).

These historical mechanisms of silencing have been refined but not
dismantled. They are embedded in laws, in institutional routines, and in
clinical reasoning. They manifest in the overprescription of
psychotropic drugs, in the routine use of physical and chemical
restraints, and in the bureaucratic flattening of suffering into risk
profiles. The state no longer requires asylums to achieve its aims. It
has found in outpatient coercion, forced pharmacological adherence, and
judicial discretion the tools to achieve the same ends through more
diffuse and insidious means. The history of psychiatry in Spain is
therefore not a story of linear progress. It is one of continuity
through transformation. What has changed are the forms, not the
functions. From medieval heresy to modern noncompliance, from
confinement to injection, from overt moralism to administrative
rationality, the thread remains. The goal has always been to suppress
what cannot be assimilated. Paupers, madwomen, transgressors, and
migrants converge in the institutional imaginary as bodies to be managed
for the sake of order. In the name of public health, psychiatry has
enacted private violence. In the name of care, it has administered
exclusion (Brydán, 2016).

This is the context from which to examine the current reality of forced
psychiatric treatment in Spain. Coercion is not an aberration but a
structural feature of the system. It is embedded in its genealogy,
sustained by its institutions, and reproduced through its discourses.
What follows is an analysis of this contemporary landscape, its legal
frameworks, clinical arguments, and sites of resistance. This analysis
begins from a clear premise. Coercion constitutes harm. The burden of
justification lies not with those who resist it but with those who
impose it. The next section asks not only what is done but why it is
permitted and how it endures.

## **1.2. Current framework: forced psychiatric interventions and institutional accountability**

****\
Forced psychiatric treatment, in the form of involuntary outpatient
commitment and compulsory medication, continues to be promoted in Spain
by certain clinical and legal actors, despite a substantial body of
evidence demonstrating its limited effectiveness and significant ethical
cost. Proposals to legislate involuntary outpatient treatment have been
presented repeatedly over the past two decades and have been
systematically rejected by legislative bodies, professional
associations, and user organizations. The arguments in favor of such
coercive measures rely on speculative claims that forced compliance with
medical regimens will prevent hospital readmissions, reduce dangerous
behaviors, and alleviate systemic pressures. These claims remain
unsubstantiated by empirical research and lack theoretical coherence
when examined within the framework of rights-based clinical practice and
evidence-based medicine.****

The most comprehensive review to date, conducted using Cochrane
methodology, found no consistent benefit of involuntary outpatient
treatment over standard care. Key outcome indicators, including hospital
readmission rates, social functioning, mental state, quality of life,
and satisfaction with care, showed no statistically significant
differences between individuals subjected to coercive outpatient orders
and those receiving voluntary treatment. Calculations of the number
needed to treat reveal ethically untenable implications. For example,
preventing a single hospital readmission may require imposing coercive
treatment on more than eighty individuals. This magnitude of
intervention would be considered disproportionate in any other domain of
healthcare or public policy. The continued defense of these measures,
therefore, cannot be grounded in scientific evidence but reflects
institutional priorities that favor control and risk management over
collaboration and patient autonomy (Sailas & Fenton, 2000).

In Spain, the resurgence of legislative initiatives to implement
involuntary outpatient treatment stems, in part, from systemic
deficiencies in community mental health infrastructure. Policymakers and
some clinical representatives argue that coercion is necessary in light
of the absence of sustained relational care and the fragmentation of
social and health support systems. This framing displaces responsibility
for structural failure onto the individual and substitutes forced
compliance for the development of comprehensive and supportive services.
Legal justifications often rely on expansive interpretations of
incapacity and risk, frequently invoking concepts such as lack of
insight or treatment refusal without operational definitions. These
categories are problematic from both clinical and legal perspectives and
are prone to subjective misuse. The attempt to reframe coercion as a
preventive measure paradoxically undermines both clinical outcomes and
the therapeutic relationship that recovery depends upon (Cañete-Nicolás
et al, 2012; Gías Gil, 2013).

By contrast, shared decision-making has consistently been associated
with enhanced clinical engagement, improved functional outcomes, and
reduced relapse rates. It is a model that affirms the individual's
capacity to participate in care decisions, even during periods of
psychological distress. The presence of a collaborative therapeutic
alliance is the most robust predictor of positive long-term outcomes
across mental health conditions. Involuntary measures tend to disrupt
this alliance, induce mistrust, and reinforce avoidance and
disengagement. The experience of being subjected to forced treatment is
associated with psychological trauma, persistent anger, and withdrawal
from support systems. These reactions are not anecdotal nor incidental
but constitute evidence of systemic harm that impairs future
help-seeking behaviors and compromises adherence to care (Pozón, 2012;
Villagrán et al, 2015; Serrano-Miguel, 2022).

Despite the continued application of coercion in psychiatric practice
and discourse, there is an emerging international consensus that
sustainable recovery requires the implementation of non-coercive
interventions. These include intensive home-based care, flexible
assertive community treatment, peer-supported crisis services, and
culturally adapted psychotherapeutic approaches. Each of these models is
grounded in voluntary engagement and recognizes the complexity of mental
suffering as relational, contextual, and often trauma-related. Their
implementation in diverse settings has demonstrated measurable benefits,
including reduced hospitalization, lower use of emergency services,
improved social functioning, and enhanced quality of life. These
interventions are not only ethically preferable but are also
cost-effective when compared to the cumulative financial and human costs
associated with repeated admissions, chronic pharmacological management,
and the judicial infrastructure required to enforce coercive measures.

****Moving away from forced treatment is not only a normative imperative
but also a practical strategy for building effective mental health
systems. The prevention of relapse and the reduction of new psychiatric
crises are best achieved by addressing the social determinants of mental
health and ensuring continuity of care. Programs that include supported
housing, community-based rehabilitation, and participatory
decision-making have demonstrated the capacity to foster autonomy and
reduce dependency on institutional care. Investment in these better ways
requires not only a reallocation of resources but also a shift in
clinical training toward relational competencies, narrative
understanding, and cultural humility. In contrast, reliance on coercion
reflects a failure of systemic imagination and a resistance to
structural change. It reinforces a cycle in which acute deterioration is
used to justify punitive interventions rather than being interpreted as
a signal of systemic neglect (Serrano-Miguel, 2020; Parrabera-García et
al, 2023).****

****

The Spanish context illustrates a persistent tension between
constitutional guarantees of liberty and the enduring custodial logic
embedded within psychiatric practice. The current legal framework
already permits involuntary hospitalization under strict conditions and
provides for substitute decision-making in cases of demonstrable
incapacity. Repeated attempts to introduce new forms of outpatient
coercion do not respond to legal vacuums but rather aim to extend
mechanisms of control into the everyday lives of individuals beyond the
institutional setting. Such expansion lacks empirical justification and
raises serious concerns under international human rights standards. The
European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly emphasized that any
restriction of liberty ought to be necessary, proportionate, and subject
to rigorous judicial oversight. In the case of forced outpatient
treatment, these criteria are rarely satisfied (SES‑PAS, 2020;
****Francisco Torres‑Gonzalez, 2022; Calcedo‑Barba et al., 2024;
Pérez‑Prieto et al., 2025****).

The path forward requires a deliberate and evidence-based transition
toward systems of care grounded in autonomy, trust, and mutual
responsibility. This transition involves not only legal and policy
reform but also an epistemic transformation in how psychiatric knowledge
is produced and applied. Clinical paradigms ought to integrate lived
experience, recognize the limitations of current diagnostic frameworks,
and abandon the presumption of incapacity that underpins coercive
practice. Medical education ought to prioritize ethical reasoning,
critical reflection, and dialogic engagement. Institutions ought to be
held accountable for harm caused by coercion and incentivized to adopt
practices that build individual capacity rather than enforce submission.
Service users, families, and communities ought to be empowered to
participate meaningfully in the design, implementation, and evaluation
of care. The objective is not merely to reduce coercion but to create
conditions under which it becomes obsolete. This is attainable through
the systematic deployment of care models that center human dignity,
relational continuity, and the right to self-determination in mental
health.

**Table 6. Systemic failures and mechanisms of institutional harm**

  -------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------
  Epistemic exclusion        Discounting of lived experience, pathologization of dissent   Power Threat Meaning Framework, patient narratives          Inclusion of experiential knowledge in clinical assessment
  Feedback failure           Lack of outcome tracking, no learning from errors             Fieldwork, malpractice cases, WHO QualityRights framework   Participatory audit systems, continuous quality improvement
  Institutional impunity     Absence of sanctions for abuse or neglect                     Ombudsman reports, legal proceedings                        Legal reform, independent oversight bodies
  Policy inertia             Disconnection between evidence and policy                     Literature review, Horizon Europe evaluations               Integration of science-policy interfaces
  Disabling governance       Decision-making without user input                            Comparative models (e.g., open dialogue)                    Deliberative participation, democratic care protocols
  Performativity of ethics   Ethics committees used as bureaucratic cover                  Field observations, case analysis                           Transparent and accountable ethical governance structures
  -------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------

Synthesizes underlying failures in governance, feedback, and legitimacy
that perpetuate harmful practices in psychiatric systems, and outlines
corresponding areas of structural intervention.

The justification for compulsory outpatient treatment in Spain has
increasingly rested on a particular construction of psychiatric
chronicity, framed as a stable and medically verifiable condition
necessitating continuous pharmacological management under professional
supervision. Arguments in favor of such measures emphasize loss of
insight and lack of adherence as diagnostic indicators of pathology.
These assertions often rely on the unexamined assumption that
individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder will
inevitably relapse without pharmacological maintenance, and that
treatment refusal is itself evidence of illness. The proposal to impose
medication in community settings does not arise from demonstrated
therapeutic superiority but from institutional logics oriented toward
risk mitigation, cost containment, and reputational management.

Within clinical discourses, psychosis is often portrayed not only as a
disruption of cognition or affect but also as a suspension of civil and
legal personhood. Autonomy is routinely invalidated by assessments that
equate dissent with incapacity. A recurrent narrative positions certain
individuals as inherently unable to act in their own best interests due
to an alleged deficit in self-awareness. Under this paradigm, forced
outpatient treatment is presented as a humane and proportionate better
to hospitalization. The language of care serves to obscure its
disciplinary function. Legal instruments redefine therapeutic goals, and
medication becomes both the intervention and the prerequisite for legal
freedom. Spain has not enacted a specific statute authorizing
involuntary outpatient treatment. Nonetheless, judicial interpretations
have enabled conditional discharges and provisional legal arrangements
that replicate its function. Proponents frequently invoke international
precedents, such as Kendra's Law in New York or the Mental Health Act in
England and Wales, to argue for legal codification of coercive
outpatient measures. The supposed benefits include reductions in
hospitalizations, improved treatment adherence, and decreased
interaction with the criminal justice system. However, these metrics
fail to capture subjective well-being or personal recovery. They rely
instead on institutional proxies of compliance and contact, rather than
on person-centered outcomes (****Watnik, 2001; Brown et al, 2023)****.

The therapeutic value of antipsychotics remains a subject of ongoing
debate, particularly in the context of long-term use. While short-term
reductions in acute psychotic symptoms have been observed, the
literature indicates a complex and often inconclusive relationship
between sustained medication use and long-term recovery trajectories.
Meta-analyses have not shown consistent differences in functional
outcomes when comparing individuals subjected to coercive treatment with
those receiving care voluntarily. The widespread assumption that
maintenance pharmacotherapy prevents relapse has not been adequately
tested under conditions of informed and uncoerced choice. The use of
long-acting injectables without consent raises significant ethical
concerns. The procedural convenience of such formulations obscures the
structural violence involved in chemically enforcing behavioral
conformity. Appeals to psychiatric chronicity are often employed to
override the preferences and agency of service users. Chronicity is
typically framed as a biological inevitability, rather than a socially
mediated and therapeutically contingent construct. This framing erases
the well-documented role of trauma, social exclusion, and institutional
betrayal in the etiology and perpetuation of psychiatric distress. It
also forecloses the possibility of meaningful recovery without
medication. Within the Spanish policy debate, it is not uncommon to hear
that families require legal instruments to compel relatives to accept
treatment. However, coercion frequently undermines trust, alienates
users from services, and reproduces cycles of disengagement and
deterioration. Assertions that forced treatment supports therapeutic
alliance are fundamentally flawed. Coercion and alliance are mutually
exclusive (Moncrieff, 2008; Kinderman, 2014; Gøtzsche, 2015).

The limited body of empirical research cited in defense of involuntary
outpatient treatment in Spain suffers from significant methodological
limitations. These include selection bias, absence of randomization,
lack of appropriate control groups, and vague or nonstandardized outcome
criteria. Such deficiencies compromise the validity and generalizability
of their findings. In contrast, the expanding literature on shared
decision-making offers robust and replicable evidence that collaborative
care planning enhances adherence, improves satisfaction, and leads to
better clinical and functional outcomes. Individuals who are heard,
respected, and engaged are demonstrably more likely to participate
meaningfully in their own recovery. Decision-making capacity is not
fixed but situational and relational, shaped by the quality of the
therapeutic environment. Coercive outpatient treatment undermines these
enabling conditions and erodes the relational infrastructure on which
sustained recovery depends (****Viadel et al, 2006; Portero, 2010;
Cañete-Nicolás et al., 2012)****.

Medication use within involuntary outpatient frameworks is typically
determined by clinical expediency rather than by individualized
therapeutic dialogue. Regimens are often standardized, with minimal
adjustment based on tolerability, side effects, or patient-reported
experience. The dominant reliance on long-acting injectables reflects a
pharmacocentric and compliance-oriented model of care. Psychological and
social interventions are nominally acknowledged but rarely
operationalized within coercive frameworks. Clinicians themselves
acknowledge that the existing infrastructure is inadequate for
delivering comprehensive, community-based recovery services. Coercion
functions as a compensatory mechanism for systemic neglect. Arguments
asserting that forced treatment guarantees stability ignore the reality
that such measures are most often deployed in environments lacking
viable therapeutic better ways (Sheridan Rains et al., 2019).

Recovery cannot be reduced to the suppression of symptoms. It involves
the reconstitution of meaning, the restoration of agency, and the
reconstruction of social roles. Coercive practices flatten this
complexity. They pathologize resistance and reframe dissent as clinical
deterioration. The result is not stabilization but the entrenchment of
epistemic and relational harm. Individuals subjected to coercion
consistently report fear, humiliation, and lasting distrust in the
health system. These responses are not signs of psychopathology but
adaptive reactions to structural violence. To claim that coercion is
care is to erase the lived experience of those most affected and to
perpetuate a model of psychiatry rooted in domination rather than
healing (Eiroa-Orosa & Rowe, 2017 ; Kalathil, 2018).

Defenses of involuntary outpatient treatment often appeal to public
safety and administrative efficiency. Yet, these are not therapeutic
aims. They reflect institutional priorities that are misaligned with the
goals of recovery and individual well-being. The discourse of risk is
itself problematic. It is often racialized, gendered, and
socioeconomically biased. The presumption that certain individuals or
groups are inherently dangerous leads to arbitrary and discriminatory
enforcement. In the Spanish context, as in others, coercive
interventions disproportionately affect those without family support,
those with limited financial resources, and those from migrant or
minority backgrounds. Structural vulnerabilities are medicalized, and
the burden of adaptation is placed on the most disenfranchised
****(Jacka & Berk, 2012; Kidd et al., 2015a; Walker et al., 2019)****.

To ensure improvements in these and all systemic failures, this
dissertation was conducted through embedded engagement in national and
international networks, including formal research actions, clinical
settings, and policy initiatives, in line with a participatory
action-research design. These collaborative environments were not
peripheral but constituted integral fieldwork sites, where knowledge was
co-produced through iterative exchange, reflexive analysis, and
goal-oriented praxis. Colleagues and participants functioned
simultaneously as key informants, critical interlocutors, and
co-generators of empirical data, interpretive frameworks, and
operational milestones. This embedded model reflects a commitment to
scientific accountability, enabling the triangulation of perspectives
and enhancing the translational potential of the findings. From a
medical anthropological standpoint, this approach aligns with the
ethical imperative to contribute constructively to the systems under
study, rather than maintaining a detached observational stance.
Constructive engagement, anchored in empirical rigor and situated
responsiveness, is not merely a methodological choice, as shown in
chapter 2, but a disciplinary obligation when investigating healthcare
structures that actively produce suffering or protection. This
orientation ensures that the work not only documents systemic
dysfunction but contributes to its resolution, in fidelity to both the
scientific method and the principles of relational care ****(Schneider,
2012; Rose, 2018)****.

In this dissertation, recovery is defined as the restoration and
sustained maintenance of physiological regulation, functional autonomy,
and psychosocial agency, assessed through multidimensional outcomes.
These include measurable reductions in pharmacological dependency where
clinically indicated, normalization of neuroendocrine and inflammatory
markers, improvement in cognitive-affective integration, and the
demonstrated ability to engage meaningfully in relational, educational,
and vocational roles. Best practices are defined as those clinical and
institutional procedures which, across populations and contexts, support
these outcomes with minimal adverse effects and maximal user engagement.
Such practices are characterized by informed consent, contextual
attunement, and dynamic accountability, enabling the calibration of care
in response to evolving individual and systemic conditions. Recovery is
conceptualized not as a fixed state but as a dynamic, processual
achievement contingent upon ecological coherence, institutional
responsiveness, and the absence of epistemic and structural violence.
Within this framework, coercion is not classified as therapeutic, but as
a mechanism of control and presumed risk management, whose continued use
in clinical settings, including in punitive or extrajudicial forms,
undermines both the legitimacy and efficacy of psychiatric care. Its
presence signals systemic failure to establish relational safety and
ethical care environments, and its eradication remains a medical, legal,
and scientific imperative ****(Mezzina et al., 2006b)****.

**1.3 Overmedication and pharmacocentrism in Spanish healthcare and
psychiatry**

****The overuse of psychotropic drugs in Spanish healthcare is not
attributable to isolated clinical errors or professional negligence, but
rather reflects the systematic implementation of a medical model in
which pharmacological management occupies a dominant, structurally
legitimised position. The persistence of overmedication reveals a
multifaceted institutional configuration, shaped by professional habits,
legislative frameworks, educational curricula, industrial influence, and
cultural norms of care. Spain ranks among the highest countries in
Europe in terms of anxiolytic and antidepressant consumption, with
benzodiazepines, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and atypical
antipsychotics prescribed at rates consistently exceeding clinical
guideline recommendations. This overuse affects diverse patient
populations, often without rigorous diagnostic substantiation, without
informed long-term risk assessment, and in contexts where the
biopsychosocial origins of distress remain unexamined. The diffusion of
pharmacological responses beyond specialist psychiatry, notably through
general practitioners and emergency services, illustrates the
institutional entrenchment of pharmacocentrism as a default reaction to
psychological and behavioural symptoms. This clinical orientation,
sustained by economic expediency and time pressure, results in a
pathological narrowing of treatment options, in which symptom
suppression replaces diagnosis, monitoring, and therapeutic alliance
(Cohen, 1975; Jiménez, 2005).****

Psychotropic prescriptions are frequently initiated and maintained in
response to life stressors, interpersonal losses, or chronic social
hardship, even in the absence of major psychiatric disorders.
Pharmacological solutions are mobilised in response to fatigue,
insomnia, anxiety, somatic complaints, and family conflict, without
adequate differential diagnosis, multidisciplinary consultation, or
provision of non-pharmacological interventions. This pattern results in
the chronic administration of medications initially intended for
short-term or crisis use. Benzodiazepines, for instance, which were
approved for transient management of acute anxiety and sleep
disturbances, are widely maintained for periods extending several years.
Spain has been consistently placed among the top
benzodiazepine-consuming countries in the Organisation for Economic
Co-operation and Development, with a prevalence that far exceeds the
epidemiological incidence of anxiety-related disorders requiring
pharmacological treatment. The consequences of this misuse include the
development of tolerance, dependence, withdrawal syndromes, cognitive
impairment, and functional decline. These biological effects are
compounded by psychological dependence, impaired agency, and the
reinforcement of passivity and medicalised identity (Cañete‑Nicolás et
al., 2015; ****Francisco Torres‑Gonzalez, 2022****).

Prescriptions issued by non-specialist physicians account for the
majority of anxiolytic and antidepressant use in Spain. This reflects a
structural configuration of healthcare that prioritises throughput,
administrative manageability, and symptomatic resolution over
person-centred assessment and care continuity. General practitioners are
routinely tasked with managing complex mental health presentations in
under ten minutes per consultation, with limited access to referral
networks, psychotherapy, or case follow-up. The effect is a system where
medication is prescribed as a stopgap measure in the absence of time,
resources, and institutional pathways for comprehensive care.
Psychotropic medication in such settings becomes an instrument not only
of symptom control, but of organisational containment. Patients who fail
to improve under these regimens are often recycled through healthcare
services with escalating doses, additional diagnoses, and polypharmacy,
without systematic review of initial assumptions or exploration of
better ways. The phenomenon is not reducible to pharmacological inertia
but ought to be understood as the functional correlate of a fragmented,
under-resourced, and risk-averse healthcare infrastructure.

****Within psychiatric services, the structural predominance of
pharmacological approaches is particularly pronounced. Antipsychotic
drugs, including long-acting injectables, are increasingly employed not
only in psychotic disorders but also in behavioural regulation across a
range of non-psychotic diagnoses, including intellectual disability,
dementia, and borderline personality disorder. These prescriptions are
frequently initiated and continued without robust clinical indication,
without documented informed consent, and without systematic evaluation
of risk-benefit ratio. Long-term administration of antipsychotics is
associated with significant adverse effects, including metabolic
syndrome, extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, cognitive decline, and
increased mortality. Despite these well-documented risks, deprescription
remains rare, and pharmacological regimens are often escalated in
response to behavioural challenges, institutional conflicts, or
professional disagreement, rather than through clinical re-evaluation.
This pattern is sustained by training deficits, liability concerns, and
the institutionalisation of pharmacological compliance as a proxy for
therapeutic success (Bobes et al., 2012; Guzmán‐Parra et al., 2018;
****Aragonés‐Calleja & Sánchez‐Martínez, 2023****). ****The issue of
overmedication ought to also be understood in relation to the absence of
integrated psychosocial interventions. Community mental health services
in Spain are unevenly distributed, under-resourced, and oriented toward
pharmacological stabilisation rather than recovery or social
reintegration. Psychotherapy, occupational therapy, peer support, and
family counselling are chronically underfunded, sporadically
implemented, and in many regions effectively inaccessible. In this
vacuum, pharmacological strategies acquire a monopoly on therapeutic
legitimacy. Patients and families come to equate care with medication,
and refusal is interpreted as irrationality or denial of illness.
Institutions internalise this logic, and physicians operate within a
framework in which prescribing is the most readily available,
reimbursed, and institutionally protected act. This creates a feedback
loop in which overmedication becomes self-reinforcing, shielded from
scrutiny by cultural expectation, institutional design, and professional
norms.

The educational system reproduces this paradigm. Medical curricula in
Spain devote limited attention to the historical, sociological, or
psychological dimensions of mental suffering. Pharmacology and
diagnostic classification are prioritised, while reflective practice,
relational skills, and trauma-informed approaches remain peripheral.
Students are not systematically trained in shared decision-making,
patient autonomy, or non-pharmacological pathways to recovery. Instead,
they are socialised into a model of care in which therapeutic success is
defined by symptom reduction and adherence. The absence of critical
pharmacovigilance, alongside limited training in deprescription, leads
to professional trajectories in which medication is employed early,
broadly, and indefinitely. Continuous education, often funded or
influenced by pharmaceutical interests, reinforces these patterns,
presenting pharmacological innovation as synonymous with clinical
progress, and obscuring the ethical and empirical limits of current
practice (Montero, 2014).

****The pharmacological management of distress is further amplified by
broader sociocultural factors that facilitate medicalisation and
discourage systemic responses. In Spain, high rates of prescription for
psychotropic drugs are not merely the product of clinical decisions but
reflect a widespread pattern of medicating social suffering. Poverty,
unemployment, precarious housing, and chronic stress linked to
caregiving responsibilities or domestic violence are frequently
translated into psychiatric symptoms within clinical encounters. Rather
than acting on the social determinants of health, the healthcare system
often absorbs their consequences through the language of diagnosis and
the mechanism of prescription. This transfer of responsibility from
public policy to the individual subject reinforces a biomedical
narrative in which structural adversity is reframed as personal
dysfunction, treatable primarily through pharmacological means. The
result is a chronic disjunction between diagnosis and reality, in which
the burden of systemic failure is redistributed as individual pathology
(Laporte et al, 1983; Bertolín-Guillén, 2021; Suleman et al., 2025).****

This phenomenon is particularly visible in primary care, where general
practitioners are expected to manage a high volume of patients in
limited time, often without access to psychosocial resources or referral
options. Within these constraints, medication becomes not only the path
of least resistance but the only available tool. Benzodiazepines and
antidepressants are routinely used to manage conditions that emerge from
socioeconomic deprivation, interpersonal conflict, and cumulative life
stress. While such medications may provide temporary relief, their
prolonged use in structurally disadvantaged populations reinforces
dependence, undermines the development of adaptive coping strategies,
and delays or displaces interventions that address underlying causes.
Chronic exposure to these drugs carries significant health risks,
particularly among older adults, for whom the risk of falls, cognitive
impairment, and iatrogenic injury is markedly increased. In this
context, overmedication becomes a vector of medical harm, sustained by
institutional indifference to the conditions that generate suffering
(Santamaría, 2020; Bertolín-Guillén, 2021; Roncero et al, 2025).

### Table 7. Systemic logic of psychiatric coercion and overmedication

  ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------
  ****1. Structural Conditions****   Sociostructural determinants (e.g., poverty, trauma)                                                       
  ****2. Initial Presentation****    Psychiatric symptom presentation                       Risk aversion and legal constraints                 
  ****3. Institutional Framing****   Framed as individual disorder                          Protocol-driven care (low variance, high control)   
  ****4. Diagnostic Assignment****   Diagnostic label assigned                              Pharmacocentric intervention                        
  ****5. Institutional Outcome****                                                                                                              Chronicity, exclusion, resistance to reform
  ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------

This table outlines the sequential institutional logic through which
social suffering is reframed as individual disorder, leading to coercive
psychiatric interventions. It demonstrates the interplay between
sociostructural determinants and legal-institutional constraints,
showing how diagnostic labeling and pharmacocentric protocols converge
to produce chronicity, exclusion, and resistance to reform. The model
reflects mechanisms of structural violence embedded in clinical
governance and highlights the need for systemic redesign grounded in
patient autonomy, ethical accountability, and recovery-oriented
practice.

From a public health perspective, the cost of this pharmacocentric
approach is substantial. Financially, the allocation of resources to
medication procurement, distribution, and monitoring diverts funding
from preventative and community-based interventions. Clinically,
overreliance on drugs contributes to unnecessary hospitalisations,
treatment-resistant presentations, and elevated rates of chronic
disability. Psychosocially, it erodes trust in the healthcare system,
stigmatises distress, and fragments the relational fabric necessary for
long-term recovery. The cumulative burden of overmedication is therefore
not limited to the patient but extends to families, professionals, and
society as a whole. Its persistence is indicative of a deeper
epistemological crisis in healthcare, where the metrics of success are
misaligned with the realities of human suffering, and where the promise
of technological precision obscures the need for ethical and contextual
sensitivity (Laporte, 1984; Díaz-Gutiérrez et al, 2018).

The evidence presented in this section confirms that overmedication in
Spanish psychiatry cannot be explained as a series of isolated errors or
unfortunate habits. It is a systemic feature of a clinical ecosystem
that privileges pharmaceutical solutions, institutional convenience, and
epistemic authority over patient experience, structural reform, and
relational care. Addressing this dysfunction requires a sustained and
multidisciplinary effort, capable of confronting both the cultural
assumptions and the institutional practices that sustain pharmacocentric
hegemony. The next section will examine the rationale, principles, and
implementation strategies of autonomous medication management and other
scientifically grounded practices that can restore clinical integrity
and advance health outcomes in a rights-based, participatory, and
ethically coherent framework.

****

**1.4 Toward autonomous medication management and evidence-based better
practices**

****International developments in psychiatric care have progressively
challenged the historical dominance of paternalistic, pharmacologically
centered, and compliance-oriented treatment ****paradigms. Autonomous
medication management has emerged in this context as a scientifically
grounded and ethically necessary framework, aiming to reconfigure
psychiatric pharmacotherapy as a dialogical and evidence-based process
rather than a unilateral imposition. In multiple health systems across
North America and Europe, empirical and longitudinal studies have
identified significant clinical and public health concerns linked to the
long-term use of psychotropic medication, including metabolic syndrome,
cardiovascular risk, neurocognitive impairment, emotional blunting, and
altered social cognition. These effects, compounded by insufficient
informed consent procedures and structurally coercive treatment regimes,
have prompted sustained critique from both academic psychiatry and
user-led advocacy. Concomitantly, policy frameworks in jurisdictions
such as Quebec, Brazil, the Netherlands, and Finland have integrated
better models of care, reflecting a shift in clinical and ethical
reasoning. These models emphasize recovery, narrative coherence,
contextual understanding, and relational decision-making, positioning
medication not as the axis of intervention but as one modifiable element
within an evolving therapeutic arrangement. This reframing has been
supported by controlled trials, real-world cohort data, and
trans-disciplinary consensus statements underscoring the necessity of
reducing medication load, implementing tapering protocols, and fostering
participatory care environments (Deegan, 2006; Chmielowska et al., 2022;
Horowitz, 2024).****

The Quebec model, notably developed through the work of Jean-François
Pelletier and Marie-Jeanne Proulx, systematized collaborative medication
management as a relational and ethically reflexive practice grounded in
the recovery paradigm. Informed by trauma research, patient autonomy,
and shared clinical accountability, this model emphasized the production
of knowledge through dialogue, the reorientation of clinical authority,
and the integration of peer support into pharmacological decisions.
These strategies were operationalized through structured dialogues,
non-hierarchical therapeutic teams, and flexible treatment planning
responsive to individual trajectories of distress and recovery. In
Brazil, the translation of these principles into a context marked by
psychosocial community care, collective health constitutionalism, and
anti-institutional reform yielded a model in which medication reduction
strategies were embedded within a broader political commitment to
deinstitutionalization and rights-based psychiatry. The Brazilian system
demonstrated that medication management cannot be decoupled from
socio-legal determinants, such as access to housing, income, and
community resources. By integrating psychotropic deprescription into a
continuum of public health and social protections, Brazil's approach
highlighted the necessity of collective supports and legal frameworks
that reinforce the legitimacy of non-pharmacological care (Canadian
Deprescribing Guidelines Project, 2024).

In the Netherlands and Finland, open dialogue practices have provided
further empirical grounding for low-medication and user-centered
psychiatric models. These practices, which integrate continuous familial
and community involvement, real-time dialogical processes, and minimal
reliance on diagnostic categorization, have yielded statistically
significant outcomes in terms of reduced hospitalization, lower chronic
medication use, and higher patient-reported recovery metrics. Despite
these outcomes, institutionalization of such models remains limited due
to systemic inertia, financial constraints, and disciplinary resistance
within conventional psychiatric governance. The comparative analysis of
these jurisdictions reveals that autonomous medication management is not
an abstract ethical ideal but a viable clinical framework that depends
on interlocking supports: clinical retraining, patient-led tools,
digital infrastructure, and legal recognition of participatory rights.
This empirical corpus establishes the conceptual, ethical, and practical
viability of a model in which medication use is not dictated by standard
protocols or institutional mandates, but co-produced in situated,
relational, and physiologically literate clinical ecosystems (Seikkula &
Olson, 2003; Olson et al., 2014; Groot & van Os, 2023).

**** ****Barriers to the widespread adoption of autonomous medication
management remain significant, particularly in contexts such as Spain
where clinical traditions, institutional protocols, and professional
hierarchies continue to privilege pharmacological intervention as the
cornerstone of psychiatric care. Despite rhetorical shifts toward
recovery-oriented principles and the formal inclusion of patient rights
in national mental health strategies, these commitments often fail to
materialize in clinical practice. Structural constraints include the
absence of training in dialogical and trauma-informed care, limited
availability of psychosocial better ways, and medico-legal cultures that
penalize clinical discretion perceived as deviant from pharmacocentric
standards. These constraints are reinforced by the design of health
information systems that track medication adherence as a proxy for
clinical improvement, thereby entrenching pharmacological compliance as
an index of successful care. The result is a clinical environment in
which patient requests to taper or discontinue medication are often
interpreted as signs of denial, resistance, or lack of insight, rather
than as expressions of informed agency. This interpretive framework not
only delegitimizes the experiential knowledge of individuals with lived
experience but also disincentivizes reflective practice among
professionals, who remain embedded in cultures of risk aversion and
diagnostic orthodoxy (****Serrano-Miguel et al, 2020; Martínez-Hernáez
et al, 2020)****.****

Further compounding the issue is the asymmetry of scientific literacy
and epistemic authority between patients and professionals. In the
absence of co-produced clinical guidelines and shared platforms for
knowledge dissemination, patients are often deprived of the information
necessary to engage meaningfully in pharmacological decision-making.
Many remain unaware of the full range of risks associated with long-term
medication use, the physiological processes underpinning withdrawal
syndromes, or the better ways supported by international evidence. The
dissemination of open-access deprescription guidelines, interactive
digital decision aids, and patient-led training modules remains limited
to specific pilot programs and rarely reaches primary or secondary care
settings. In Spain, the integration of these tools into routine care is
further hindered by fragmented governance, insufficient policy
coordination across autonomous communities, and the dominance of
pharmaceutical industry interests in continuing medical education and
guideline development. The lack of independent evaluation mechanisms and
the near absence of patient-controlled documentation systems exacerbate
this problem, resulting in an institutional environment that
structurally inhibits the operationalization of best practices in
medication management (****Sanguineti et al., 2025****).

Scientific consensus increasingly recognizes the need to redefine both
the content and process of psychiatric care to accommodate the epistemic
plurality and physiological variability inherent in real-world clinical
populations. Rather than framing medication adherence as a binary
outcome or marker of engagement, contemporary best practices emphasize
the use of feedback-informed treatment planning, co-defined clinical
endpoints, and metrics that incorporate both physiological and
psychosocial dimensions of recovery. These include cognitive
functioning, metabolic health, narrative coherence, affect regulation,
and social role fulfillment. Evidence from longitudinal studies suggests
that such outcome measures are better predictors of sustained well-being
than traditional symptom checklists or diagnostic criteria alone.
Consequently, the scientific justification for maintaining
pharmacocentric treatment models without rigorous re-evaluation has
weakened considerably. The persistence of these models in Spain reflects
not an absence of better ways, but a failure to implement those better
ways due to institutional inertia, legal ambiguity, and the
marginalization of critical perspectives within psychiatric education
and governance (****Kuhl, 2019****).

The consolidation of pharmacocentric paradigms in Spanish psychiatry,
despite accumulating international evidence of their limitations, ought
to be understood as a product of deeply embedded institutional logics
that extend beyond individual clinical encounters. Professional
cultures, regulatory environments, and reimbursement schemes
collectively sustain a framework in which the prescription of
psychotropic drugs is not only normalized but structurally incentivized.
Reimbursement policies favor short, medication-focused consultations
over time-intensive psychosocial interventions. Legal and administrative
protocols often prioritize risk minimization through rapid
pharmacological containment rather than comprehensive contextual
evaluation. Training curricula in medicine and psychology continue to
privilege symptom-based diagnostic categories and neurochemical
explanatory models while neglecting integrative approaches to trauma,
embodiment, and social determinants. This constellation of forces
reinforces a clinical habitus that marginalizes non-pharmacological
knowledge, restricts therapeutic imagination, and produces epistemic
conditions hostile to dialogical and participatory care (Toro et al,
2006).

Crucially, the normalization of long-term psychopharmacological
treatment in Spain persists despite its well-documented iatrogenic
consequences. Chronic exposure to antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood
stabilizers, and anxiolytics has been associated with a wide range of
adverse effects, including but not limited to metabolic dysfunction,
cognitive impairment, emotional blunting, movement disorders, hormonal
dysregulation, and sexual dysfunction (Simopoulos & Trinidad, 2013).
Beyond physiological sequelae, prolonged medication use often leads to
psychosocial dependency, erosion of self-efficacy, and impaired identity
development, particularly in adolescents and young adults. These
outcomes are rarely monitored systematically and are frequently
minimized or pathologized when raised by patients. Instead of prompting
critical reflection on the appropriateness of treatment plans, reports
of adverse effects are often met with diagnostic escalation or
polypharmacy. This practice not only amplifies risk but entrenches a
clinical cycle wherein patient concerns are reinterpreted as evidence of
disorder rather than valid input into therapeutic decision-making. Such
dynamics illustrate how the pharmacocentric model operates not merely as
a treatment strategy but as a disciplinary mechanism, shaping patient
subjectivity, professional identity, and institutional norms (Dencker et
al, 1986; Gotzsche, 2019).

The ethical implications of this model are significant. When clinical
systems prioritize biochemical intervention over relational
understanding, the result is a degradation of therapeutic integrity and
a systematic erosion of informed consent. True consent requires not only
the provision of information but also the freedom to decline or modify
treatment based on evolving needs and goals. In the current Spanish
context, this freedom is often nominal, constrained by structural
scarcity, normative pressure, and the medical-legal framing of deviation
as deviance. Autonomy becomes performative rather than substantive,
preserved in rhetoric but denied in practice. To counter this tendency,
evidence-based better practices in medication management ought to be
embedded within a broader transformation of psychiatric epistemology and
governance. This transformation entails not only revising treatment
protocols but reconfiguring the systems of knowledge production,
professional accreditation, and institutional accountability that
sustain them (****Whitaker, 2005; Rose, 2007)****.

This dissertation contributes to such reconfiguration by articulating
the scientific, ethical, and operational foundations of autonomous
medication management, rooted in comparative fieldwork, empirical
evidence, and the lived expertise of those affected. Through
multi-scalar analysis and trans-disciplinary integration, it exposes the
structural determinants of pharmacocentric persistence and outlines
actionable pathways toward clinical practices that are both more
effective and more just. The next section delineates the medico-legal
and constitutional frameworks necessary to support this transition,
identifying the normative, procedural, and institutional conditions
under which pharmacological care can be rendered compatible with human
rights, clinical excellence, and democratic legitimacy.

****

**1.5 Legal, epistemic, and scientific foundations of the research
problem**

****The persistence of coercive practices and pharmacocentric treatment
models in contemporary psychiatry reflects a complex intersection of
legal ambiguity, epistemic asymmetry, and scientific limitation. These
elements sustain a structural configuration in which patient autonomy,
informed consent, and bodily integrity are subordinated to institutional
convenience, professional discretion, and risk management protocols. The
foundational problem addressed in this dissertation is not limited to
clinical overreach but concerns the systemic reproduction of coercion
through embedded legal norms, scientific validation mechanisms, and
decision-making hierarchies that obscure the boundary between care and
control. Despite international human rights instruments affirming the
principle of free and informed consent in medical treatment, national
legal frameworks often contain exceptions that permit involuntary
intervention on the basis of presumed incapacity, risk, or diagnostic
classification (Hemper et al, 2024). These exceptions, while formally
regulated, are subject to broad interpretive discretion and rarely
subjected to external verification or retrospective audit. In the
Spanish context, the organic laws governing civil incapacity,
guardianship, and mental health intervention permit medical and judicial
actors to override patient preferences without requiring real-time
justification rooted in contemporary scientific standards. This legal
permissiveness enables coercion to function as a normalized clinical
strategy rather than as a last resort (Desviat, 2011; ****Ferreirós,
2013; ****Ramos-Pozón et al, 2025).****

The epistemic structure of psychiatry reinforces this dynamic by
locating clinical authority within a diagnostic system that remains
descriptively based and not etiologically validated. The prevailing
nosological models used in Spain and across most high-income health
systems are grounded in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental
Disorders and the International Classification of Diseases. These
classifications rely on symptom clusters without mechanistic grounding,
rendering diagnostic attribution vulnerable to subjectivity,
sociocultural bias, and administrative utility. The absence of objective
biomarkers or reproducible physiological indicators undermines the
epistemic reliability of psychiatric diagnosis and weakens its claim to
medical legitimacy under the standards of falsifiability and mechanistic
transparency expected in other domains of health science. Nevertheless,
these classifications carry significant legal and social weight,
functioning as gatekeeping devices for civil status, capacity, and
access to entitlements or restrictions. In practice, they authorize
interventions that may include forced hospitalization, involuntary
medication, and long-term institutionalization, often without recourse
to independent appeal or longitudinal re-evaluation. This tension
between epistemic uncertainty and legal determinacy constitutes a core
dimension of the research problem addressed in this dissertation
****(Moncrieff, 2010; Frances, 2013)****.

The institutionalization of psychiatric knowledge occurs within a
regulatory architecture that confers normative status to clinical
opinion without subjecting it to the same evidentiary thresholds applied
in other domains of biomedicine. In the absence of mechanistic
specificity or outcome-based validation, clinical authority is derived
primarily from institutional position, professional credentialing, and
codified protocols. These protocols are themselves frequently based on
consensus rather than on controlled empirical evaluation and often
reflect the influence of pharmaceutical interests, risk containment
priorities, and medico-legal defensibility rather than therapeutic
efficacy or patient-defined recovery. This dynamic produces a closed
epistemic loop wherein deviation from established pharmacological or
diagnostic practice is interpreted as clinical error, administrative
liability, or patient irrationality. Within such a system, innovation,
dissent, or adaptation is structurally discouraged, and relational or
contextual data is deprioritized in favor of quantifiable symptom
management. Clinical decisions are thus governed by algorithmic logic
informed by population averages and extrapolated trial data, rather than
by person-specific trajectories, life histories, or situated capacities
for choice (Kirk & Kutchins, 1992; Kirk et al., 2013).

The scientific literature on coercion and psychiatric harm has expanded
over the past two decades, but its integration into clinical and legal
praxis remains limited. Meta-analyses and large-scale observational
studies have documented the long-term consequences of coercive
practices, including learned helplessness, treatment disengagement,
iatrogenic injury, and elevated suicide risk. Nevertheless, the
incorporation of these findings into policy reform or clinical training
has been partial and inconsistent. Scientific evidence of harm is often
neutralized by institutional narratives of risk mitigation or patient
safety, which present coercion as a necessary response to clinical
urgency, despite the lack of predictive validity in psychiatric risk
assessment tools. Scientific critique of pharmacocentric practices,
including the long-term inefficacy of certain drug classes and the
underreporting of adverse effects in industry-sponsored trials, has
likewise struggled to produce sustained shifts in clinical behavior or
regulatory standards. This indicates a structural dissociation between
knowledge production and institutional change, a gap this dissertation
aims to expose and address through embedded, empirically informed, and
system-sensitive research (Moon, 2000).

Within the Spanish context, the convergence of legal permissibility,
scientific ambiguity, and clinical discretion creates a structural
environment where coercive practices are not episodic but constitutive
of psychiatric governance. Civil codes, health statutes, and
jurisprudence allow for involuntary interventions based on broad
interpretations of risk, incapacity, or presumed medical necessity,
without requiring the presentation of individualized harm thresholds or
evidence-based justification. Judicial endorsement of clinical
recommendations is often automatic, reflecting the judiciary's reliance
on psychiatric expertise and the absence of independent oversight or
epistemic counterbalance. This arrangement consolidates the authority of
the psychiatric institution while limiting avenues for patient
contestation, legal redress, or external review. In such a
configuration, the patient's capacity to object is undermined not only
procedurally but conceptually, as dissent is pathologized and
interpreted as a symptom of illness rather than as a legitimate
expression of agency. Diagnostic instruments, clinical notes, and risk
assessments function not as descriptive aids but as technologies of
capture, generating administrative legitimacy for interventions whose
scientific basis remains weak or untested (Szasz, 2007; Whitaker, 2010).

These systemic conditions are reinforced by the epistemological division
between objective and subjective evidence, in which first-person
accounts of harm or injustice are routinely discounted as unreliable or
non-clinical. This marginalization of lived experience undermines the
empirical scope of psychiatric inquiry, narrows the definition of valid
data, and restricts the development of participatory or phenomenological
models of care. It limits the potential for system feedback and error
correction, as mechanisms for reporting harm are underdeveloped,
institutionally internal, or perceived as adversarial. When adverse
outcomes do occur, including iatrogenic deterioration, suicide, or
chronicity induced by cumulative intervention, institutional responses
prioritize liability management over truth reconstruction, preventing
meaningful learning or procedural reform. In this environment, the
legitimacy of psychiatric practice is maintained through normative
inertia, credential-based authority, and bureaucratic insulation from
user critique. The resulting gap between clinical rhetoric and
institutional practice constitutes a core pathology of governance and a
critical object of analysis for this research (Burstow, 2015; Held,
2020; Markus, 2020).

The structural features outlined above define not only the object of
study but also the methodological constraints and ethical obligations
under which this dissertation has been developed. The convergence of
legal authority, clinical autonomy, and epistemic opacity requires a
research design capable of operating within contested institutional
spaces while maintaining analytical rigor and procedural integrity. This
entails a scientific framework that treats lived experience as data,
institutional discourse as evidence, and clinical practice as situated
behavior subject to empirical analysis. It also demands a methodological
position that does not reproduce the asymmetries it critiques, but that
enables observation, documentation, and engagement without reproducing
harm or epistemic exclusion (Sanati & Kyratsous, 2015). The research
problem is thus not limited to identifying instances of coercion or
overmedication but extends to mapping the normative architectures that
sustain them and to tracing the conditions under which these
architectures might be transformed. Such transformation cannot occur
solely through clinical innovation or legal amendment but requires a
reconfiguration of epistemic hierarchies, procedural safeguards, and
institutional accountability mechanisms. These dimensions will be
addressed in the following chapter, which outlines the methodological
strategy adopted, the design of field instruments, and the analytical
frameworks used to examine coercion, agency, and psychiatric governance
in real-world contexts. The aim is to generate scientific knowledge that
is empirically grounded, legally relevant, and operationally useful in
advancing ethically defensible models of mental health care (Houlders,
Bortolotti, & Broome, 2021).

****

**1.6 Systemic failure, structural violence, and the challenge of
reform**

****The current structure of psychiatric care in Spain is shaped by
entrenched institutional paradigms that prioritise pharmacological
containment over biopsychosocial integration. Despite the increasing
availability of global frameworks for rights-based care, including the
World Health Organization's QualityRights program, and the widespread
dissemination of trauma-informed principles and patient-centred care
models, the dominant clinical responses to mental distress remain
largely pharmacocentric and reactive. This discrepancy reflects a
fundamental misalignment between emerging standards in global health and
the operational norms within much of Spanish psychiatry. The sustained
use of psychotropic drugs, particularly for long-term treatment of
non-acute mental health conditions, continues to occur without
consistent application of participatory decision-making protocols,
interdisciplinary evaluation, or structural risk assessment. While
professional societies increasingly recognise the importance of
ecological, neuroendocrine, and relational factors in shaping mental
health outcomes, these insights are yet to be translated into routine
practice. The continued dominance of reductionist paradigms not only
limits clinical efficacy but systematically undermines the rights,
autonomy, and long-term recovery prospects of patients, particularly
those most marginalised by poverty, trauma, and social exclusion. The
absence of meaningful dialogue between disciplines, the limited
implementation of rights-based training, and the persistent framing of
non-compliance as clinical deviance all contribute to an institutional
landscape in which pharmacological interventions become the default
response to distress, regardless of context, history, or patient
preference. In this setting, structural violence operates not as an
aberration, but as a consequence of standardised practice, revealing the
urgent need for paradigm correction guided by scientific integrity and
ethical obligation (Paradis-Gagné et al., 2021; Gill et al., 2024).****

****Efforts by the Spanish central government and some regional ones,
such as the Catalonian one, to address the disproportionate reliance on
pharmacological interventions have gained visibility through the recent
national mental health strategies, which emphasise the importance of
community-based care, interdisciplinary coordination, and preventive
approaches. These policy instruments acknowledge the overuse of
psychiatric medication and advocate for non-pharmacological responses,
especially in primary care and non-acute settings. However, the
translation of these priorities into practice remains partial and uneven
across regions. Institutional inertia, uneven training of healthcare
professionals, insufficient infrastructure for psychosocial support, and
the persistence of hierarchical clinical cultures continue to impede the
realisation of these policy objectives. Without substantive reform in
how medical decisions are made, documented, and followed up, the stated
goals risk becoming performative. The emphasis on mental health as a
public health priority ought to not be reduced to rhetorical
commitments. It requires the allocation of resources to
multidisciplinary teams, the reorganisation of care pathways to enable
continuity and choice, and the development of measurement systems that
