Table summarizing the validation processes, cultural adaptations, and
ethical protocols applied to the three central survey instruments of the
dissertation. The approach emphasizes scientific rigor, epistemic
justice, and ethical research practice in contexts marked by historical
and structural asymmetry.

The deployment of these instruments occurred under conditions of
profound institutional and infrastructural precarity. The resulting
systems had to ensure GDPR-compliant anonymization, timestamp logging,
and encrypted access, highlighting the level of operational autonomy
required for research in ethically sensitive but structurally
unsupported terrains, and so those did, using mostly only open source
tools or institutionally available ones to gather responses anonymously.
The first survey, adapted from UK materials, served as a pilot for the
participatory principles and mixed question architecture later adopted
across instruments. The open dialogue survey followed, with an emphasis
on national outreach and policy engagement, leading to a peer-reviewed
publication. The final and most intricate instrument, on shared
decision-making, consolidated lessons from the prior tools and
incorporated advanced ethical provisions, conceptual robustness, and
alignment with WHO QualityRights and international deprescription
frameworks. Each instrument\'s refinement fed into the next, forming a
cumulative methodological arc that supported the broader action-research
structure of the dissertation (Lehmann, 1998a; Lehmann, 2010).

All instruments were constructed and validated in line with
action-research principles. Initial drafts were reviewed by expert
panels that included clinicians, anthropologists, legal professionals,
and psychiatric survivors. Pilot testing with target respondent groups
allowed refinement of item clarity, cultural appropriateness, and
conceptual scope. The surveys were made accessible through digital
platforms, and technical barriers, were met with infrastructural
adaptations to preserve data integrity and accessibility (Ladkin, 2007).
Each instrument incorporated informed consent procedures based on
dynamic consent principles. Respondents were provided with full
disclosure of the study's aims, scope, data protection measures, and
options to withdraw. No personal identifiers were collected, and all
responses were anonymized at point of entry. Given the researcher's
status as both insider and survivor, ethical oversight included detailed
reflexive protocols and independent review by senior academics.
Integration across the three instruments was conducted using thematic,
narrative, and comparative techniques (Lassiter, 2005). While each
survey addressed distinct issues, labeling, dialogical practice, and
medication governance, they also functioned as intersecting diagnostic
tools within the broader research architecture. The quantitative and
qualitative material collected through open questions, complemented the
ethnographic data and was used to corroborate findings emerging from
participant observation, legal analysis, own witness, and
testimony-based research.

The three surveys incorporated in this dissertation were constructed and
validated through a rigorous process combining clinical, scientific, and
lived-experience expertise: the first survey, i****nquiry into the
'Schizophrenia' Label (ISL)****, was originally developed in the United
Kingdom under the leadership of Dr. Suman Fernando and other critical
psychiatrists and survivor-advocates. It was part of a broader inquiry
into the epistemic, social, and clinical consequences of psychiatric
labeling and contributed significantly to the eventual renaming of ISPS,
International Society for Psychological and Social Approaches to
Psychosis, which officially removed the term schizophrenia from its
title in recognition of its problematic and stigmatizing legacy. The
Spanish adaptation used in this thesis was reviewed and revalidated by
local experts, whose contributions ensured contextual relevance,
terminological clarity, and epistemological alignment with Spanish
clinical, legal, and social realities. This validation process included
both linguistic adjustments and content calibration to prevent
inadvertent reinforcement of diagnostic violence or cultural distortion.

Delving in deeper depth in the first major survey informing this
dissertation, the iquiry originally coordinated in the United Kingdom by
a distinguished team of survivors, professionals, and critical scholars
including ****Professor Suman Fernando, Dr. Jayasree Kalathil, Dr.
Philip Thomas, and Dr. Janet Wallcraft, we find**** an unprecedented
initiative to systematically document the personal, institutional, and
social consequences of receiving a diagnosis of alleged schizophrenia,
with the aim of exposing its damaging effects and questioning the
legitimacy of its use in modern mental health systems (Kalathil &
Fernando, 2012). The ISL was built through testimony-based research,
inviting submissions from those with lived experience of the label,
their families, and professionals across the United Kingdom. It was
widely disseminated and remains a landmark in user/survivor-led
knowledge production, combining deep epistemological insight with
political urgency. The report had a transformative impact on public and
academic discourse, helping to precipitate the ****International Society
for the Psychological and Social Approaches to Psychosis (ISPS)****
decision to remove alleged schizophrenia from its name. It also helped
consolidate a paradigm shift toward trauma-informed, rights-based, and
culturally sensitive better ways to diagnostic psychiatry.

The Spanish version of this Inquiry was launched and adapted
independently by the present researcher during the early stages of
postgraduate study, prior to the official beginning of this doctoral
work, with input from members of the Spanish collective LoComún
(Fernández, 2018). We expanded the number of question, adapting it to
the Spanish reality. However, it was methodologically consistent and
ethically aligned with the original effort, and became a central
component of this dissertation's evidentiary base. The ****survey was
distributed both online and by post****, following open science
principles and open-source technical implementation. Thousands of
individuals across Spain -including professionals, survivors, users, and
family members -were reached via a comprehensive distribution effort to
almost all public mental health centers, support associations, some
direct contacts, and most known activist networks. This adaptation
retained the testimonial richness and critical openness of the original
Inquiry, with items focusing on the meaning of diagnosis, its perceived
effects, the experience of coercion, and the perceived better ways to
current systems. It foregrounded the voices of those marginalized and
criminalized by diagnostic practices, and thus contributed directly to
the core aims of this research: exposing systemic violence, contesting
the epistemological dominance of biomedical psychiatry, and advancing a
model of shared decision-making and patient autonomy rooted in ethics,
dignity, and justice.

The second survey, focused on *open dialogue in Spain*, was validated by
a national team of practitioners and researchers actively involved in
open dialogue implementation, dissemination, and training. Its
development followed a consultative model grounded in the lived
expertise of clinicians engaged in dialogical practices, particularly
those who participated in national meetings and postgraduate education
programs facilitated by the researcher. Given the diverse institutional
pathways through which open dialogue has been introduced in Spain, the
survey was carefully reviewed to reflect the heterogeneity of
implementation experiences and regional regulatory differences
(Valtanen, 2019). In the context of Spain, where overdiagnosis,
overmedication, and systemic institutionalization remain widespread, the
open dialogue model has emerged as both a therapeutic and sociopolitical
better. It provides a culturally grounded and clinically viable
framework for resisting coercion and fostering collective
responsibility. Terminological choices, questions on training access,
and institutional barriers were refined to enhance resonance with the
Spanish professional and administrative context (Parrabera-García et al,
2023).

Before launching the survey, the team actively participated in a
****national census effort led by HopenDialogue****[^3], a European
project promoting dialogical practices across health systems. This
census aimed to document all professionals, services, and informal
initiatives linked to open dialogue in Spain (Pocobello et al, 2025). As
part of that process,the researcher contributed a comprehensive list of
contacts gathered over years of engagement -comprising ****hundreds of
clinicians, educators, researchers, and activists**** who had expressed
sustained interest in dialogical care. Through this participatory
mapping, the team reached nearly every professional in the country who
had either trained in or supported the open dialogue approach. The
census established a baseline, documenting the scattered but growing
community of dialogically trained professionals and their placement
within public and private services. Building upon this foundational
work, the o****pen dialogue Professionals Survey**** was conceptualized
as a second-stage empirical effort. Its objective was not simply to
assess knowledge or compliance, but to explore the lived tensions,
ethical obstacles, and latent potential of dialogical care within
Spain's often rigid institutional landscape. It asked: What happens
after the training ends? How do professionals navigate moral distress,
institutional contradiction, and patient expectations in daily practice?
The survey, designed and distributed in 2023, was structured around six
thematic axes: (1) exposure to coercive practices in institutions; (2)
fidelity to dialogical principles in practice; (3) ethical tensions and
institutional resistance; (4) experiences with shared decision-making;
(5) perceptions of patient voice and autonomy; and (6) systemic and
legal barriers to transformation. A total of ****35 questions****
-including multiple open-ended prompts -were included, allowing for
qualitative and quantitative insight.

The third survey, *Shared Decision-Making and Medication Use in
Psychiatry*, was subjected to the most extensive international
consultation process. Over one hundred experts, including senior
psychiatrists, social scientists, policymakers, and user-survivors,
provided feedback. Notably, Peter Lehmann (2010), internationally
recognized advocate for psychiatric drug withdrawal and ethical
medication governance, contributed targeted feedback that led to the
strengthening of sections on responsible deprescribing, autonomy, and
trauma-informed practice. This survey incorporated best practices from
global deprescription research and was adjusted to accommodate the
particular tensions within the Spanish system, including resistance to
non-pharmacological care and the lack of national guidelines on shared
decision-making. Distributed during an ongoing governmnetal national
debate on responsible use of psychiatric drugs, the survey presented,
among other questions, the following scenarios that brought to attention
some of the failure points and sources of controvery of the current
system:

National review of the use of neuroleptics in children and adolescents****                                 Addresses developmental and ethical risks in pediatric neuroleptic use, often without sufficient differential diagnosis.           To document professional stances on deprescribing in young populations, perceived risk-benefit ratios, and the educational, familial, and systemic supports required for safer transitions.
  ****8. Ending the use of neuroleptics for non-psychiatric indications in general medicine****                     Challenges routine but clinically inappropriate neuroleptic use in general hospital and somatic care contexts.                     To assess inter-specialty communication, guideline awareness, and mechanisms for error correction and deprescribing in non-psychiatric settings.
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This table outlines eight hypothetical scenarios included in the
national survey to explore professionals' responses to ethically,
medically, and institutionally significant reform propositions. Each
scenario was designed to elicit reactions to systemic shortcomings,
ranging from diagnostic practices and interdisciplinary coordination to
institutional violence and overmedication, and to assess readiness for
change, ethical positioning, and structural awareness. The scenarios
served as a methodological tool to examine not only individual attitudes
but also the perceived feasibility of implementing rights-based,
evidence-informed reforms within psychiatric and general medical
practice.

Across all three instruments, ethical safeguards were prioritized.
Informed consent was implemented dynamically, with detailed information
about the purpose, data use, and confidentiality protocols provided
upfront. Respondents could exit at any point, and anonymity was ensured
using encrypted data collection platforms. Ethics review followed a
multi-layered strategy involving informal advisory from international
collaborators and rights-based research collectives, compensating for
the absence of consistent institutional support during the study period.
These validation and ethical measures ensure that the surveys do not
merely gather data, but constitute methodologically sound, contextually
attuned, and ethically grounded instruments of action-research. These
surveys provided not only empirical depth but also participatory
legitimacy to the thesis\'s central claim: that psychiatry in Spain
ought to transition from coercive and opaque structures toward
collaborative, transparent, and rights-based systems of care. Through
these instruments, the research established a multi-voiced archive of
institutional critique and constructive proposals, grounded in
scientifically sound, ethically robust, and culturally adapted
methodology.

Across the three surveys deployed during the research, the combined
reach extended to several thousand individuals, yielding a total of
approximately seven thousand responses; 400, 200, and 90 respectively.
This included broad national dissemination within Spain and targeted
engagement with professionals, users, and advocates across relevant
networks. The final survey alone, focused on shared decision-making,
psychiatric medication, and deprescribing, was answered in full by
ninety professionals and experts, many of whom contributed extensive
narrative responses. Based on average response duration, over 41
minutes, the accumulated time dedicated to answering this instrument
exceeded by far the one hundred hours of expert input poured in. This
represents a formidable repository of grounded, contextualized, and
profession-specific knowledge, barely tapped in the present
dissertation, as the wealth is enourmous and spans beyond the thesis
topic. The vast majority of invitees to this last survey were members of
the **Asociación Española de Neuropsiquiatría** (AEN)[^4], widely
recognized as the primary professional association for critical and
community psychiatry in Spain, CIBER members, the excellence mental
health national network, and Spanish published experts in psychistry.
Most are respected authors of peer-reviewed scientific papers and
influential books on psychiatric practice, ethics, and systemic reform.
Their contributions capture the current dilemmas and barriers within the
Spanish psychiatric system, as well as articulations of best practice
and proposals for structural change. These surveys, therefore,
constitute more than data collection tools: they are participatory
instruments of knowledge production that generate a high-density,
multidisciplinary archive of ethical, clinical, and systemic insights
indispensable for the translational objectives of this dissertation.

Additionally, an informal fourth exploratory survey was sent via email
to all non-Christian religious organizations officially registered in
Spain, aiming to gather indicative data on their mental health
challenges, structural marginalization, and access to spiritual
practices in a context predominantly shaped by Christian norms and
secular public institutions. The responses---although limited in number
and unevenly distributed across traditions---offered valuable insights
into the lived experiences of religious minorities, including a small
number of Buddhist, Hindu, and other non-mainstream international
communities. The aim was gauging how minorities feel and operate in the
country. Most organizations reported significant constraints in
accessing dedicated spaces for prayer, meditation, or retreat, often
facing bureaucratic obstacles, neighborhood resistance, or neglect in
municipal planning. These limitations were described as directly
affecting the psychological well-being, community cohesion, and
intergenerational transmission of cultural identity. This survey was
inspired by the use of sensory rooms in some wards in Sweden, and the
need to have such safe spaces to meditate, relax and find inner peace,
reflect and recollect, in urban settings, out-patient, open for
everyone, beyond regular church. While the sample was not representative
in a statistical sense, the findings aligned with broader themes in this
dissertation regarding the structural invisibility and epistemic
marginalization of non-dominant groups. Respondents highlighted that the
lack of institutional recognition and culturally safe spaces for
contemplation or spiritual care contributed to distress, alienation, and
a diminished capacity to support members facing mental health crises.
These testimonies reinforce the relevance of a bio-cultural and
rights-based approach to mental health, one that includes freedom of
belief, ritual, and narrative as essential elements of psychological
resilience and human dignity. The results of this survey will be
presented in Chapter 3, as part of the broader empirical mapping of
exclusion, silencing, and unmet care needs within plural Spanish society
(Heim, 2016).

In addition to yielding empirical data, the surveys function as
translational outputs in themselves. Their validated versions, adapted
to the Spanish context and ethically reviewed, can be re-used in
clinical teaching, professional training, or rights-based service
evaluation across Spain and comparable contexts. Their public
availability, where permitted, contributes to the open science agenda
articulated in this dissertation. All instruments are now available in
the dissertation annexes, and will soon be made available in the
dissertation online repository. Their structure and content already
serve as foundation for expert systems and computational models proposed
in later chapters, particularly in the areas of medication governance,
legal mapping, and user-professional negotiation interfaces. In this
way, the surveys link qualitative inquiry with scalable implementation
tools, demonstrating methodological continuity from lived experience to
system-level intervention. On top of this use, experts had the chance to
request participating in further research and trainings, and most did
so, allowing for further participatory action-research informed by them
in the future.

It must be noted that a very significant majority of those surveyed,
comprising both mental health professionals and service users, expressed
shared concerns regarding the pervasive overreliance on pharmacological
interventions within current care systems. Participants consistently
pointed to a systemic tendency to prioritize medication as the primary,
and often sole, response to psychological distress. This was frequently
accompanied by a striking lack of access to better modalities of care,
particularly those rooted in psychological and social support. The
findings suggest a widespread recognition of the limitations inherent in
medication-centric models, with calls from both groups for more
comprehensive, person-centered approaches that include talk therapies,
community-based resources, and socially grounded interventions (Holmes &
Marcus, 2008).

## **2.4 Field strategy and sites of observation**

The methodological architecture of this dissertation emerges from a
deliberate fusion of medical anthropology, clinical ethics, bio-cultural
analysis, open science, and trans-disciplinary action-research. It is
not a retrospective narrative nor a technical compartmentalization of
methods, but a structured epistemological and political act of knowledge
production grounded in conditions of systemic adversity. The research
design and dissertation construction were developed as interconnected
dimensions of the same scientific process, governed by explicit
theoretical commitments and the ethical imperative to intervene, not
merely describe. These commitments informed every procedural decision,
from field engagement to analytical validation, ensuring that the study
remained faithful to the complex, often violent realities it was
constructed to document and transform. Core frameworks introduced in the
first sections of this chapter, as well as Chapter 1, provided the
foundational logic of integration. The bio-cultural paradigm demanded
that mental suffering and resilience be read as co-constituted by
social, environmental, legal, and biological forces. The open science
infrastructure ensured that all methodological iterations, decisions,
and evidence trails were timestamped, logged, and in many cases publicly
accessible through encrypted or version-controlled systems. This
transparency was not aesthetic or bureaucratic, but protective and
epistemologically necessary, as the research was repeatedly threatened
by institutional repression, material loss, and personal harm. Human
rights principles, epistemic justice theory, and structural violence
analysis further defined the ethical stakes of the work, guiding not
only data collection and analysis, but the very legitimacy of the
categories, interpretations, and claims advanced throughout the study
****(Peterson & Runyan, 2010)****.

The work of Paul Farmer, Nancy Scheper-Hughes, Suman Fernando, and Byron
Good, among others, underpinned a methodological commitment that
rejected the position of detached observer. Instead, the research was
carried out through embedded participation in collectives, policy
processes, professional task forces, and activist-scientific coalitions
(****Good, 1994; ****Fernando, 2017). These included the coordination of
EU-level networks, the leadership of scientific actions, and ongoing
roles in field-defining working groups in Spain, Indonesia, and beyond.
Methodologically, this positioning enabled a form of analytical access
and ethical fidelity that no detached standpoint could replicate. Like
Farmer, the researcher's commitment to proximity and engagement provided
not only data, but critical insight into how institutions respond, fail,
adapt, or silence in the face of ethical challenge. This was not
auxiliary to the research, it was the field, the method, and the
validation. Each phase of writing, coding, and synthesis was embedded in
this logic of engaged knowledge. Scientific representation was
continuously cross-checked against testimonies, policy materials, and
expert consultations, ensuring internal coherence and external
accountability. Drafts were developed through recursive cycles of
analysis and revision, grounded in feedback from survivors, clinicians,
legal scholars, anthropologists, and community networks. This recursive,
multi-modal process allowed the dissertation to evolve in parallel with
the field conditions, without compromising scientific rigor or empirical
traceability. Methodological decisions were subjected to version control
and meta-analytical commentary, ensuring that the structure of the
dissertation reflected not only its content but its conditions of
emergence.

A full paper by the researcher on ethics in qualitative research is
added in the annexes. What distinguishes the methodology employed is not
only its grounding in formal frameworks, but its embodiment of the
ethics those frameworks demand ****(Miles & Freedman, 2023)****. In the
face of erasure, displacement, and systemic retaliation, methodological
fidelity required resilience, creativity, and adaptive precision. The
dissertation includes not only data analysis, but the documentation of
the conditions under which knowledge was produced. These include forced
mobility, chronic threat, physical violence, and institutional betrayal.
Despite these conditions, or precisely because of them, the research
protocols remained intact through protective networks, epistemic
tracking tools, and collective memory practices. These are not marginal
notes, they are the necessary infrastructure of research in conditions
of organized neglect and political denial. Throughout the development of
this dissertation, institutional support was not simply absent, it was
at times actively obstructive (Roberts, 2000). Critical phases of the
research were marked by hostility, neglect, and disavowal from
universities, medical institutions, and public authorities, even while
certain government bodies in Mexico, Catalonia, and Spain expressed
official interest in inviting the researcher, supporting mental health
transformation. This contradiction underscores a deep structural
inconsistency, in which the declared commitment to scientific progress,
public health, and global agendas such as Madrid proposing itself once
to become in its entirety a blue zone, is rendered meaningless by the
refusal to ensure the basic safety of researchers, informants, and
participants -the researcher keeps on persevering; supporting the true
commendable, working on through stronger networks and better funding
****(Miles & Freedman, 2023)****. The disconnect between rhetorical
promises and operational reality, though, is not only a tragic
administrative oversight that almost cost its life and that of many
others -all, never achieving the best strived to achieve-, it is an
ethical and epistemic failure. It is impossible to produce or apply
meaningful reform if those responsible for documenting harm are
simultaneously exposed to new harm by the very systems they aim to
improve (Gupta‑Wright, 2018).

The methodological frameworks developed in Chapter 1 and grounded in the
principles articulated at the beginning of Chapter 2 were not optional
lenses but essential tools for navigating and resisting this reality.
The integration of medical anthropology, action research, human rights,
and open science created a scaffold from which to both protect and
articulate the work of knowledge production under siege. The logic of
this dissertation is inseparable from the political and structural
conditions in which it was written. Rather than compromise its
scientific validity, this embeddedness strengthens its claim to
relevance, rigor, and necessity. Each theoretical commitment, from
epistemic justice to trans-disciplinary ethics, was enacted through
methodological decisions that resisted extraction, protected vulnerable
knowledge-holders, and sustained the ethical obligation to intervene
when life and dignity were at risk. Crucially, the methodological stance
adopted throughout this research moves beyond passive observation and
toward the embedded, collaborative, and translational engagement
championed by figures such as Paul Farmer. Just as Farmer insisted that
medical anthropologists and clinicians ought to position themselves not
as neutral observers but as active agents of systemic change, this
dissertation was constructed through direct participation in research
networks, advocacy platforms, survivor collectives, and scientific
consortia. These included leading and contributing to transnational
efforts such as EU COST actions ReMO[^5], and FOSTREN[^6], where the
researcher's role was never marginal but consistently generative,
strategic, and co-responsible, never mere academic endeavours. This
collective work allowed for scientific cross-checking, mutual
verification, and iterative design refinement, often in contexts where
traditional institutional support had collapsed or turned punitive.
These networks became not only research environments but ethical
shelters, allowing the work to continue when isolation and erasure
threatened its very possibility.

Under such conditions of extreme duress and sadistic enjoyment of others
on the researcher suffering, the call for justice is not an abstraction.
It is an operational precondition for the continuity of any ethical and
scientifically robust system of knowledge production (Bolade-Ogunfodun,
Soga, & Laker, 2023). No society can legitimately claim a future of
peace, sustainability, and social flourishing while criminal impunity,
institutional complicity, and structural neglect remain unchallenged.
What is required is not generosity from systems that have long failed,
but enforcement of the law and the removal of actors who have undermined
truth, well-being, and the possibility of health itself. The demand is
not naive, it is technical, ethical, and necessary. This dissertation,
forged in adversity and shaped by solidarity, documents the costs of
current dysfunctions and proposes a pathway for their systemic
transformation. Its methodology, grounded in situated action, scientific
rigor, and participatory ethics, is itself part of the infrastructure
needed to reach the future that policy documents and public discourse
claim to pursue. Only through full recognition of these truths can the
academic, clinical, and social systems begin to align with the values
they profess to defend.

The coming chronological exposition, structured year by year and month
by month, is a methodological extension of this architecture. It reveals
how research unfolded, not as a neutral progression of inquiry, but as a
series of ruptures, accelerations, and strategic adaptations. It traces
how ethics, science, and survival were managed simultaneously, and how
embedded engagement with institutional and grassroots actors made the
work not only possible, but scientifically and ethically credible
(Kidder, 2003). In this way, the dissertation enacts a methodology of
refusal against silence, extraction, and institutional complicity, and
affirms the power of bio-cultural, action-oriented science to generate
not just knowledge, but the possibility of justice.

In 2020, despite continuous institutional violence and a context of
coercion, including forced medication, psychiatric abuse, and severe
bodily violations, the researcher secured a national predoctoral
contract and began work at Universitat Rovira i Virgili under six-year
ministerial funding. Throughout 2020, during COVID-19 lockdowns, they
participated in high-level international collaborations, including with
SURE at King's College London, the Mexican Parliament Forum on mental
health and human rights, and the EU COST FOSTREN action on ending
coercion. The researcher also co-coordinated a postgraduate course on
Open Dialogue at Blanquerna-Ramon Llull University and was appointed
global liaison for **Mad in America**. These achievements took place
under conditions of ongoing confinement and systemic abuse, highlighting
both the resilience and the precarity of academic engagement under
extreme duress.

The researcher barely survived the year 2022. In September 2022, the
researcher conducted one month of immersive ethnographic fieldwork in
Trieste, Italy, following a preparatory phase of local familiarization.
Using shadowing and key informant interviews within a medical
anthropology framework, the study documented real-time practices in
WHO-recognized community psychiatry settings. Embedded in daily routines
across residential units, community centers, and mobile teams, the
researcher observed non-coercive care dynamics and institutional
cultures shaped by deinstitutionalization. Supplemented by interviews
with professionals and service users, and participation in public
forums, the fieldwork yielded critical insights into relational care,
governance, and the operational tensions of the Trieste model.
