In 2024--2025, the researcher prepared ethnographic fieldwork in
Indonesia as a visiting scholar at Universitas Muhammadiyah Yogyakarta
(UMY), focusing on the abolition of **pasung, **the domestic confinement
of people in mental distress. Through interviews and observation, the
study framed **pasung** as a structural outcome of systemic neglect,
mirroring global psychiatric coercion under different guises. The
research connects historical colonial violence, gendered oppression, and
mental health inequality, calling for the abolition of all forms of
coercive care through rights-based, culturally rooted, and community-led
approaches.

The fieldwork conducted in Trieste and Yogyakarta grounds the research
questions in two distinct yet structurally connected settings. In
Trieste, sustained observation and interviews within a historically
non-coercive community-based mental health system revealed the fragility
of reform when bureaucratic demands and clinical discretion challenge
relational care. This directly informs the questions on how coercion
persists despite formal commitments to rights-based models. In
Indonesia, the study of pasung illuminated coercion as a symptom of
systemic abandonment, where families resort to confinement in the
absence of safe and trusted services. This reframes coercion as not only
institutional but domestic and structurally induced. Both cases
reinforce the central research aim: to identify how coercive practices
are produced, legitimized, or resisted across systems, and what
conditions are required to support ethical, participatory mental health
care.

## **2.5 Ethical protocols and methodological dilemmas**

The ethical governance of this research was conducted under conditions
of structural violence, institutional complicity, and personal
endangerment that render conventional research ethics committee
procedures insufficient (Banks et al., 2013). The normative assumption
of institutional neutrality, stability of context, and the disconnection
between researcher and researched does not hold in inquiries involving
prolonged human rights violations, coercive psychiatric practices, and
institutional retaliation. Under such circumstances, procedural approval
from standard committees offers limited epistemic or protective
validity. It was necessary to develop a parallel framework of ethical
rigor based on relational responsibility, trauma-sensitive engagement,
and scientific accountability (Schneider, 2012). The ethics applied in
this study exceed institutional compliance and instead reflect the
substantive moral architecture needed when research is itself situated
in fields of harm and resistance (Minkler & Wallerstein, 2008).

Three principles structured the ethical design. The first was relational
ethics, grounding scientific work in responsibility to those whose
suffering and testimony constitute the material of inquiry. This
required that every stage of data collection, from surveys to field
observation, include embedded mechanisms for participant control,
opt-out, and narrative refusal. The second was trauma-informed ethics,
acknowledging that engagement with survivors and professionals in
contexts of iatrogenesis, institutional betrayal, or legal abandonment
demands methods that minimize re-traumatization (Kemmis & McTaggart,
2000). Open-ended questions were structured to permit selective
engagement and avoid prescriptive formats that might trigger collapse,
dissociation, or distress. The third was the principle of non-extractive
ethics, in which participants\' contributions are not treated as passive
data sources but as co-generators of critical epistemology. This ethical
model required the researcher to approach participants as interlocutors
within a shared diagnostic, legal, and social terrain, producing
knowledge about psychiatric governance from within its zones of friction
and denial.

Methodological dilemmas arose continuously and were resolved through the
implementation of dynamic ethical protocols (McTaggart, 1991). These
protocols governed situations in which participants disclosed ongoing
risk, exposure to violence, or systemic abandonment. Rather than
applying mandated reporting frameworks that risked reinforcing
psychiatric control or institutional containment, the researcher
prioritized informed support measures grounded in consent and
non-reinstitutionalizing logic. In parallel, epistemic verification
structures were constructed to protect the empirical integrity of the
data under conditions of legal precarity, potential censorship, and
retrospective institutional erasure ****(Kortmann, 2010)****.
Timestamping of field interactions, public versioning of survey
instruments, and mirrored data storage ensured that both participant
accounts and analytical conclusions would be resilient against loss,
tampering, or suppression. These mechanisms reflect a scientific
commitment to both traceability and justice in knowledge production,
extending the obligations of academic transparency into fields where
formal ethics procedures have proven structurally inadequate
****(Flaherty et al., 1988)****.

Given the researcher's direct exposure to long-term psychiatric
coercion, institutional retaliation, and physical and psychological
endangerment, safety procedures were indispensable not only for personal
survival but also for the continuation of research. Protective
strategies included the use of shared coworking environments to reduce
vulnerability, strict structuring of movement and working hours,
nutritional monitoring to mitigate cognitive decline or exhaustion, and
avoidance of any contact with actors linked to prior aggression or legal
manipulation ****(Hollan, 1997)****. These protocols were not optional
but structurally imposed by the research context itself, in which the
investigator operated under prolonged exposure to threats that
constituted not hypothetical risks but documented and ongoing harm
(Russo, 2012). Under such conditions, ethics becomes not an external
requirement but the precondition for the possibility of knowledge at
all. The researcher\'s dual positionality as professional, survivor, and
target demanded constant negotiation between the commitment to rigorous,
reproducible analysis and the need for self-preservation in a
compromised and adversarial system (Baum, MacDougall, & Smith, 2006;
Honey et al., 2020).

The operationalization of these ethical foundations is further
elaborated in a scientific article accepted for publication in a leading
international journal, as already noted Rose, 2008). That work
formalizes the conceptual and methodological model underlying this
thesis, offering a framework for future research conducted under
analogous conditions of structural and institutional violence. The
innovations presented in this dissertation, including the integration of
trauma-informed consent, dynamic field response protocols, and epistemic
protection mechanisms, constitute an applied ethical infrastructure
capable of supporting scientifically robust, politically accountable,
and humanely grounded psychiatric research. The work affirms that it is
not sufficient to avoid harm. It is necessary to document it, name it,
and construct scientific systems that refuse to reproduce it in silence
or complicity. This ethical architecture undergirds the entire research
design and defines its scientific integrity. The ethical dimension of
this dissertation cannot be confined to conventional formulations or
institutional templates. It emerges instead as a direct response to a
research process carried out under sustained personal and professional
duress, marked by exposure to psychological torture, structural
violence, and the ongoing degradation of basic legal and human rights.
These are not isolated episodes but defining conditions of the field
itself. This section therefore presents a reflexive reconstruction of
what was ethically required but often unavailable, what was enacted in
place of absent protections, and what future research ought to
institutionalize to avoid replicating the violence it seeks to describe
(Tadesse et al., 2022).

**Table 28. Ethical infrastructure developed under conditions of
structural violence**

  -------------------------------- ------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ****Informed consent****         One-time, static consent                   Assumes stability, lacks adaptivity to trauma or ongoing risks          Dynamic, revisable consent with continuous option to withdraw; consent embedded in narrative flow
  ****Risk assessment****          Anticipatory, based on hypothetical harm   Ignores real-time and systemic risks, particularly from institutions    Situational risk protocols, field reflexivity, and real-time monitoring of retraumatization signals
  ****Participant protection****   Anonymization, withdrawal rights           Inadequate under surveillance, legal persecution, or medical coercion   Multi-site encrypted archiving, role-adapted anonymity, and external verification to prevent deletion
  ****Ethical oversight****        Approval by centralized REC                Non-responsive to evolving abuses, often inaccessible or politicized    Peer-reviewed ethical documentation, network-based advisory from survivors and professionals
  ****Researcher safety****        Presumed unnecessary or external           Researcher exposed to torture, defamation, and institutional violence   Structured safety routines (nutrition, space, timing), embedded protection practices, withdrawal from high-risk zones
  ****Duty to intervene****        Prohibited in many REC guidelines          Ethical paralysis under documented harm                                 Justified ethical action: alerts to authorities, protective coordination, direct advocacy for at-risk individuals
  ****Data integrity****           Institutional data storage                 Risk of deletion, falsification, or obstruction                         Timestamping, public versioning, decentralized storage, open science mirroring and backups
  ****Trauma sensitivity****       Basic care to avoid retraumatization       Incomplete without survivor-led input                                   Co-designed instruments, trauma-informed narrative structuring, optionality in expression
  -------------------------------- ------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Summary of the limitations of conventional ethics frameworks and the
better procedures developed in this dissertation to uphold scientific,
relational, and trauma-informed integrity under systemic threat. This
infrastructure reflects a research ethics adapted to real conditions of
institutional betrayal, psychiatric violence, and professional
retaliation, where both researcher and participants faced risks of
silencing, misrepresentation, or death.

The research was undertaken -at times- in spaces where harm was not
hypothetical, where others had been institutionalized against their
will, misdiagnosed, or subjected to irreversible pharmacological damage,
while the researcher, too, faced threats to life, health, and legal
personhood (Lehmann, 2024). Others remained at risk throughout the study
period, and their testimonies required careful handling not only for
ethical reasons but for reasons of basic safety. In such circumstances,
conventional ethics approval procedures offered little. Research ethics
committees operate from a presumption of institutional safety and
stability that was structurally incompatible with the real conditions of
the work. Their protocols presume that risks are discrete, containable,
and primarily emotional or procedural (****Fisher, 2012****). They do
not address how to proceed when the risk is systemic, unrelenting, and
politically embedded. As such, this research adopted an ethics
infrastructure grounded in necessity and iterative adaptation.
Relational ethics were prioritized throughout, establishing trust
through extended contact, cultural sensitivity, and sustained presence.
All consent was treated as dynamic rather than static, with participants
able to revise or withdraw their input at any stage. Trauma-informed
principles were applied not only to protect participants but to ensure
that the research process itself did not reproduce the harm it sought to
document. These principles guided the design of interview protocols, the
structure of surveys, and the researcher's conduct in high-risk
situations (Hultman & Hultman, 2023).

Survival strategies became integral to the research method. These
included strict attention to nutrition, sleep, environmental control,
digital hygiene, and the strategic use of coworking spaces to avoid
isolation and exposure (Meloni et al., 2015). Such routines were not
accessories to the fieldwork but preconditions for continuing it
(Gabriel & Casemore, 2022). The physical and psychological toll of
documenting systemic violence from within cannot be overstated
(Clandinin, Caine, & Lessard, 2018). In many instances, the continuation
of the research depended not on institutional support but on the
cultivation of micropractices of endurance and minimal restoration.

These notes do not propose an better ethics framework as a complete
solution. Rather, they document the real procedural and epistemic gaps
that emerge when ethics is reduced to compliance. The annexes of this
dissertation include a peer-reviewed scientific contribution that
systematizes these insights. Here they are presented as a necessary part
of methodological transparency. Ethics under structural duress requires
a new infrastructure, one that begins not with the assumption of
institutional safety but with the recognition of its absence (Hemer,
2023). Until such systems are in place, the burden of ethical innovation
will continue to fall on individual researchers working beyond
protection, in terrains where knowledge production is inseparable from
survival. This is not sustainable. It is also not avoidable. For
research to be ethical under real conditions of harm, it ought to become
a tool of active protection, not passive observation. The procedures
developed here represent one such attempt, made under constraint, with
full awareness of its insufficiencies and with the hope that it may
serve others working in conditions where silence has become fatal.

## 

## **2.6 Data integration and analytical logic**

The integration and processing of data in this dissertation were carried
out under conditions that profoundly disrupted the basic assumptions of
continuity, safety, and institutional support typically underlying
empirical research ****(Rose & Webb, 1997)****. At various stages, the
researcher was subject to repeated acts of physical and psychological
violence, including episodes consistent with clinical definitions of
torture (Mollica, 2004; Méndez, 2013). These conditions of violence led
too to the loss of digital equipment, personal records, and project
materials. Several computers were irretrievably damaged or confiscated,
backups destroyed or rendered inaccessible, and analytic environments
had to be repeatedly reconstructed in the aftermath of coercive
displacement or forced migration. These experiences, far from
peripheral, constituted the factual terrain of research execution
(Hermann & Provost, 2003). They informed not only methodological
constraints but also the interpretive logic that underpins the thesis.
The baseline conditions of knowledge production were those of exposure,
violation, and degradation. Under such circumstances, the preservation
of analytic coherence and the continuity of triangulation were not
guaranteed by infrastructure but required improvisational resilience,
adaptive logic, and trans-disciplinary solidarity.

Data management protocols were necessarily reduced to their most
essential and recoverable components. No centralized institutional
infrastructure could be used. Confidentiality was preserved through
decentralized storage systems and physical partitioning of content
across trusted jurisdictions. No identifiable information was retained
in active analytic corpora. Manual encryption methods were deployed
where digital tools were unavailable, and content-sensitive materials
were handled with protocols designed not only to comply with ethical
expectations but to avoid further endangering the lives of collaborators
or respondents. Digital notebooks, when operational, were maintained in
modular snapshots, allowing for asynchronous reconstruction of
analytical steps. Version control was applied manually through dated
annotation in plain text and locally encrypted files. Every document was
treated as potentially subject to intrusion, erasure, or forced
disclosure (Michener, 2015). Data minimization was enforced as a
structural requirement, not as a methodological preference.

Open-science principles were upheld to the extent compatible with
safety. Documentation was maintained in reproducible form, but
distribution remained restricted until the relevant risks abated. The
researcher's role in coordinating and leading various international
networks and task forces, particularly under the EU BEACON One Health
Education initiative and related COST Actions, proved essential in
safeguarding analytic validity (Sullivan et al., 2019). These roles
provided access to experts across psychiatry, anthropology,
computational ethics, and legal studies, who offered feedback,
methodological review, and triangulation support when institutional
resources were unavailable or actively obstructive (Simmons, 2025).
Collaboration with these experts was not a formalized institutional
process but a strategic necessity to ensure the epistemic integrity of
the work. These alliances allowed the research to continue through
episodes of forced displacement, institutional harassment, and prolonged
interpersonal destabilization caused by individuals enacting cruelty
under the guise of caregiving, victimhood, or professional concern.
(Allen & Mehler, 2019) The violence experienced was not only physical
but structural, extending its corrosive effects to the ethical standing
and practical continuity of the research.

Triangulation was achieved through analytical proximity rather than data
volume. Thematic confirmation was accepted only when the pattern was
traceable across at least three data layers and consistent with external
literature or practitioner testimony ****(Farmer, Robinson, Elliott, &
Eyles, 2006)****. Particular emphasis was placed on the correlation
between first-person accounts and legal-structural conditions. For
example, narrative reports of institutional silence or coercion were not
only coded as testimonial evidence but assessed against statutory
protections, clinical guidelines, and observed professional behavior
within field settings. Discrepancies between institutional claims and
lived experience were analytically foregrounded, not treated as
interpretive anomalies. These divergences were mapped and indexed within
the coding system to document the structural dissonance between official
policy and actual practice.

Reflexivity was not articulated in abstract epistemological terms but
constituted a methodological core. The analytic stance of the researcher
evolved through cycles of loss, reassembly, exposure, and partial
recovery (Munir & Staats, 2020). Shifts in interpretive position were
recorded in marginalia and analytic logs. Reflexive annotations were
revisited at each synthesis stage to determine whether interpretive
adjustments reflected epistemic maturation, trauma distortion, or
strategic recalibration (Dingwall, 1997). These annotations were not
post hoc justifications but concurrent field entries, forming part of a
real-time record of analytic experience under threat. Particular
attention was given to the limits of interpretation during acute periods
of violence or malnutrition. Analyses produced during such periods were
subject to later verification, checked against both literature and
external expert commentary, and retained only when their methodological
soundness could be independently confirmed. Cross-checking procedures
included direct engagement with the literature, correspondence with
academic and clinical experts, and critical comparison with
institutional documentation. Published guidelines, peer-reviewed
studies, and national legal instruments were used as reference points
for verifying thematic claims. Where thematic codes intersected with
known psychiatric controversies or legal precedents, documentary review
was intensified to avoid extrapolation (Alvesson & Sköldberg, 2000).
Informants with institutional or clinical experience were consulted
through anonymized exchanges to validate the contextual interpretation
of field-derived material. No claim was incorporated into the final
analytical corpus without at least one layer of corroboration beyond the
initial data source.

This dissertation's analytical logic, therefore, reflects not only the
complexity of the subject matter but the existential and epistemological
conditions of its own emergence. Knowledge was not extracted but
salvaged, not observed from a distance but reconstructed from within a
collapsing architecture of care and research. The analytic outputs that
follow do not represent an ideal analytic pathway but an ethically
necessary and scientifically rigorous traversal through contexts of
obstruction, degradation, and partial restoration. The triangulated
structure, reflexive protocols, and distributed verification model
embedded in this chapter constitute both a methodological map and a
procedural archive of knowledge produced under repression.

## **2.7 Limitations, adverse conditions, and scientific validity**

The execution of this research was marked by continuous and often
life-threatening exposure to violence, coercion, and institutional
betrayal. These adverse conditions were not episodic disruptions but
systemic and cumulative, shaping every phase of the study. The fieldwork
was conducted under conditions of extreme duress, including physical
assault, forced sedation, psychological degradation, and repeated
displacement across jurisdictions. At various stages, the researcher was
subjected to medical procedures without consent, including drugging,
misdiagnosis, and acts of chemical restraint. These events occurred
within a broader context of institutional complicity, whereby legal
systems, healthcare institutions, and academic structures either failed
to offer protection or actively contributed to the ongoing harm. These
failures included the refusal of due process, denial of access to
justice, confiscation or destruction of research materials, and
systematic obstruction of scholarly continuity. No university provided
sustained support, no ethics committee assumed responsibility for
mitigating the risks, and legal mechanisms proved structurally incapable
of recognizing or responding to the scale of abuse. It took a lot,
almost the research own life, to document the abuses, torture ongoing,
after that many years of being a reported active crime. This fact is
testament of how urgent and important it is to address and redress the
legal loopholes that allow for victims to be left more and more
vulnerable, and criminals acting with full inpunity.

The psychological consequences of this exposure were not abstract but
somatically and cognitively registered. Periods of executive
dysfunction, memory impairment, and physical exhaustion affected
analytic pacing, material recovery, and documentation integrity. In
several instances, work had to be reconstructed from memory,
reformulated in exile, or safeguarded through encrypted correspondence
with peers. The researcher was at times homeless, reliant on temporary
shelter or hostile environments, and suffered from untreated medical
conditions as a consequence of deliberate neglect and obstruction. These
circumstances represent not merely obstacles to scientific work but a
radical exposure of the political and biopolitical conditions under
which knowledge about psychiatry is allowed to be produced. In a field
concerned with human suffering, coercion, and systemic injustice, the
absence of protective infrastructures for researchers immersed in such
environments constitutes a structural paradox with deep epistemic
implications.

Despite these conditions, the scientific validity of the research
remains intact and demonstrable. The methods applied were not only
adequate to the questions asked but strengthened by the ethical
imperative and existential urgency that accompanied their deployment
(Singer & Baer, 2007). The triangulation between surveys, testimonies,
field observation, and legal documentation ensured analytic robustness.
The research questions were pursued through multiple independent
sources, and claims were only retained after critical comparison with
expert judgment, field evidence, and published literature. Where data
loss occurred due to displacement or material destruction, the
researcher maintained procedural continuity through distributed
verification, iterative cross-checking, and ethical reflexivity
(Scheper-Hughes & Lock, 1987). Every remaining fragment of analysis was
subjected to methodological scrutiny, and interpretive caution was
applied in all inferential steps (Gravlee, 2022). The infrastructure may
have failed, but the epistemic scaffolding was not compromised. This is
evidenced not only in the internal consistency of findings but in the
alignment of results with international evidence, peer-reviewed
consensus, and practitioner testimony.

Far from weakening the study's validity, these conditions intensify its
authenticity and historical relevance. The fact that knowledge was
produced in the same structural context that the study aims to describe,
marked by medical violence, epistemic disqualification, and
institutional abandonment, confers upon the research a depth of
embeddedness and phenomenological fidelity that no idealized academic
distance could replicate. The methodological strategy emerged in
response to adversity, and the knowledge produced reflects the embedded
complexity of living, researching, and surviving within sites of
organized harm. This reflexive entanglement does not dilute the
objectivity of the analysis but clarifies its ethical trajectory. The
research makes no claim to omniscience, but it claims, without
hesitation, its place as a rigorous, ethically anchored, scientifically
coherent intervention into a domain where neutrality has often served to
shield violence. This chapter does not propose that trauma guarantees
truth, nor that suffering in itself validates epistemic claims. It does
argue, however, that scientific knowledge cannot remain blind to the
conditions of its own production, and that structural violence endured
by researchers is not an extrinsic event but an intrinsic aspect of
inquiry in contested fields. The scientific validity of this
dissertation lies not in its adherence to abstract protocols but in its
demonstration that rigorous, participatory, and empirically grounded
research is possible even under repression. The work therefore
constitutes not a deficit model of knowledge, but a contribution to the
methodology of research under structural adversity. It offers both a
diagnosis of systemic failure and a model of survival-informed,
ethically rigorous, and scientifically validated knowledge production.

To ensure scientific rigor while documenting systemic injustice, several
bias-mitigation strategies were employed throughout the research
process, always keeping in check the reality of others in the systems
the researcher endured as a victim. Despite the absence of classical
interviews or audio recordings, excluded to protect participants and the
researcher under conditions of coercion and risk, public expert
presentations and thematic dialogues were conducted and archived,
serving as open-access data sources and triangulation tools, to the best
of the researcher abilities, despite loss of resources being common. The
methodological framework was grounded in mixed methods and action
research theory, but its application in this context required adaptation
to conditions of duress, epistemic risk, and institutional hostility
that rendering almost impossible to keep the materials intact for long
periods of time. The protocols developed, including an online knowledge
base, a public repository for backups and transparency, real-time
analytic profiles, and document triangulation using open source
resorces, are replicable in other constrained research environments and
offer a transferable architecture for future studies documenting
structural violence.

## **2.8 Methodological contribution to transformative open science**

This dissertation concludes its methodological exposition by advancing a
situated and operational framework for transformative open science.
Beyond the mere application of existing protocols, the work constructs
new methodological standards that serve not only scientific validity but
structural justice. The commitment to open data, reproducible
instruments, and version-controlled documentation has been grounded in
an active ethics of participation, reciprocity, and repair. The
methodological logic underlying the project is one of epistemic
inclusivity: recognising that knowledge is not the preserve of
institutions alone, but a shared human capacity forged in experience,
testimony, and struggle. This work integrates both citizen and
non-citizen science. It affirms that the right to produce, access, and
act upon scientific knowledge cannot be restricted by documentation
status, social class, or historical exclusion. Scientific capacity
exists across all groups and can be developed when conditions of dignity
and recognition are established. The research includes those who have
been administratively silenced, forcibly displaced, or institutionally
erased, acknowledging that their knowledge and experience are essential
to understanding systemic violence and generating authentic solutions.
The co-design of instruments, living fieldnotes, and feedback mechanisms
has drawn directly from participants with no formal academic background
but whose embodied knowledge of harm and recovery far exceeds that of
many formally accredited professionals. This integration is not
symbolic. It is structural. Without it, the research would lack
validity, depth, and purpose.

The study introduces a set of methodological and technological tools
grounded in open-source standards and community validation under
development still. Multisited ethnography, structured through saturation
and event-mapping thresholds, is cross-validated through surveys, legal
frameworks, and historical-political context. Testimonial matrices
transform raw notes into actionable syntheses, not through external
abstraction but through dialogical iteration with those directly
affected. The digital infrastructure developed through the EU COST
Action BEACON One Health Education supports this architecture (Simmons,
2025). This is the brain-child of the research Platforms, expert
systems, and co-educational modules are under active construction,
designed to remain openly available and responsive to user feedback
until at least 2029. The approach is modular, integrative, and
inherently adaptive, with interfaces for both professional users and lay
contributors, and with safeguards against institutional capture.

A core methodological innovation is the proposal of continuous feedback
loops at all levels of decision-making and care, and an open costant
invitation to bring feedback by different ways. These loops are not
limited to clinical processes but extend to institutional governance and
policy design. Communities are not invited after the fact but
structurally positioned as co-creators of knowledge and care, learning
from each other. Survivors of coercion, communities abandoned by the
welfare state, and youth deprived of educational opportunity are no
longer considered passive beneficiaries of reform. They are framed as
active epistemic agents and future scientific actors. This dissertation
explicitly argues that the most promising scientific and civic
leadership will emerge from these very groups when structural violence
is interrupted and reparative systems are put in place.

The action-research model articulated here contributes to a science that
prevents harm, rather than merely documents it. It promotes
infrastructures that restore capacity and dignity, and that build
resilience across generations. The research supports the emergence of
children from adverse conditions -- including poverty, abuse,
institutionalisation, forced migration, or racial exclusion -- as future
scientists, educators, clinicians, and decision-makers. It defends their
right not only to be protected from harm, but to flourish, to be heard,
and to lead. This requires new norms of authorship, recognition, and
leadership in science, inclusive of non-traditional trajectories, of
historically excluded identities, and of knowledge forged under
oppression.

The EU BEACON One Health Education action, initiated during this
dissertation process, embodies these principles. It proposes that no
child be condemned to silence, erasure, or structural inferiority. That
no future student, professional, professor, anyone at all in our
societies be lost to psychiatric violence, educational exclusion, or
institutional betrayal; they, the professionals and professors of
tomorrow, fully engaged and supported from early on, as far as we can
continue forward our careers in peace; we work to ensure it all has a
chance to happen. Open science is not a matter of access alone, but of
transformation. It is about building systems that recognise, support,
and elevate the capacities of those long denied visibility and voice.
The methodological contribution of this work, then, lies not only in its
rigor, but in its refusal to separate science from justice, or care from
governance. It offers a blueprint for a participatory, integrative, and
emancipatory science, one that is capable of learning from those most
harmed, and rebuilding with them the institutions that once excluded
them.

## **2.9 Reflexive meta-methodology and scientific protocols for dissertation construction**

The narrative architecture of the dissertation is governed by the
empirical sequence and ethical imperatives of the research itself. The
ordering of survey data, ethnographic reporting, testimonial
incorporation, and legal analysis is not arbitrary but reflects the
temporal escalation of inquiry from exploratory mapping to embodied
survival, from systems critique to translational proposal. Each chapter
corresponds to a lived phase of research, demarcated not only by topic
but by epistemic urgency. The writing process itself functioned as a
recursive, multi-modal act of synthesis, drawing from live field notes,
encrypted correspondence, digital testimony archives, peer-reviewed
manuscripts, policy papers, and formal presentations. These modalities
were not integrated as appendices or accessories but woven into the
analytic corpus in accordance with a protocol of epistemic fidelity and
dialogical construction. Such integration was governed by coherence, not
by hierarchy of form. Legal citations and narrative witness statements,
statistical tabulations and anthropological commentary, co-exist not as
competing genres but as interdependent elements of a bio-cultural
diagnostic grammar. Reflexivity in this context is not performative
introspection but a structural and continuous engagement with the
political and material implications of each knowledge claim. The work
does not presume the neutrality of its categories, nor the innocence of
its interpretations.

The ethical grounding of the dissertation is inseparable from the
anthropological lineage it draws upon, including the field-defining
contributions of Paul Farmer, Nancy Scheper-Hughes, and Byron Good, each
of whom recognized the moral imperative of research that refuses
detachment in the face of organized suffering. Their influence is not
merely cited but embedded in the design logic of this dissertation. At
every phase, the question of what ought to be named, what ought to be
protected, and what ought to be transformed has guided not only what is
written but how it is written. The dissertation rejects the view that
ethical research in psychiatry can be extracted from the terrain of
conflict without becoming complicit in the very systems it purports to
study. Instead, it insists that rigorous, transparent, and relationally
responsible research is itself an act of healing, if conducted under
proper conditions of care, recognition, and epistemic parity.

Collaboration is central to this research design, though authorship is
formally singular. The knowledge presented is co-produced through
dialogical exchange with psychiatric survivors, field interlocutors,
legal scholars, digital mental health innovators, clinicians, and
educators from multiple continents. The networks coordinated or
co-founded by the researcher, including EU BEACON, ReMO, and FOSTREN,
functioned not only as dissemination channels but as infrastructural
nodes for scientific co-production. Task forces and working groups
within these consortia supported peer validation, ethical oversight, and
triangulation of findings. Such trans-disciplinary involvement allowed
for distributed epistemic authority and diversified validation,
embedding each analytic output within a wider scientific ecology. This
does not diminish the accountability of the author but anchors it in a
collective matrix of knowledge stewardship.

The dissertation's construction was shaped by extreme conditions of
persecution, violence, and physiological disintegration. It was produced
during periods of medical torture, forced displacement, and digital
erasure. At times the researcher had no access to basic housing,
electricity, or medical care. Productivity and health was maintained,
despite the violence endured, through health tracking, micronutrient
supplementation, digital compartmentalization, and intermittent fasting,
alongside the strictest work ethic, exercise to the extent the
researcher could, and continuous short, mid and long term efforts at
self and family protection moving away from harm; always keeping the
motivation to help other victims by achieiving to doctorate. These
strategies are described not to dramatize but to affirm that the
epistemic labor required to document, resist, and propose better ways to
psychiatric violence ought to include survival as a method. The
dissertation is therefore not only an academic contribution, but a
testimonial and methodological intervention into what it means to
research psychiatry from within the circuits of its failure. This
reflexive meta-methodology affirms that knowledge can be produced
ethically, coherently, and scientifically even when institutional
guarantees are absent, when bodily integrity is under attack, and when
silence is the expected price of survival. It is this refusal of
silence, anchored in rigor and relational accountability, that allows
the dissertation to serve not only as a documentation of abuse but as a
testomony and collective blueprint for repair.

# **Chapter 3. Survey findings: patterns, perceptions, and psychiatric practice**

**Summary: **This chapter presents the results of three interconnected
surveys, conducted with users/survivors, professionals, and mixed-role
respondents, designed to assess perceptions, practices, and
institutional dynamics within psychiatry in Spain and across
transnational contexts. The integrated analysis reveals systemic
patterns of coercion, professional disempowerment, loss of trust, and
calls for structural reform. The simultaneous presentation is
methodologically justified as it enhances triangulation, clarifies
asymmetries, and supports systems-level diagnosis.

> **

## **3. Introduction to the surveys' results presentation**

## ****This chapter presents the integrated analysis of three coordinated surveys conducted among users and survivors of psychiatry, mental health professionals, and respondents with mixed or dual roles. Their combined structure provides a triangulated perspective on the Spanish psychiatric system and transnational analogues, enabling a relational diagnosis of clinical, ethical, and structural breakdowns. The rationale for presenting these data together lies in the shared thematic architecture, centered on trust, coercion, medication, consent, and institutional norms, and in the analytical strength derived from mapping convergences and divergences across groups.****

Methodologically, the surveys were distributed through academic,
activist, and clinical networks, collecting anonymised data with
informed consent. Their results were validated through triangulation
with fieldwork presented in Chapter 4, legal frameworks examined in
Chapter 6, and broader epistemic analysis. The user-survivor survey
reveals high levels of perceived coercion, forced medication, and
seclusion, described as traumatic and unjustified. Professional
responses confirm that coercion is a routinized, not exceptional,
practice, often legitimized by risk management logics and institutional
pressures. Mixed-role respondents, such as professionals with lived
experience, highlight the moral and epistemic dissonance within
practice. The moral framing diverges between what institutions present
as protective and what is widely experienced as degrading and harmful.
Ethical constraints are central. Professionals report widespread
burnout, institutional complicity, and the absence of avenues for
ethical dissent or non-coercive care. Users speak of betrayal,
disbelief, and systemic gaslighting. Both groups identify the existing
legal and ethical frameworks as disconnected from lived reality.
Relational trust is reported as structurally absent, broken by time
scarcity, hierarchical decision-making, and diagnostic opacity. Shared
decision-making around medication, although theoretically endorsed by
professionals, is rarely implemented. Users demand informed consent,
autonomy, tapering options, and full risk disclosure, demands that
professionals largely share but feel institutionally unable to fulfill.
Structural constraints dominate. Fear of reprisal, lack of protocols,
and professional isolation reinforce a status quo of epistemic and
ethical erasure.

Throughout the responses, demands for transformation coalesce around
legal safeguards, participatory care models, dialogical and
trauma-informed practice, and deep institutional change. Professionals
call for time, supervision, and reflective spaces. Users demand justice,
reparation, and structural recognition. The surveys collectively show
that current psychiatric configurations produce coercion and
disempowerment as systemic outcomes, not accidents of practice. Ethical
care under these constraints is rendered structurally impossible. Yet,
across all respondent groups, a shared horizon of transformation
emerges. The findings form the empirical backbone for the legal critique
developed in Chapter 6 and the systemic redesigns proposed in Chapter 7,
particularly through the implementation of the EU BEACON One Health
Education infrastructure. The chapter thus not only documents harm but
establishes a scientifically grounded mandate for institutional
redesign, grounded in lived knowledge and trans-disciplinary analysis.

## **3.1 Introduction: integrated survey architecture and purpose**

****This section presents the rationale for an integrated analytical
treatment of the three surveys conducted as part of this research: one
addressed to users and survivors of psychiatric services, one to mental
health professionals, and one to respondents who occupy hybrid roles,
including clinicians with lived experience or survivor-advocates working
within the system. Rather than treating these groups in isolation, the
design deliberately presents them together, both to facilitate empirical
triangulation and to reflect the relational configuration of psychiatric
care. Clinical decisions, user experiences, and institutional norms are
not produced in vacuum but are co-constituted through situated
interactions shaped by law, ethics, diagnostic authority, and historical
trauma. This methodological choice supports a multilevel systems
analysis in which divergence is as analytically valuable as
convergence.****

The surveys are built upon a shared thematic framework that centers
trust, coercion, consent, medication, and ethical practice. These five
dimensions correspond to the core concerns raised across decades of
international critique of psychiatric governance and align closely with
the central thesis of this dissertation. That is, the structural
character of coercion, the erosion of autonomy, and the epistemic
violence embedded in routine psychiatric interventions. By comparing and
contrasting how each group understands and experiences these dynamics,
the research generates a composite diagnosis that integrates user
suffering, professional disillusionment, and systemic inertia.

Presenting the three surveys together not only facilitates comparative
analysis but reflects the lived complexity of psychiatric systems. These
are not composed of isolated actors but of entangled positions where
asymmetry, responsibility, and vulnerability are co-produced. The
inclusion of mixed-role respondents enhances this frame by capturing the
voices of those who have moved between system-defined categories. Their
responses often highlight institutional contradictions, identify points
of epistemic and ethical collapse, and reveal how formal roles can
obscure relational and moral insight. These positionalities are
methodologically valuable, as they bridge the experience of harm with
the exercise of professional responsibility.

The surveys were designed with clear operational objectives. First, to
document the lived experience and structural perception of psychiatric
treatment as understood by those most affected, including both
recipients and providers of care. Second, to identify the key ethical,
legal, and epistemological tensions that compromise the legitimacy and
effectiveness of psychiatric services. Third, to amplify the voices of
both professionals and users as sources of institutional critique and
contributors to structural redesign. These objectives were not derived
abstractly but are rooted in the action-research logic underpinning the
dissertation, which seeks to advance participatory, evidence-based
reform. The surveys thus serve as an empirical foundation for the
proposals developed in later chapters and establish a baseline from
which systems-level redesign can proceed.

To clarify the alignment between these survey objectives and the
overarching goals of the dissertation, the following table
cross-references the integrated survey purpose with the main research
questions and aims articulated in Chapter 1:

****Table 29. Alignment of integrated survey with dissertation aims and
operational questions****

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Document lived experience and structural perception of psychiatric treatment               Contribute to the development and implementation of participatory mental health systems grounded in rights and justice   What forms of systemic violence and institutional failure are occurring in psychiatric governance, and how can they be corrected?
  Identify ethical, legal, and epistemological tensions undermining psychiatric legitimacy   Realign psychiatric care with empirical coherence, user dignity, and procedural accountability                           What are the structural and epistemic conditions that enable or block ethical practice and user autonomy?
  Amplify professional and user voices as legitimate sources of critique and reform          Support co-designed, dialogically grounded clinical and institutional models                                             What participatory mechanisms and evidentiary tools can inform and sustain systems-level transformation?
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This table shows how each of the three core survey objectives
contributes to the broader research architecture of the dissertation.
Each objective is functionally aligned with one or more of the central
aims and addresses a corresponding operational research question. The
integration confirms that the surveys are not merely exploratory but
serve a strategic role in evidencing the system's failures and in
designing responsive better ways.

The survey results are neither descriptive addenda nor isolated
empirical instruments, but structurally integrated into the
dissertation's conceptual and methodological logic. Their concurrent
presentation enables a relational analysis of the psychiatric system,
grounded in multivocal evidence and attentive to positional complexity.
Each layer of data speaks not only to the harms endured or witnessed,
but to the possibility of reconfiguring care through shared knowledge,
distributed responsibility, and epistemic repair. This logic carries
into the chapters that follow, where each major thematic finding is
revisited through fieldwork, testimony, and normative analysis. The
architecture of the surveys responds not only to thematic coherence but
also to methodological demands for internal consistency, comparative
reliability, and epistemological rigor. By structuring each instrument
to explore both shared and distinct dimensions of psychiatric
experience, the study ensures that responses can be analyzed across
multiple axes, including professional constraint, user harm, relational
breakdown, and normative conflict, while still preserving the
singularity of each respondent group. The users and mixed-role
respondents answered open-ended as well as multiple-choice questions to
express their lived experiences in their own terms, particularly in
domains where institutional language has proven insufficient or harmful.
Professionals, by contrast, responded to structured prompts designed to
interrogate their alignment or dissonance with legal, ethical, and
clinical norms, thereby facilitating both internal comparison and
cross-group triangulation. The methodological design allowed not only
for horizontal contrast across roles but also for vertical integration
with the broader action-research architecture. Importantly, the surveys
are not an isolated data collection mechanism. They are embedded within
a broader continuum of fieldwork and collective engagement. Many of the
respondents had previously taken part in shared spaces of learning and
action, including seminars, clinical training sessions, all events, and
advocacy campaigns. Many were reached through direct connections formed
during the ethnographic phase, including professionals who had attended
workshops facilitated by the researcher, students who later became
colleagues, and fellow survivors who chose to remain in contact for
mutual support and collaboration. Likewise, many of those who
participated in the surveys gave their consent to remain involved in
follow-up or parallel processes, including the policy translation of
findings and the pedagogical dissemination of tools. The surveys thus
serve as both a source of empirical data and a relational node within a
living network of individuals and institutions committed to mental
health transformation.

The next section presents the specific methodological and procedural
logic that underpins this integration. It details the construction,
dissemination, and ethical oversight of the three surveys, and
elaborates on how data quality was ensured through triangulation with
observational fieldwork, legal review, and narrative confirmation. The
section also clarifies how participants were anonymised, how consent was
obtained, and how each survey functioned within the broader framework of
open, participatory, and justice-oriented inquiry. Far from being
detached instruments, the surveys exemplify a collaborative and
reflexive research process, grounded in direct contact with those who
seek, provide, and reform mental health care, and who have experienced
first-hand its failures and possibilities.

## **3.2 Methodology: instruments, sample, and triangulation logic**

The survey methodology employed in this study reflects a deliberately
plural and layered approach to data collection and analysis, designed to
capture the complexity of psychiatric systems as lived, governed, and
contested. Three distinct instruments were developed, each tailored to
the positionality and situated knowledge of its respondent group, yet
aligned through a shared thematic and analytical architecture. The first
survey, addressed to users and survivors of psychiatry, included a
combination of open-ended and multiple-choice questions aimed at
documenting experiences related to diagnosis, treatment, agency,
perceived harm, and access to justice. The design of this instrument
privileged narrative expression and allowed respondents to articulate in
their own words how psychiatric interventions had shaped their lives,
relationships, and sense of self. Special attention was given to
epistemic injustices, forced treatment, and the absence of mechanisms
for repair. The second survey was constructed for mental health
professionals, including psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, social
workers, and other clinical or institutional staff. This instrument
employed a more structured format, focusing on clinical constraints,
ethical dilemmas, experiences of coercion, legal responsibilities, and
organizational norms. The aim was to capture the internal dissonance
many professionals face when working within systems that often prevent
the implementation of what they themselves regard as ethical and
effective care. The third and final survey was designed for individuals
who occupy mixed or transitional roles, such as professionals with lived
experience of psychiatry, peer support workers, activist clinicians, or
survivor-academics. This hybrid instrument combined both formats and
enabled the documentation of experiences that transcend binary
categories, thereby contributing to a more nuanced understanding of
institutional complicity, resistance, and transformation.

Distribution of the surveys occurred digitally, relying on professional,
academic, activist, and survivor networks operating within Spain, Latin
America, and other European Union contexts. Invitations were
disseminated through open channels, including mailing lists, social
media platforms, and direct contact with organizations engaged in mental
health advocacy, professional development, and policy reform.
Respondents were not selected based on diagnostic labels or
institutional affiliation but through voluntary participation and shared
concern for the themes addressed. Many were already in connection with
the researcher through fieldwork settings, clinical teaching, mutual
projects, or public events, while others entered the study through
snowball referrals and transnational networks dedicated to reducing
coercion and enhancing user rights.

To ensure scientific validity, all responses were anonymized and
gathered with explicit informed consent for use in the research. Ethical
approval had been previously obtained, and all protocols followed the
university's and national standards for participatory and
vulnerable-population research. The resulting data were subjected to
systematic triangulation, following the logic set out in Chapter 2.3.
Patterns were validated through convergence, divergence, contradiction,
or marked silence, with attention to structural asymmetry and epistemic
power differentials. Triangulation occurred not only across respondent
groups but also between surveys, field observations, testimony, and
legal analysis. Themes raised by survey respondents were frequently
echoed in informal conversations, formal interviews, or institutional
documents collected during ethnographic fieldwork.

The integration of survey data with broader fieldwork practices was not
a posterior analytical step but an embedded feature of the research
process. Many of those who participated in the surveys were also present
in participant observation settings, including academic workshops,
clinical training sessions, activist assemblies, international
conferences, and institutional reform meetings. Others had been key
informants, collaborators, or students who engaged in the research over
extended periods. Conversely, the surveys also generated new contacts
and expressions of interest that fed back into the fieldwork, policy
advocacy, and ongoing co-educational processes associated with the
dissertation. This reflexive and circular movement between inquiry,
testimony, and systemic engagement constitutes one of the core strengths
of the methodology and underscores the emancipatory orientation of the
research as a whole. The following sections will elaborate the findings,
beginning with the experiential and institutional dynamics of coercion,
as reported and interpreted by respondents across all three instruments.

This chapter presents a synthesis of the most salient patterns
identified through structured surveys distributed among diverse groups
of mental health professionals, users, and mixed populations. The
findings substantiate key research questions identified in Chapter 1 and
are methodologically consistent with the mixed-methods architecture
detailed in Chapter 2. The data confirms a widespread perception of
systemic failure across the domains of psychiatric decision-making,
patient autonomy, medication use, and institutional trust. Participants
across demographics reported experiences of coercion, epistemic
exclusion, and the normalization of pharmacological dependency, often in
the absence of transparent clinical reasoning or consent.

The results speak not only to individual clinical encounters but to
entrenched institutional and educational shortcomings. They document a
persistent disconnection between normative ethical commitments and lived
realities in mental health systems, further aggravated by deficits in
public education, legal accountability, and interdisciplinary practice.
These findings call for a dual response: pedagogical reconstruction to
align training with evidence-based, rights-oriented models of care, and
legal reform to ensure enforceable protections, transparency, and
scientific integrity. As will be further developed in Chapters 5 and 6,
the survey data provides critical justification for educational and
legislative interventions designed to restructure the psychiatric field
in accordance with constitutional mandates and human dignity.

  Underreporting or denial of adverse effects and trauma linked to psychiatric treatment   Epistemic suppression of patient narratives and post-intervention harm              Training in critical appraisal of psychiatric literature and long-term treatment outcomes              Legal obligation to document, report, and review harm linked to psychiatric interventions
  General perception of structural impunity and lack of accountability mechanisms          Absence of oversight structures enabling harmful or negligent practices             Ethics education focused on institutional design, transparency, and collective responsibility          Creation of independent complaint, review, and restitution mechanisms linked to health and justice systems
  Minimal knowledge of non-coercive better ways among both users and professionals         Poor dissemination of existing non-coercive models and community practices          Public and professional education campaigns on better ways to coercion                                 Policy endorsement and funding for non-coercive community mental health programs
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **3.3 Perceived coercion and institutional violence**

The survey data collected from users and survivors of psychiatry reveal
a consistent and deeply troubling pattern of perceived coercion across
all stages of psychiatric intervention. A majority of respondents report
having been subjected to forced medication, physical or chemical
restraint, seclusion, and involuntary hospitalization, often without
clear justification, legal documentation, or accessible channels for
appeal. These practices are not described as isolated or exceptional but
as foundational to their experience of the psychiatric system. Forced
medication, particularly through long-acting injections, is cited as one
of the most traumatic events, often administered under conditions of
fear, confusion, or explicit threat. Respondents frequently state that
they were not informed of the purpose, dosage, or risks of the
substances administered, and that refusal was equated with lack of
insight or oppositional disorder, rather than respected as a right to
bodily autonomy. Seclusion and mechanical restraint are described as
degrading and dehumanizing, with participants recounting episodes where
they were isolated for hours or days without explanation, therapeutic
accompaniment, or post-incident review. In several cases, users report
having been subjected to these measures repeatedly, without any
meaningful better being proposed, nor a single debriefing conducted
afterward.

****Table 31. Survey-based systemic dynamics and structural
recommendations ****

Synthesis of survey-derived insights highlighting critical discrepancies
between lived experience and ethical psychiatric practice. Each observed
dynamic is paired with corresponding thesis recommendations, developed
in response to the empirical evidence and aligned with the broader
research questions of the dissertation. The right-hand column provides
positive systemic actions proposed in Chapters 5 and 6 to correct the
identified institutional failures.

The psychological impact of these interventions is described as lasting
and severe. Participants recount experiences of fear, helplessness,
humiliation, and enduring mistrust toward clinicians and institutions.
Many describe the psychiatric environment not as a place of healing but
as a carceral space, structured around control, surveillance, and
punishment. Coercion is experienced as epistemic as well as physical:
many respondents report that their attempts to explain their distress,
resist a treatment, or propose an better perspective were systematically
discredited, often pathologized as symptoms of illness. This discursive
invalidation compounds the trauma of physical coercion, as individuals
are denied not only control over their bodies but also recognition of
their meaning-making. The lack of legal remedy or institutional
accountability exacerbates the sense of vulnerability, with respondents
expressing that they were often left without recourse or protection,
even in the face of what they considered violations of basic rights.
Many report that complaints were ignored, staff were dismissive, and
judicial mechanisms, if accessed at all, deferred to medical authority
without independent scrutiny. These testimonies align with broader
critiques of psychiatric impunity and signal a crisis of legitimacy
within the system.

The data from mental health professionals confirm, from within the
system, that coercion is not only present but structurally embedded in
routine psychiatric care. A substantial portion of professional
respondents acknowledged that involuntary treatment is applied
regularly, often without clear legal thresholds or robust ethical
deliberation. While some framed these interventions as necessary under
extreme conditions, many expressed discomfort and ethical dissonance,
citing that coercion often arises not from therapeutic need but from
systemic failure. Specifically, professionals highlighted a combination
of structural pressures, insufficient time, limited staff, lack of
crisis better ways, and institutional culture, as key drivers of
coercive practice. The inability to provide sustained relational care or
to negotiate meaningfully with distressed individuals was described not
as a personal deficit but as a systemic constraint. Some respondents
admitted that decisions to medicate by force or to initiate seclusion
were made under conditions of ambiguity and exhaustion, often with
little confidence that such actions were in the best interest of the
patient.

Legal ambiguity was repeatedly cited as a compounding factor.
Professionals reported uncertainty about the exact legal requirements
for involuntary interventions, and described how institutional protocols
often operate in parallel to, or in disregard of, the formal legal
framework. Many indicated that the fear of blame in the case of a future
adverse event, such as suicide, violence, or public complaint, plays a
significant role in tipping the decision toward coercion. This
risk-deflection logic, embedded in defensive institutional practice,
leads to coercion being employed pre-emptively or excessively,
particularly in the absence of clear better ways. Several professionals
described how the expectation to control behavior, rather than address
suffering, results in an over-reliance on pharmacological containment
and physical separation, especially in acute units. This is further
compounded by the absence of reflective supervision, ethical
deliberation spaces, or trauma-informed infrastructure, leaving many
professionals to navigate these decisions in isolation. The result is a
culture in which coercion is normalized, internal resistance is
suppressed, and ethical dissonance is treated as inevitable rather than
as a signal for reform.

Respondents occupying mixed or dual roles, such as
survivor-professionals, peer support workers, or critical clinicians,
provided a particularly revealing perspective. Their position at the
intersection of institutional practice and lived experience allowed for
a sharp articulation of coercion's multifaceted harms. Many entered the
mental health field following personal experiences of involuntary
treatment, driven by the intent to transform the system from within.
Their testimonies displayed both a heightened ethical sensitivity and a
nuanced understanding of the systemic pressures that constrain reform.
Some reported feeling complicit in the very practices they had once
endured, citing role expectations and institutional inertia as barriers
to providing viable better ways. Others described a permanent tension
between professional norms and ethical clarity, including implicit or
overt demands to reinforce risk management logics and suppress
divergence from established treatment pathways.

These findings support the thesis hypothesis that clinical discretion is
often exercised within structurally coerced environments, rather than as
free ethical deliberation. Nevertheless, this same group of respondents
offered glimpses of possible systemic transformation. Several proposed
the design of incentive structures oriented not toward symptom
containment but toward sustained recovery and functional reintegration.
Among the most novel ideas reported was the concept of
public--professional partnerships modeled loosely on performance-based
incentives, where clinicians or teams would be rewarded with state-saved
resources when patients previously under coercive care achieved robust,
medication-free stability. In this framework, the 'bounty' would be the
measurable reduction in cost to the public health and welfare systems,
often thousands of euros monthly, achieved through effective, voluntary,
and person-centered care. This framing reverses the conventional
trajectory of career prestige and resource allocation, no longer tied to
chronicity and dependence but to outcomes in restored autonomy and
reduced harm.

Participants emphasized that such a shift ought to not obscure
structural injustices that currently render deprivation itself a
prerequisite for accessing support. Multiple respondents indicated that
psychiatric diagnosis is sometimes the only route to housing, disability
benefits, or material assistance, particularly under austerity regimes.
While calling for deeper socio-economic reform, they also insisted that
no benefit system should rely on the perpetuation of illness or enforced
compliance as eligibility criteria. Health, understood as the capacity
to live autonomously and contribute meaningfully, ought to be decoupled
from surveillance logics and framed as a public good. Participants
proposed pilot programs combining housing, nutritional support,
educational resources, and professional development opportunities for
service users wishing to exit the psychiatric system. Such proposals
resonate with broader calls for longitudinal studies based on informed
consent and genuine free will, targeting both early and complex cases
without discrimination or resignation. No group should be excluded from
recovery trajectories based on severity, age, or diagnostic category.
The ethical horizon is clear: no profession should depend for its
existence on the perpetuation of suffering, and no state should treat
despair as an acceptable outcome of systemic design.

These mixed-role accounts were also among the most detailed in
documenting the epistemic effects of coercion. They emphasized how
diagnostic authority is used to discredit dissent, how consent is
routinely undermined, and how institutional legitimacy is preserved
through denial or minimization of harm. Several noted the absence of
formal structures for professionals to report or contest coercive
practices without risking retaliation or career damage. These
respondents highlighted how systemic coercion operates not only on
patients but also on clinicians, through role confinement, emotional
suppression, and the normalization of ethical compromise. In doing so,
they exposed a critical dimension of structural violence within
psychiatry: the production of moral disengagement as a professional
norm. Many expressed that meaningful change is unlikely to arise from
within isolated institutions and called for trans-disciplinary
alliances, user-led initiatives, and external accountability mechanisms.
Their narratives also pointed to the therapeutic and political
importance of remembering one's own experience, resisting institutional
amnesia, and restoring ethical clarity through shared reflection and
coordinated action.

The triangulated analysis of the three surveys reveals that coercion is
not an exception within psychiatric systems but a normalized and
routinized feature of their structure, culture, and discourse. Across
respondent groups, coercive interventions, forced medication, seclusion,
physical restraint, and involuntary hospitalization, are described as
common, institutionally sanctioned, and often executed without
meaningful consent, transparent communication, or post-event
accountability. The data show that while professionals frequently
recognize the ethical and clinical limitations of these practices, they
remain structurally constrained by systemic pressures, resource
scarcity, ambiguous legal frameworks, and defensive institutional
logics. The moral framing of coercion diverges markedly between groups:
professionals often refer to it as a form of safety or necessary
containment, whereas users and survivor-professionals characterize it as
avoidable harm, trauma, and institutional violence. It ought to be
noted, about half of respondents to the last survey requested their
responses not to be shared, even if made anonymous, explicitly. Fear is
a key component of current state of affairs, as witnessed during
field-work, by most if not all players not exercising violence
themselves, as reprisals with harshest consequences are common.

justifications, and experiential framings across respondent groups**

  --------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ****Forced medication****               Widespread, described as traumatic, dehumanizing, poorly explained, often long-acting injections     Reported as frequent, institutionally normalized, used under pressure and fear of liability            Described as unnecessary in most cases, linked to trauma, used to suppress dissent
  ****Seclusion and isolation****         Experienced as punishment, used to silence or intimidate, without therapeutic support                Seen as a last resort, yet often used in absence of better ways or staff capacity                      Recognized as retraumatizing, often unreviewed, with no restorative function
