reform.

These results also clarify the epistemic tensions at the core of
psychiatric knowledge production. Professional ideology, built on
assumptions of expertise, benevolence, and compliance, is systematically
contradicted by user narratives of harm, exclusion, and mistrust. What
is marketed as person-centered care frequently manifests as
surveillance, control, and diagnostic capture. The surveys document not
isolated violations but a field-wide epistemic fracture that
delegitimizes the knowledge claims of users while overvaluing
technocratic decision-making. This gap is not only cognitive but
operational, shaping institutional policies, legal frameworks, and
therapeutic practices.

The analytical implications of these findings are substantial. First,
they justify the methodological use of testimony, narrative mapping, and
trauma-informed coding not as auxiliary tools, but as central analytical
devices capable of capturing harm that escapes statistical or procedural
documentation. Second, they ground the dissertation's conceptual and
policy redesign proposals in lived data rather than ideological
critique. Third, they establish the empirical authority of the author
not only as a researcher but as an embedded witness and ethical actor
navigating coercive systems. Fourth, they position the thesis as a
translational effort, moving from descriptive documentation to
epistemically legitimate proposals for reengineering psychiatric care
within a rights-based, dialogical, and bio-culturally grounded
framework.

Ultimately, the scientific integrity of this research resides not only
in the breadth and depth of its empirical base, but in its capacity to
confront the institutional refusal to learn from those harmed. The
surveys provide the evidentiary and conceptual scaffolding upon which
the next chapter builds its systemic critique and its grounded
propositions for ethical psychiatric transformation. The data affirm
that the current configuration of psychiatric governance is incompatible
with ethical care and that an better horizon, rooted in respect,
autonomy, and epistemic justice, is both imaginable and empirically
necessitated, though structurally obstructed.

****This dissertation is designed not only to document and analyze
systemic dysfunctions in psychiatric practice but to actively contribute
to their redress through scientifically grounded, ethically mandated
translational strategies. The methodological architecture has been built
to ensure that the findings, derived from lived experience, professional
testimony, and legal scrutiny, do not remain confined to academic
interpretation. Instead, they are structured for strategic deployment in
pedagogical, clinical, legal, and policy settings. Each dataset
collected and each analytical step undertaken was oriented toward
relevance in implementation, with an explicit focus on institutional
redesign, ethical restitution, and health system transformation.****

The three surveys provide modular, verifiable, and thematically
integrated repositories of evidence, capable of informing multiple
levels of intervention. The first survey on psychiatric labeling
supplies forensic material suitable for legal advocacy, educational
reform, and rights-based service redesign. The second survey on open
dialogue documents implementation challenges and professional readiness,
offering a diagnostic resource for systems planning, curriculum
development, and regulatory restructuring. The third survey on
medication management and shared decision-making offers operational
pathways for deprescription protocols, ethical prescribing guidelines,
and patient-led monitoring systems. Each survey includes codified user
needs, actionable reform proposals, and emergent professional consensus,
forming a robust, scalable basis for systemic transformation. This
document is also set as an online one, as living one on a git
repository, with additional interactive statistics, graphics and
results, made available in the open.

The ethnographic and legal fieldwork data complement the surveys by
illuminating the everyday environments where policy fails, rights are
suspended, and institutional betrayal is normalized. These findings
serve not only as documentation but as input for digital systems design,
clinical ethics training, and administrative monitoring. By
cross-referencing narrative content, institutional documents, and
professional discourse, the dissertation generates analytic tools that
can be used to prototype transparent, accountable, and rights-compatible
mental health infrastructures. These include open-source expert systems,
quality assessment indicators, and policy simulation models, all
outlined in the implementation-focused final chapters. Everyone is
encourage to join in to help.

The translational value of the work lies in its capacity to intervene
where traditional scientific publishing has failed to effect change. The
layered design of this dissertation, combining rigorous data analysis
with action-research methodology and network-based implementation
strategies, ensures that its findings are not only publishable but
actionable. International networks such as EU BEACON, FOSTREN, and ReMO
serve as dissemination pathways and ethical infrastructure for deploying
the thesis results in practice, across borders, and within health,
legal, and educational systems. In this sense, the dissertation is both
a scientific document and a translational instrument. It seeks to
realign psychiatric practice with ethical mandates, legal obligations,
and lived human experience. Its strategic goal is to support the
emergence of a new evidentiary and institutional order, one that
recognizes dignity, autonomy, and care as non-negotiable conditions of
health system legitimacy. The evidence presented in this chapter, and
throughout the thesis, is not simply informative. It is constitutive of
the moral and operational case for systemic psychiatric reform.

# **Chapter 4 -- Fieldwork and Testimony: Lived Structures of Betrayal**

**Summary: **This chapter presents findings from long-term participant
observation, narrative reconstruction, and firsthand documentation
across institutional, professional, and familial contexts. It traces the
continuity of psychiatric violence from diagnosis to detention and from
systemic neglect to epistemic silencing. The chapter gives voice to
trajectories of betrayal, medical, legal, social, and familial, while
also highlighting moments of resistance, ethical courage, and the slow
recovery of agency.

****4. Introduction and positionality****

****This chapter begins with direct field observation from the public
event Jornada Drets bàsics en els internaments psiquiàtrics involuntaris
(Conference on Basic Rights in Involuntary Psychiatric Internment), held
on Friday 18 March 2022 at the Col·legi de Metges de Barcelona, the
official Medical Council of the city. The event was organized by the
Ethics Committee of the Catalan Mental Health Congress Foundation, an
interdisciplinary platform dedicated to policy development and debate in
the mental health field. Its stated aim was to examine the legal
framework governing involuntary internment and to reaffirm the normative
and protective roles of existing legislation, including Spanish national
law and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities. ****Opening addresses were delivered by Josep Vilajoana,
then president of the Foundation, Sílvia Ventura, jurist and president
of the Ethics Committee specializing in psychiatric legal matters, and
Joan Vegué, director of the Catalan Government's Mental Health and
Addictions Master Plan. The keynote by Fernando Santos, a public
prosecutor in Córdoba and advocate for disability rights, focused on Law
8/2021 as a turning point toward ethical support rather than substituted
decision-making. He was followed by Alberto Vásquez, Peruvian jurist and
former adviser to the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Health, who
stressed the disjunction between formal legal commitments and prevailing
institutional practices in psychiatric care. Later, Sílvia Ventura and
Montserrat Hierro, both experts in legal capacity and psychiatric
detention, introduced the committee's internal publication *Coneixements
jurídics bàsics en relació als ingressos psiquiàtrics involuntaris*
(Basic Legal Knowledge on Involuntary Psychiatric Admissions). The
document sought to clarify the minimum legal requirements under
international law and was presented as a tool to align clinical
procedures with human rights standards.

The researcher attended this event under conditions of recent exposure
to institutional torture and acute psychological distress, which
resulted in the loss of all personal notes and materials. Despite this,
the atmosphere remains vividly remembered. Some participants had
previously provided support in managing the adverse effects of forced
medication, demonstrating ethical commitment beyond institutional
constraints. Others, however, exhibited marked discomfort at the notion
that legal safeguards should be mandatory and enforceable. Judicial
oversight was perceived not as a protective necessity but as a threat to
professional autonomy. This reaction revealed an entrenched belief in
clinical discretion as a sufficient and unchallengeable basis for
deprivation of liberty and treatment, irrespective of independent
review. Although publicly framed as an occasion for ethical
deliberation, the congress revealed itself to be a key ethnographic site
where the instrumentalization of legal language was used to protect,
rather than dismantle, extrajudicial psychiatric authority. This was not
visible in the official transcripts but was evident in the informal
refusal to acknowledge systemic harm. While legal principles were
affirmed in discourse, their institutional application remained
selectively suspended. The need for enforceable safeguards emerged not
as a theoretical aspiration but as a structural requirement to prevent
ongoing violations under the guise of care.

Such events of institutional visibility and density were rare across the
fieldwork period, due to the researcher's extended exposure to coercive
contexts, limitations on movement, and lack of secure resources. On the
few occasions where safe participation was possible, professional
gatherings of this kind repeatedly exposed the discrepancy between
declarative ethics and operational accountability. These were not
anomalies but consistent patterns. Forums ostensibly dedicated to rights
and protections often functioned as platforms of denial, where legality
was invoked symbolically while mechanisms of redress and enforcement
were resisted or dismissed.

****By the time of this event, two years had passed since the beginning
of the fieldwork. The societal lockdown imposed during the COVID-19
pandemic was already receding into memory, but another form of
confinement had intensified. The use of psychiatric drugs as chemical
restraints had given way to more overt forms of physical violence. The
researcher, having momentarily escaped the numbing effects of enforced
medication, a contemporary form of non-surgical lobotomy, faced
escalating brutality. These beatings, increasingly frequent and
unconcealed, were not isolated acts but manifestations of a deeper
systemic collapse, where control substituted care and punishment
replaced ethics. What was inflicted was not only unlawful but
structurally normalized through the absence of accountability. That such
injuries were not irreversible is an exception, not a guarantee. Under
the current conditions, irreparable harm remains likely, not because the
law allows it, but because it is routinely ignored. All our health
requires common sense being sanity. Sanitation. ****

As legal scholar, Escalada has repeatedly emphasized, informed consent
ought to be a continuous and meaningful process, not a formality
administered once, if at all. When individuals are subjected to coercive
treatment without recurrent opportunities for valid, informed agreement,
legal protections are not merely bypassed, they are systematically
dismantled. Any framework that permits such practice under the guise of
clinical discretion undermines the core legal principle that life and
liberty ought to be protected without exception. To hold someone captive
through the force of unchecked authority, while claiming legal
legitimacy, is to erode the very foundation of democratic justice.
Fieldwork observations and testimonies beyond this one instance, across
diverse settings spanning five long and intense years, confirmed this
same pattern of concern on the need for better protections, and the need
to stop the regarding the pervasive overreliance on pharmacological
interventions within current care systems. Almost all consulted
individuals, whether users, peer advocates, or practitioners described
similar dynamics of overmedication coupled with neglect of social and
psychological dimensions of care. My own experience mirrored these
findings: I encountered a system where active listening was absent, and
where family members were able to exert coercive influence, pushing for
punitive treatments that escalated into institutionalized abuse, and
neither anamnesis nor any meaningful formulation was ever attempted,
destroying my own persona and true history in the medical records -an
achievement for the perpetrators. The mental health system, rather than
offering protection, was weaponized at their insistence, obstructing any
attempt to report clear instances of violence. Structural gaps,
particularly the lack of coordination with law enforcement, judicial
mechanisms, and victim support services, further compounded the harm.
Overmedication, rapidly inducing cognitive and physical impairments,
served to deepen vulnerability, making it easier for ongoing abuse to
occur unchecked. In my case this systemic cruelty intensified
intensified over, often reaching thresholds that could be classified as
psychological and physical torture. In general, a constant observation
was the need for true conversations and dialogues with patients, to
ensure the reality perceived by the professional matches that of the
lived experience, in fuller depth, to ensure proper consensual effective
support.

**4.1 Methodological continuity and scope**

****The researcher acknowledges that not all data gathered during the
five years of fieldwork could or should have been recorded, preserved or
disseminated according to open science standards, nor law allows for,
nor morals do, to share in complete full transparency. Names will be
often avoided, for one or other reasons and prudence. Much of the
material was produced under conditions involving repeated institutional
violence, forced interventions and sustained personal risk. This
included documented episodes of psychological and physical torture, the
use of psychiatric authority to suppress resistance and escalating
threats involving weapons and bodily harm. These circumstances do not
constitute a methodological limitation but are intrinsic to the observed
reality. The findings presented are inseparable from the environment in
which they were generated.****

The dynamics of coercion extended far beyond psychiatric facilities,
permeating family systems and broader sociocultural structures. Across
multiple settings including domestic, educational, judicial and welfare
domains, the same mechanisms of control, silencing and exclusion were
observed. These dynamics formed a continuum, reinforcing each other and
producing long-term harm. Ongoing fieldwork focused on pasung practices
exemplifies how such forces continue to operate outside institutional
psychiatry, revealing persistent gaps in legal enforcement and clinical
accountability. This investigation aims not only to document but also to
support the development of legal mechanisms that prevent harm, improve
public health governance and promote educational and community systems
that protect human capital and cultivate resilience.

Within the integrative paradigm of one health, individual health
outcomes are inseparable from social, political and ecological
determinants. Medical science, grounded in physiological evidence,
affirms that sustained poverty, exclusion and institutional violence
increase susceptibility to illness through immunological, metabolic and
neuroendocrine disruption. These mechanisms are well documented and
clinically relevant. Current mental health systems often fail to
incorporate such findings into practice, instead reinforcing models
centered on pharmacological symptom control without addressing
structural causes. The result is the continued prescription of
treatments whose long-term effects can undermine recovery, while
non-pharmacological pathways grounded in evidence from nutritional
psychiatry, psychoneuroimmunology, trauma research and metabolic
medicine remain underused or institutionally discredited.

These failures are not incidental but systemic, shaped by gaps in
scientific publication, distorted incentive structures and a lack of
transparent methodological standards. The overprescribing environment,
resistant to critical scrutiny, continues to medicalize the
physiological effects of deprivation and distress while offering limited
tools for sustainable healing. Scientific and legal structures ought to
be aligned with the imperative to reduce harm, ensure integrity and
promote effective care based on current evidence.

The present chapter responds to the core research questions set out in
Chapter 1 and adheres to the methodological architecture defined in
Chapter 2. It offers a synthesized presentation of findings under the
constraints of academic format, drawing from the most consistent and
verifiable observations. These results are not only relevant to the
specific contexts studied but are generalizable across comparable
systems where psychiatric discretion is exercised without enforceable
safeguards. Chapters 5 and 6 will respectively develop the educational
and legal-political responses necessary to ensure that institutional
knowledge, clinical practice and social structures converge toward
conditions that promote health, safety and human flourishing.

As outlined in Aristotelian thought, the law ought to govern where
ethical self-regulation is absent. When injustice is structurally
normalized, legal frameworks are not only necessary for deterrence but
indispensable for correction. Psychiatric systems, like all systems of
power, ought to be subjected to transparent limits, and these limits
ought to be informed by scientific knowledge, constitutional rights and
the lived reality of those most affected. The integrity of science and
the dignity of human life both require it. This chapter presents a
synthesis of empirical results derived from long-term, multi-sited
ethnographic fieldwork across psychiatric, institutional, domestic, and
community contexts. It answers, as stated, the core research questions
identified in Chapter 1 and adheres to the methodological framework
outlined in Chapter 2. The approach is necessarily integrative and
selective. Given the structural and documentary constraints of the
thesis format, the chapter does not attempt to reproduce the totality of
observations but instead refines and consolidates the most critical
patterns, convergences, and deviations into a scientifically grounded
response. The findings reveal persistent mechanisms of coercion, legal
ambiguity, and clinical discretion that facilitate harm in the absence
of effective oversight.

Clear clinical contradictions were identified throughout the fieldwork.
While some practitioners endorsed and documented full recovery through
trauma-informed, nutritional, and metabolic interventions, others
continued to enforce medication regimens disconnected from the evolving
scientific evidence. The marginalization of psychoneuroimmunology,
nutritional psychiatry, and metabolic approaches remains symptomatic of
a broader failure to integrate available biomedical knowledge into
standard practice. This disjunction is sustained by systemic weaknesses
in the current scientific publication system, where structural bias,
underreporting of adverse outcomes, and commercial pressures continue to
obstruct the screening and consolidation of critical findings. As a
result, well-substantiated better ways are excluded or delegitimized,
and harmful practices persist, including those already regarded as best
ways, ought never to be mere optional conditionals.

This chapter is committed to presenting results with methodological
precision and without ideological mediation. Purest medical output, as
should always be. Its purpose is to clarify what has been observed,
establish its scientific relevance, and prepare the ground for the
normative and practical dimensions of the work. Chapters 5 and 6 will
elaborate the necessary socio-educational and politico-legal responses,
respectively. What follows here is an account of what is, as observed,
documented, and verifiable, in commitment to scientific integrity and
human dignity.

Next section establishes the fieldwork settings and methodological
framework, distinguishing between public psychiatric hospitals in Spain
and Italy, domestic environments in Catalonia and Sweden, community and
NGO care networks, and digital and legal spaces of observation. It
articulates a methodology executed under adverse conditions, rooted in
the protocols described in previous chapter, yet shaped by real-time
ethical demands, coercive constraints, and personal endangerment. The
positionality of the researcher as survivor, professional, and embedded
actor enabled access to critical dimensions of institutional violence
and systemic failure often shielded from standard inquiry. Analytical
tools included micro-event mapping, epistemic triangulation, field
notes, and testimonial cross-verification, integrated through a forensic
anthropological and narrative reconstruction approach. Scientific
replicability, ethical safeguards, and evidentiary robustness were
ensured through documentary convergence, contradiction analysis, and
methodological reflexivity under pressure.

Section 4.2 details the institutional logic of psychiatric violence,
examining how diagnosis, labeling, and administrative practice create a
cycle of coercion, narrative foreclosure, and impunity. Through direct
observation and reconstruction of specific cases, it reveals how
unverified diagnoses are recycled, anamnesis ignored, and restraint or
forced treatment applied without procedural or clinical justification.
The complicity of professionals, often silent or constrained by
administrative hierarchies, illustrates how harm is perpetuated not
through ignorance but through institutional design. The field evidence
confirms that what is presented as care frequently functions as
containment, producing archival erasure and moral injury.

Section 4.3 shifts the analytical lens to familial betrayal and its
intersection with institutional violence. It documents how psychiatric
mechanisms are mobilized by families to control, discredit, or exile
relatives, often with the support or indifference of professionals. The
research identifies structural analogues to pasung in Spain and Sweden,
with confinement, medicalization, and exclusion enacted in private
homes. Gendered and generational asymmetries are central to this
dynamic, with women, children, and elders most frequently targeted. The
findings show that far from acting as a protective counterforce,
institutions often amplify familial harm, prioritizing parental or kin
narratives over the subject's lived account, especially in contexts of
economic dependency or social stigma.

Section 4.4 addresses the epistemic consequences of coercion,
emphasizing how psychiatric practice frequently produces the erasure of
personhood. This is achieved through diagnostic reductionism, rejection
of cultural or biographical meaning, and dismissal of explanatory
frameworks that challenge psychiatric hegemony. The material collected
through observation, document analysis, and survivor testimony
illustrates how resistance, spirituality, grief, or somatic expressions
are pathologized and depoliticized. Loss of rights, social abandonment,
and fear of retaliation are recurrent outcomes of this silencing. This
section operationalizes forensic discourse analysis and epistemic
mapping to reveal the mechanisms through which subjectivity is
transformed into administrative data and moral agency into medical
noise.

Section 4.5 centers practices of resistance, recovery, and ethical
witnessing. Despite the pervasive harm documented, numerous participants
demonstrated creative and courageous strategies to reclaim narrative
control, challenge institutional dominance, and survive against
dehumanizing forces. Acts of self-managed care, testimonial writing,
symbolic escape, and covert professional solidarity are analyzed not as
anecdotal exceptions but as key components of a counter-archive. These
practices constitute the foundational elements of an better
infrastructure of dignity and care, one that exists in parallel and
often in opposition to the formal system. They are essential to
understanding how recovery becomes possible where systems fail.

Section 4.6 synthesizes the field-based evidence into systemic insight,
confirming that the patterns observed are not isolated irregularities
but structural features of current psychiatric, legal, and familial
systems. Institutional betrayal emerges as a recurrent phenomenon, not a
breakdown but a function of design. Fieldwork reinforces the
survey-based findings presented in Chapter 3 and prepares the ground for
Chapter 5, where betrayal is theorized as a core logic of the
institutional order. The convergence of narrative, legal, and
ethnographic data confirms the need for deep legal, pedagogical, and
clinical restructuring. This chapter thus completes the empirical
groundwork of the dissertation by documenting the lived experience of
injustice and the scientific imperative to transform the systems that
produce it.

****

****4.2 Fieldwork settings and methodological implementation****

This section deepens the analytical thread of Chapter 4 by detailing the
implementation of the methodological architecture outlined in Chapter 2,
in direct response to the research questions established in Chapter 1.
Rather than reiterate principles already presented, it clarifies how
knowledge was generated under conditions of coercion, institutional
betrayal, and epistemic exclusion, and how this process remained
scientifically accountable despite structural impediments.

Field sites were selected for their diagnostic salience in relation to
psychiatric coercion, pharmacological overreach, legal voids, and
structural violence. These included public psychiatric hospitals in
Spain and Italy, community mental health centers and NGO-affiliated
clinics, family homes, especially in Catalonia and Sweden, and digital
and legal spaces that functioned as informal archives and discursive
arenas. Site selection followed the presence of recurring coercive
dynamics, low legal oversight, and systemic failures in clinical
accountability, not convenience or access. The researcher's position,
simultaneously as professional, survivor, and embedded subject, was
intrinsic to the generation of findings. Rather than a methodological
bias, this positionality allowed access to real-time coercive practices,
legal ambiguities, and social silencing rarely documented in
institutional settings. Observation included external behavior and
internal responses to repeated threats, assaults, and chemically
enforced submission, transforming bodily experience into an additional
vector of analysis. This aligns with a strand in medical anthropology
that affirms the scientific legitimacy of situated, reflexive inquiry
under oppressive conditions.

Methodologically, the research employed embedded presence, constrained
journaling, structured field notes, and retrospective reconstruction
using institutional documents, legal files, and testimonies
cross-verified through survivor networks. Standard interviews and
recordings were largely precluded by risk, replaced by multi-source
triangulation. Validation was achieved through convergence across field
data, survey findings (Chapter 3), and documented clinical and legal
records. Recurrence tracking, contradiction analysis, and micro-event
mapping enabled detection of structural patterns, while
positionality-aware coding safeguarded against interpretive distortion.

Three axes of triangulation were central: alignment between field
experience and survey data; comparison of observed practices with
documented legal and clinical frameworks; and validation of testimonies
against historical and published patterns of psychiatric harm,
diagnostic inflation, and judicial impunity. Expert feedback from
clinicians, survivors, and legal scholars further reinforced analytic
coherence. The methodological stance adopted here was not only adaptive
but necessary. In contexts where formal protections failed, and consent
mechanisms were routinely subverted or weaponized, ethical research
demanded procedural flexibility and forensic attention to traceable
harm. This required transforming research from documentation alone into
a protective mechanism, a means of registering abuses too easily erased
from official record.

This section thus demonstrates the feasibility and necessity of rigorous
field research under constraint, answering how psychiatric coercion
persists despite formal safeguards, how personhood is disqualified
through institutional discourse, and how scientific inquiry can uphold
integrity when legal protections and human dignity are under systemic
threat. It reaffirms that methodological exactitude and reflexive
engagement are not mutually exclusive but essential companions when
documenting structurally produced suffering. While Chapter 2 lays the
theoretical foundation of multi-sited ethnography, critical
phenomenology, and action-research logic, this section serves a distinct
function: to provide standalone justification for the application of
those frameworks in hostile and unpredictable field conditions. This
includes the ethical and analytic safeguards employed to protect
vulnerable informants, the forensic logic guiding data retention and
integrity under threat, and the methods of triangulation used to ensure
credibility and analytic rigor in the absence of conventional interview
protocols or institutional support. The methodological rigor applied
here was calibrated to the exceptional constraints of live coercive
settings, where audio recording or overt consent processes would have
placed informants or the researcher at risk of retaliation, psychiatric
detention, or reputational harm. Instead, the research relied on
embedded presence, real-time ethical appraisal, and retrospective
cross-validation with institutional documentation, survivor networks,
and thematic congruence across data sources.

Triangulation was a recursive and relational process, not a static
technique. It operated across three principal axes: first, comparison of
field experiences with survey findings obtained in the earlier phase of
the research; second, alignment of observed practices with institutional
documents, clinical records, and policy frameworks; third,
cross-checking of testimonies against known patterns of psychiatric
violence, epistemic injustice, and legal neglect. Validation was
achieved through documentary convergence, contradiction analysis,
recurrence tracking, and the active involvement of survivors,
clinicians, and legal experts in verifying plausibility, coherence, and
consistency across narratives. While the chapter draws on legal-forensic
techniques developed in response to systemic impunity, it also applies
epistemological humility, ensuring that power differentials are not
replicated in the representation of suffering.

The methodological logic executed in this chapter is not only consistent
with, but a live enactment of, the commitments outlined in the
theoretical and ethical scaffolding of Chapter 2. It demonstrates how
scientific inquiry can remain rigorous under duress, how abuse can be
documented without reproducing it, and how positionality can be
transformed from liability into epistemic strength. This fieldwork
constitutes not only data collection but a methodological testimony to
the violence of the systems examined and the necessity of developing
inquiry methods that can withstand and document such conditions with
integrity and precision.

## **4.3 the institutional cycle of violence: psychiatric control and complicity**

****A scientifically validated analysis of contemporary psychiatric
systems reveals a persistent and reproducible cycle of institutional
violence that operates both within formal treatment frameworks and
across the wider sociopolitical terrain. This cycle is neither
accidental nor anomalous, it is structurally embedded in the
administrative logic, juridical justifications, and clinical routines
that frame psychiatric interventions as therapeutic, even when their
outcomes are profoundly injurious. The disciplinary function of
psychiatry, particularly in Spain but observable across transnational
field sites, remains linked to broader patterns of domestic and
structural coercion. These patterns are legitimized by institutional
languages of care, while in practice they reproduce systems of control
that deny autonomy, bodily integrity, and epistemic agency.****

The mechanisms of this cycle include forced drugging, unjustified
restraint, involuntary hospitalization, and the systematic denial of
basic procedural guarantees. These measures are often enacted without a
proper anamnesis or diagnostic reevaluation, relying instead on recycled
diagnoses drawn from earlier and frequently unverifiable records. In
multiple documented cases, individuals were subjected to long-term
psychiatric control on the basis of records that had never undergone
scientific or legal scrutiny, yet were cited as definitive. The logic of
these interventions does not align with therapeutic aims, but rather
with risk management, administrative expedience, and symbolic
containment. These mechanisms align not with healing but with
incapacitation and the reproduction of stigma, serving the institution
more than the individual.

This cycle of psychiatric containment is neither confined to clinical
spaces nor reducible to isolated professional decisions. It is deeply
embedded in a broader societal configuration that delegates moral
responsibility and political authority to the psychiatric institution as
a mechanism of social regulation. The violence of such a delegation lies
precisely in its perceived neutrality: family courts, police
departments, schools, and even human rights bodies often reproduce the
same narrative assumptions that psychiatry establishes. Once a person
has been diagnosed and institutionalized, the social field tends to
withdraw critical engagement, acting instead as an amplifier of
exclusion. The effect is cumulative: relatives, coworkers, and even
friends come to interpret emotional expression, resistance, or refusal
not as legitimate responses to adversity or abuse, but as symptoms of
illness to be controlled or silenced.

This social complicity consolidates the institutional cycle, functioning
through omission as much as commission. Families overwhelmed by
unresolved intergenerational trauma or abuse histories may
instrumentalize psychiatry as a means of avoidance, preferring the
medicalization of dissent to the confrontation of violence. Educational
professionals, pressed for time and lacking adequate support, refer
students to mental health services without investigating environmental
or systemic causes. Courts and legal actors, unfamiliar with the
epistemic and ethical limitations of psychiatric judgment, defer to it
as expert truth. As such, a continuum is established, in which domestic
violence, systemic neglect, and institutional abuse are managed through
a shared infrastructure of coercion that presents itself as care.

The psychiatric institution, in this configuration, does not merely
respond to mental health needs, it assumes a disciplinary role by
absorbing and deflecting the contradictions and failures of other
societal systems. When political, familial, or economic structures fail
to provide safety, dignity, or justice, psychiatry becomes the de facto
solution. Yet, rather than addressing the source of distress, it often
redirects blame to the individual, administering interventions that
erase testimony, obscure causal chains, and collapse complex life
histories into decontextualized symptom clusters. In doing so, it
produces what this dissertation identifies as a politically protected
form of epistemic and bodily violence, carried out with clinical
language, scientific pretension, and institutional immunity. The
perpetuation of institutional abuse in psychiatry cannot be fully
understood without examining the societal complicity that sustains it.
Psychiatric institutions do not function in isolation. Rather, they are
enmeshed in a broader sociopolitical ecosystem that grants legitimacy to
coercive practices under the guise of care. Schools, social services,
law enforcement agencies, and even families play decisive roles in
initiating and reinforcing psychiatric control. Teachers referring
disruptive students to psychiatric assessment, judges relying on
psychiatric reports to justify coercive treatment, and families
deferring responsibility to institutional frameworks all contribute to a
diffuse system in which coercion is normalized, expected, and seldom
questioned.

The family, in particular, becomes both the origin and amplifier of
psychiatric labeling, often driven by dynamics of rejection,
misrecognition, or moral panic. It is common in field data that the
first contact with psychiatry was not due to clinical symptoms in a
strict sense, but rather to sociocultural nonconformity, dissent, or
perceived burden. Once labeled, the individual enters a cycle of
containment where professional voices lose autonomy under administrative
directives, and institutional priorities shift from therapeutic support
to disciplinary regulation. This dynamic mirrors historical models of
social control, psychiatry here functions as an enforcer of normality, a
mechanism of silencing rather than understanding, and a buffer against
structural accountability. In such contexts, metabolic,
neurodevelopmental, or ecological dimensions are disregarded in favor of
bureaucratic expediency, a clear departure from any rigorous application
of one health or translational ethics principles.

The epistemological collapse within the system manifests through the
erosion of clinical rigor and the predominance of documentation over
diagnosis. Anamnesis, which in best practices should form the backbone
of any legitimate medical or psychiatric evaluation, is systematically
omitted or replaced by circular, recycled narratives that have long lost
clinical value. Diagnoses are reproduced mechanically, not in response
to observed reality but as bureaucratic expedients serving institutional
agendas. These may stem from outdated files, vague allusions, or prior
coercive encounters, and are rarely verified with the subject or updated
with new evidence. This archival inertia facilitates impunity: once
labeled, the person is framed through a lens of risk, not need, and
their account is dismissed as lacking credibility.

Practitioners often participate in this process indirectly, under
pressure from institutional priorities that favor documentation
compliance and administrative performance over ethical care. Field
observations and testimonies repeatedly reveal that professionals who
object to these practices or attempt to reduce coercion face isolation,
professional sanction, or subtle disqualification. Conversely, those who
follow orders and silence dissent are rewarded with promotions or
institutional support. This incentive structure displaces clinical
responsibility toward risk management and liability avoidance, resulting
in harm. The system values coherence with past documentation over
correspondence with present clinical truth. This detachment between
diagnostic acts and actual health status constitutes not only
malpractice but a structural breach of the bioethical principles of
beneficence and non-maleficence. The very tools of medicine are turned
against those they are meant to serve.

Findings from extended ethnographic fieldwork into contrasting negative
and positive dynamics, tied directly to the thesis research questions
and validated through embedded observation. It draws from
cross-contextual analysis across psychiatric institutions, familial
systems, legal frameworks, and informal care settings. The positive
proposals are detailed in the thesis as necessary reforms to ensure
lawful, ethical, and scientifically grounded care.

These dynamics give rise to a broader coercive loop, sustained by a
structural logic of entrapment. It begins with a triggering episode,
frequently a situation of social, familial, or interpersonal
vulnerability, which is interpreted through a pathologizing lens rather
than addressed contextually. A diagnosis is assigned, often without a
thorough examination or proper anamnesis, locking the individual into a
frame from which exit becomes nearly impossible. Once this
classification is recorded, it initiates a self-reinforcing circuit:
treatment decisions reference prior records, not current realities, and
coercive interventions are justified by the presumed risk inferred from
the diagnosis itself. This cyclical process, diagnosis, coercion,
containment, narrative closure, repeats across institutions and
practitioners, shielding the system from accountability and foreclosing
any meaningful reassessment.

The process of narrative closure is central to this mechanism. Rather
than supporting recovery, it systematically erases dissenting voices.
Testimonies of abuse or objections to diagnosis are marked as symptoms
of illness. Complaints are reframed as paranoia or resistance. Requests
for review or better care are taken as evidence of lack of insight. This
not only dehumanizes but also medicalizes resistance, undermining any
possibility of structural redress. Events such as forced medication,
physical restraint, and even severe bodily harm become absent from the
medical record, or else are transcribed in passive voice, divorced from
agency or accountability. The archival erasure of violence, whether
through omission, euphemism, or distortion, solidifies impunity and
perpetuates cycles of harm. It is not merely an ethical failure but a
structural epistemicide, where the knowledge and lived experience of the
person are systematically silenced by institutional record.

The convergence of coercion and impunity is not a malfunction but a
defining feature of psychiatric institutional practice under current
frameworks. Administrative priorities are dictated less by therapeutic
logic than by legal defensibility, reputational risk management, and
operational efficiency. The psychiatric file, rather than functioning as
an evolving clinical tool, becomes a legal shield, designed to preempt
liability, justify interventions, and silence potential controversy.
Professionals are not only discouraged from questioning past entries but
may be disciplined for raising concerns that contradict dominant
narratives. The written record assumes a juridical function that
overrides its medical purpose, and the epistemic authority of psychiatry
is deployed to naturalize systemic violence.

Such dynamics are not limited to clinical institutions. Family members,
educational staff, and social workers often contribute, willingly or
inadvertently, to the entrapment cycle. Families overwhelmed by care
duties or drawn into cultural scripts of deviance and rehabilitation may
interpret distress as pathology and demand institutional response.
Schools and social services, unequipped or unwilling to accommodate
non-normative behaviour, default to referral and diagnosis. In many
cases, their testimonies are given more weight than that of the
individual subjected to treatment, especially when social standing,
gender, ethnicity, or language are used, explicitly or implicitly, to
discredit self-report. The continuity of institutional control is thus
enacted across a network of actors, all linked by a tacit agreement that
containment is safer than understanding, and erasure preferable to
accountability.

The reinforcement of violence through interconnected institutional
layers reveals a systemic disregard for foundational principles of
biomedical ethics and human rights law. The persistent use of coercion,
especially in the form of involuntary treatment, sedation, and forced
hospitalization, is rationalized through a distorted application of the
principle of beneficence, often detached from both patient will and
long-term outcomes. This misapplication reflects a broader
epistemological corruption: the substitution of clinical uncertainty
with administrative certainty, and of complexity with binary labels. In
effect, psychiatry becomes the operational arm of social control,
disguising repression as care and trauma induction as stabilization.

This process is neither random nor rare. It reflects a stable system of
incentives whereby documentation is weaponized and consent rendered
performative. Practitioners report being routinely pressured to fill in
records in a manner that protects institutions rather than truthfully
reflects events. These distortions are structurally embedded: adverse
incidents may be reclassified or omitted, with the assumption that
patients' narratives are unreliable, emotionally distorted, or
irrelevant. Testimony is pathologized rather than verified. At the same
time, families and external actors are encouraged to contribute to the
shaping of records without oversight, reinforcing a cycle of
interpretative closure. This closure ensures that psychiatric violence,
once initiated, is maintained and validated through self-referential
systems of documentation, despite contradicting observable health
outcomes or lived realities.

The harm produced by such cycles is cumulative. Each act of
misdiagnosis, force, or negation of personhood amplifies prior trauma
and closes further avenues for legal or clinical redress. Individuals
subjected to this regime describe a sense of epistemic obliteration: to
speak is to invite reinterpretation, and to resist is to confirm
pathology. The psychiatric system not only disciplines the body but
rewrites the subject. By severing access to narrative, it denies
identity, continuity, and ultimately, the possibility of recovery as
defined by the individual, not by the institution. These mechanisms do
not operate in isolation within psychiatric institutions but are
mirrored across legal, familial, and educational systems that cooperate,
actively or passively, in the enforcement of the same coercive logics.
Schools, social services, and judicial bodies often defer to psychiatric
authority without scrutiny, reinforcing a presumption of validity for
all psychiatric narratives regardless of origin, revision, or
contradiction. This deferral generates what may be termed a *delegated
authoritarianism*, wherein non-medical systems legitimize psychiatric
action without bearing the ethical or scientific responsibility for its
outcomes. Children and adolescents are especially vulnerable within this
configuration, as disciplinary interventions at school may trigger
psychiatric referrals, and vice versa, initiating a cycle of diagnosis,
labeling, and control that transcends any one institution's boundaries.

Family systems, particularly under stress, conflict, or structural
disadvantage, may act as the initial and most enduring enforcers of
psychiatric violence, whether through explicit demands for
institutionalization or through subtle delegitimization of the child's
or relative's speech. The delegation of caregiving responsibilities to
psychiatric systems becomes a form of social outsourcing, often driven
by exhaustion, fear, or misinformation. This handover reinforces the
fantasy that healing can be enacted through control, and that suffering
can be silenced through medication. It also creates a cycle wherein
relational problems are depoliticized and re-individualized, allowing
structural harms, poverty, violence, discrimination, to be reinterpreted
as internal defects in those who suffer their effects. Those systems, as
any other institution, is suspect.

This multi-institutional complicity creates what can be described as a
continuum of coercion and epistemic erasure, within which individual
dissent or resistance is systematically reframed as symptomatology. Even
when harm is visible, bruises from restraint, cognitive deterioration
from overmedication, dissociative collapse from forced hospitalization,
the response is often a doubling-down on control mechanisms. Any
questioning of psychiatric authority, particularly from those already
labeled, is dismissed as a lack of insight. This not only delegitimizes
opposition but functions as a trapdoor logic: the more harm one resists,
the more pathology one is said to embody.

In this setting, institutional betrayal is not a breakdown of a system
meant to care, but the expected result of a system designed to obscure
responsibility through distributed impunity. Rather than being
exceptional or accidental, betrayal is embedded in the way information
is structured, decisions are made, and records are curated. This
architecture of violence hides in plain sight, operating not at the
margins of psychiatry but through its procedural core.

This architecture of violence is maintained through a sophisticated
entanglement of symbolic authority, operational opacity, and
pseudo-scientific ritual. Professional protocols, legal documentation,
and diagnostic language produce an illusion of rigor, objectivity, and
care, while obscuring the actual power dynamics at play. Clinical files
often contain circular logic, diagnosis justifying treatment, and
treatment justifying further containment, without empirical reassessment
or patient-led narrative. The process becomes one of bureaucratic
self-replication, whereby errors and omissions are not corrected but
solidified through accumulation and procedural sanctification. These are
not passive oversights but mechanisms of control grounded in material
effects: they produce disability, dependency, and social exclusion.

Meanwhile, structural barriers to redress remain nearly absolute.
Victims of psychiatric violence, even when aware of their rights, face
insurmountable hurdles in accessing justice. The courts often rely on
the very psychiatric institutions under scrutiny to provide evidence or
expert testimony, reproducing conflicts of interest and shielding
impunity. Mechanisms of appeal are either inaccessible, undermined, or
symbolic, resulting in institutional closures rather than systemic
accountability. Even public complaints or critical reporting are defused
through administrative delay, fragmented responsibility, and the
psychological pathologization of the complainant.

This state of epistemic and institutional capture has profound
consequences for both science and ethics. When entire populations are
excluded from knowledge production, when their speech is erased, their
pain misread, their resistance recoded as pathology, the scientific
enterprise collapses into circularity. Validity, in such a context, is
not established through falsifiability, replication, or lived
applicability, but through repetition, authority, and institutional
endorsement. Psychiatry, as critiqued here, loses its capacity to heal
because it ceases to listen. It becomes an instrument not of care but of
containment, whose effects are sustained by law, economics, and social
consensus.

To break this cycle, the dissertation calls for a paradigmatic shift
grounded in bio-cultural integrity, epistemic justice, and participatory
design. The path forward is not merely regulatory or technocratic, but
existential and civilizational. It requires an unmasking of the routines
of violence that hide beneath clinical euphemism, an ethical
reconstruction of medical authority, and the restitution of narrative
sovereignty to those whose lives have been managed instead of heard. The
subsequent chapters explore how such transformation can begin, rooted in
the collective intelligence and scientific testimony of those too long
excluded from both protection and authorship; always co-authorship, in a
society, from responsible co-authorizators and criminal ones.

## 

## **4.4 Familial betrayal and the domestic-institutional continuum**

In contemporary psychiatric ecosystems, the family is often positioned
rhetorically as a site of support, emotional stability, and
post-discharge care. However, data from this research and others show
that the family frequently operates as a primary vector of coercion,
particularly in domestic environments marked by gender asymmetries,
economic dependency, or social stigma. Numerous accounts collected
throughout this study document the use of psychiatric frameworks to
silence, discredit, or remove kin whose behavior diverges from normative
expectations. This includes not only overt forms of coercion, such as
forced hospitalization requests or collusion with legal guardianship
mechanisms, but also subtle, long-term strategies of narrative
manipulation. In such contexts, psychiatric diagnosis becomes a tool of
symbolic violence, transforming dissent into pathology, critique into
delusion, and vulnerability into dangerousness.

The medicalization of familial conflict generates a systematic
misalignment between clinical narratives and subjective experience. When
families initiate psychiatric referrals under coercive conditions, the
diagnostic process itself is contaminated by strategic omissions,
exaggerations, or falsified behavior reports. These narratives, once
codified in institutional records, acquire a procedural inertia that
becomes almost impossible to reverse. The subject's voice is displaced
by a curated pathology, reified by repetition across medical, legal, and
social service systems. Such dynamics are particularly prevalent in
Spanish and Swedish institutional cultures, where the family retains a
normative legitimacy as a proxy decision-maker, even in the absence of
accountability mechanisms or oversight. Clinical records reflect this
structural bias, often echoing initial accusations or claims without
independent verification.

The data gathered through ethnographic immersion and narrative
reconstruction reveal that many psychiatric referrals are initiated not
in response to clinical crisis but as a means of social exclusion.
Behavioral deviance, intergenerational conflict, or non-normative
sexuality are reframed through psychiatric lenses as disorder. The
widespread practice of leveraging mental health systems to impose
domestic control, particularly over women, adolescents, and elderly kin,
aligns with global literature on the gendered and generational
deployment of psychiatry. The framing of concern as care masks a deeper
logic of social containment, frequently endorsed by institutional actors
who regard family narratives as more trustworthy than the contested
accounts of those diagnosed.

The pathologization of unwanted, despised, enjoyed upon kin does not
occur in a vacuum. It is amplified by broader sociocultural dynamics,
including structural sexism, normative ableism, and a persistent
cultural fear of deviance. Social contagion, in this context, refers to
the discursive and procedural replication of exclusionary logics across
institutions. Once a psychiatric label has been affixed, particularly
one carrying implications of unpredictability or violence, media
representations, school systems, and welfare agencies tend to align with
the family's version of reality, further isolating the individual. This
recursive affirmation of the initial coercive frame fosters a totalizing
narrative structure, often impervious to clinical revision or judicial
challenge.

The mimicking of pasung-like confinement conditions within European
homes has emerged as a recurring pattern in this research. Although
pasung, or shackling, is officially recognized as a human rights
violation in Indonesia and elsewhere, domestic psychiatric restraint
practices in Spain and Sweden remain under-documented and unregulated.
Multiple accounts detail confinement, chemical restraint, and social
isolation implemented informally within households, particularly in
cases involving elderly dependents, disabled family members, or those
with contested gender identities. These conditions persist in part due
to institutional complicity: health and social service professionals
frequently defer to familial authority, despite indications of abuse or
false reporting.

This chapter thus examines familial betrayal and sadistic crime,
enslavement, other and all tortures, not as an interpersonal failing but
as a structural interface between domestic and institutional power. The
role of the family in psychiatric control cannot be fully understood
without accounting for the clinical inertia that ensues when unverified
histories, lies, are embedded into medical records. Early demise. The
following parts will expand on the epistemic closure mechanisms, legal
reinforcement dynamics, gendered dimensions, and consequences for
clinical and scientific integrity.

Once a psychiatric so-called narrative is initiated by familial actors
and institutionalized through documentation, the medical apparatus often
becomes complicit in the maintenance of that narrative, regardless of
its empirical validity. Clinical inertia refers to the resistance of
diagnostic and treatment protocols to change, even in the presence of
new evidence or the withdrawal of initial complaints. In psychiatry,
this inertia is not merely a matter of professional oversight or
bureaucratic delay. It is a systemic property rooted in the asymmetry of
credibility between patients and institutional gatekeepers. When a
diagnosis is formulated in response to familial pressure or
misinformation, subsequent clinical encounters tend to reaffirm rather
than reassess the initial conclusions. This produces a cascade effect in
which each entry in the medical record reiterates, amplifies, and
legitimizes the original frame of deviance, thereby reducing the
possibility of diagnostic revision or ethical intervention. Loathing on
lives, with clinical histories a facade.

**Documented dynamics of psychiatric control and betrayal within
domestic-institutional continuums, with reinforcement loops and
medical-institutional silencing operating transgenerationally.**

The epistemological closure is facilitated by a culture of bureaucratic
risk aversion and medico-legal defensiveness. Practitioners, under
pressure to ensure continuity and compliance with prior documentation,
often replicate rather than interrogate the assumptions embedded in past
assessments. This dynamic is particularly evident in situations where
patients contest their diagnoses or treatment plans. Rather than
triggering re-evaluation, resistance is typically interpreted as a
symptom of pathology, reinforcing the need for control. In this way, the
possibility of error is institutionally neutralized. The narrative
established by the family becomes a self-fulfilling clinical protocol,
sanctioned by layers of medical documentation that exclude the patient's
account from epistemic legitimacy. Loathing on lives, again, with those
anamnesi and formulations, a travesti.

This process is exacerbated by digitalization and the widespread
integration of interoperable health records across care systems. In
contexts such as Spain and Sweden, once a psychiatric diagnosis is
entered into the digital system, it becomes accessible to a range of
actors across multiple domains of care. The diagnostic label, often
imprecisely defined or based on contested family reports, is treated as
fact. Each clinician accessing the record becomes a node in the
replication of that narrative, further embedding the initial coercive
logic into the institutional memory. Clinical inertia, in this sense, is
not simply a failure of individual judgment. It is a structural effect
of digital epistemology, whereby the first narrative becomes the only
one that can be credibly cited and reproduced.

The implications for scientific integrity are profound. Data collected
in such environments do not reflect objective symptomatology but rather
the echo chamber of institutional consensus, generated through coercion
and sustained through repetition. The diagnosis, stripped of its
original contested context, is used to justify interventions ranging
from medication to detention, without independent reassessment. This
undermines not only the therapeutic relationship but also the validity
of psychiatric science itself, which becomes reliant on recycled and
institutionally reinforced errors. The credibility gap between medical
records and lived experience widens into an epistemic chasm, in which
patient suffering is pathologized but never heard, and clinical truth
becomes indistinguishable from bureaucratic inertia. Early demised,
histories to be, lives lost. Destroyed.

In subsequent parts, the analysis will move toward the sociocultural and
gendered dimensions of these dynamics, highlighting how institutional
actors reinforce familial authority despite evidence of abuse, and how
such entrenchment impairs the capacity of psychiatric systems to correct
or even acknowledge foundational error. The systemic entrenchment of
psychiatric narratives initiated within coercive or abusive familial
contexts reveals not only a clinical vulnerability but a foundational
legal and epistemological void. This void is filled not by empirical
rigor but by deference, often uncritical, to proxies of moral authority,
namely the family and its representatives. In this dissertation, such
patterns are analyzed not as anomalies, but as predictable outcomes of
institutional architectures that prioritize procedural efficiency and
legal insulation over truth-seeking or reparative justice. As shown in
the preceding ethnographic reconstructions and supported by
interdisciplinary literature, psychiatric institutions often become the
extension of domestic control mechanisms when clinical autonomy is
compromised by structural bias and narrative inertia. Rather than
providing oversight or independent evaluation, these institutions
reproduce and amplify familial coercion under the guise of care,
particularly in contexts where law fails to differentiate protection
from collusion. From all accounts, literature and expert witnessing:
crimes.

At the core of this betrayal lies a refusal to acknowledge that neglect
is not merely the absence of care, but a form of harm with biological,
psychological, and legal implications. From a physiological standpoint,
sustained emotional neglect and coercive control induce maladaptive
neuroplastic changes, affecting limbic structures, prefrontal
connectivity, and stress-response systems, that predispose individuals
to chronic illness and psychological collapse. This is not a
metaphorical collapse, but a cascade of pathophysiological processes
including immune suppression, neuroendocrine dysregulation, and
neurodegenerative thinning linked to allostatic overload. The social
brain, as an embodied organ, deteriorates when relational meaning is
replaced by systemic invalidation, and when the very institutions
mandated to protect are complicit in the enactment of epistemic and
psychological violence. The path from relational trauma to institutional
betrayal is often paved through a grey legal zone, where acts of
coercion, confinement, and psychological assault remain undetected or
unpunished because they are perpetrated within private spaces, domestic,
clinical, or otherwise. This legal opacity has historical roots in
colonial and patriarchal governance systems that naturalized the family
as a moral authority and shielded intra-familial harm from state
intervention. Echoes of this history are present in the ongoing
tolerance of pasung-like conditions in Europe and globally. Whether
through physical restraint, chemical sedation, or narrative erasure, the
core mechanism is the same: suppression of autonomy through the
instrumentalization of care. The rule of law is suspended not through
formal declarations, but through routinized omission, by omitting to
ask, to verify, to listen.

The practice of violence within family units is not only a modern
anomaly, it is deeply rooted in historical and cross-cultural protocols.
In some monarchic and aristocratic systems, the elimination of kin was
institutionalized as a legitimate means to secure succession and
inheritance rights. European royal houses routinely engaged in
fratricide or regicide, often under the guise of state necessity.
Ottoman princes were subject to fratricide by law, whereby the enthroned
sultan was authorized to kill his brothers to secure dynastic
continuity. Similarly, in ancient China, purges of rival family members
during imperial transitions were sanctioned by court ritual and dynastic
tradition, often with public legitimization. This cultural embedding of
intra-familial killing as protocol illustrates how power and inheritance
have historically overruled relational ethics, even as those acts were
cloaked in legality and tradition.

In contemporary times, though absolute monarchies have largely faded,
the residual logic persists in less institutionalized forms, such as
domestic inheritance disputes in South Asia where familial violence
peaks in contested succession, or in certain communal traditions where
property rights trump individual dignity. These contexts reveal that the
legal grey zone around family violence is not limited to negligence or
psychiatric coercion, it extends to premeditated, politically sanctioned
harm cloaked in kinship legitimacy. To underscore how family structures
across cultures can condone or conceal severe violence, here are case
summaries from diverse traditions accounted:

**Table 42. Historical and cross-cultural patterns of familial
violence**

  ---------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Ottoman empire                     Fratricide by law                                          Succession stability; seen as state ritual, rarely legally challenged
  Imperial china                     Elimination of rival princes                               Political cleanse in name of dynastic harmony
  South asian joint-family systems   Violence over inheritance distribution                     Internal arbitration, minimal legal scrutiny
  European aristocracies             Poisoning, execution of heirs                              Political expedience, noble privilege shields crimes
  Manson family style cults          Familial murder sanctioned by patriarchal cult structure   Internal hierarchy, blurred moral/legal boundaries
  ---------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------

This table synthesizes findings from multi-sited ethnographic research
and cross-sector survey data gathered for this dissertation. It
illustrates how familial structures, across historical periods and
cultural contexts, have functioned as sites of violence, not exception.
Patterns identified through testimonies, case narratives, and field
documentation highlight that such violence is often legitimized by
tradition, obscured by legal grey zones, or reframed as care. These
insights demonstrate the need for a scientific and legal reframing of
the family not as a sanctuary, but as a potential site of sanctioned
harm requiring full human rights oversight.

This catalog demonstrates that familial violence, including lethal
forms, is not external to history or legality; it is often **constituted
by them**. The modern family remains a legally ambivalent institution,
where proximity and intimacy justify a different threshold for what is
considered crime. As in the cult cases, and often normalized structural
hierarchies as traditionally mandated ones, abuse within a family-like
group is often protected by a presumption of autonomy and privacy until
extreme violence forces intervention; boundaries trespassed almost if
mandatory, pride and honor being killing or maiming one in the pride,
the troop, the murder of crows, as survey respondents got it when naming
their own. Now all able to afford a bed, as if princeling cubs battling
for inheritance, those subject to criminal ones reported. Across most
traditions and legal systems, the family is the primary context where
the gravest interpersonal crimes occur, including homicide, sexual
abuse, and long-term psychological harm. Intimate partner violence,
child maltreatment, and elder abuse are consistently more frequent
within familial settings than in public or institutional spaces.
Cultural ideals of loyalty, privacy, and honor often shield such crimes
from scrutiny or prosecution, particularly where patriarchal or
hierarchical norms dominate. In Spain, despite formal legal protections,
domestic violence, including gender-based violence and coercive
psychiatric interventions, remains underreported and frequently
tolerated within both family systems and institutional frameworks.
Mental health law is particularly vulnerable to exploitation due to its
reliance on subjective clinical judgments, asymmetrical credibility
between professionals and patients, and legal assumptions that equate
risk with illness and family with benevolence. In practice, vague
criteria for involuntary treatment or guardianship, such as perceived
danger or lack of insight, allow for expansive discretionary power,
often exercised without robust procedural safeguards. These structural
ambiguities facilitate the silencing of dissenting voices and the
institutionalization of private conflicts, especially when family
members initiate the process. The widespread legal fiction that
psychiatrists act solely in the best interest of the patient, and that
families are protective by default, creates a permissive environment for
coercion, false testimony, and narrative manipulation. Without
enforceable checks, such as independent review, legal aid, or
evidentiary thresholds, mental health legislation becomes a tool easily
gamed by those with access, status, or intent to control.

By the time the abuses are self-evident, it often is too late, held by
lies and mutual benefit, that being pleasure and profit, status as
hierarchical control against the kin or alleged kin, blood tied or
brothers, sisters, parents in law as step parents, not respecting the
legality but their own desires. The pathologization and criminalization
of dissenting family members -that being the victims, not the
perpetrators, most often- through psychiatric means, wherein a son,
daughter, or sibling is declared mentally ill and confined due to the
suffering inflicted, medicated and socially excluded, becomes an updated
form of symbolic violence; a very useful way to discredit and silence,
keep caged. These acts mirror the outright eliminations of the past;
they are not exceptional but structurally equivalent: both shift power
into the hands of a gatekeeper, whether a king, priest, or clinician,
masking domination with legitimacy. Whether through poisoning, shackles,
or pharmaceuticals, the outcome remains the same: one individual is
forcibly removed, silenced to maintain an existing order, a will.
