## **Chapter 6 - Legal and ethical dimensions: norms, violations, and accountability**

**Summary: **This chapter examines the legal and normative frameworks
that govern psychiatric intervention in Spain, assessing their
constitutional foundations, systemic failures, and international
obligations. Drawing directly from empirical evidence, it interrogates
how formal guarantees are undermined by subjective criteria, procedural
gaps, and institutional drift, producing systemic impunity. The goal is
not activist advocacy, but restoration of a functional, evidence-based
feedback loop between law, ethics, clinical practice, and research.

**6.** ****Introduction - legality of coercive care as standard****

The psychiatric-legal interface, as evidenced by the empirical body of
this dissertation, reveals a structurally codified set of normative
assumptions that permit, and in many cases catalyze, medically induced
harm under the guise of therapeutic intervention (Dixon, 2015). Contrary
to the constitutional and clinical expectation that all procedures in
medicine serve restorative, proportional, and least-restrictive
functions, the operative legal architecture in contemporary Spain, and
in parallel, other European jurisdictions, permits the routinization of
involuntary, non-consensual, and pathologizing interventions through a
matrix of exceptions that have become functional norms. These structural
conditions enable epistemic capture, clinical inertia, and multiscalar
violations of bodily, cognitive, and social autonomy.

The most critical and recurrent legal indeterminacy emerges from the
discretionary authority granted to clinicians, institutional
administrators, and non-forensic psychiatric personnel to suspend the
rights of individuals, often indefinitely, without adversarial
mechanisms or independent review. This discretionary framework allows
the suspension of basic rights, including those enshrined in the
European Convention on Human Rights and the Spanish Constitution, via
subjective interpretations of mental status, risk, and non-collaborative
behavior. These judgments are frequently derived from third-party
reports, especially familial actors whose interests may conflict with
those of the person targeted. Empirical data presented in this
dissertation demonstrate that psychiatric certifications and diagnostic
procedures frequently rely on unverified or manipulable information that
is then codified into medical records with institutional inertia. These
codifications function as irreversible inscriptions within digital
medical systems, reproducing systemic bias across clinical contexts,
emergency interventions, judicial proceedings, and social services
(Goffman, 1961).

Concomitantly, the legal system authorizes the delegation of custodial
and decisional power to family members, irrespective of abuse
indicators, relational conflict, or historical evidence of harm. This
delegation is presumed protective yet frequently results in prolonged
exposure to domestic control mechanisms that mimic institutional
constraint. Such familial control is often legalized through
guardianship laws, forced admission procedures, or consent waivers, all
lacking trauma-informed criteria or forensic scrutiny. These provisions
constitute a biopolitical collapse between intimacy and governance,
whereby the domestic sphere becomes an unregulated zone of psychiatric
intervention, particularly when supported by institutional actors that
do not conduct independent assessments (Ehrenberg, 2010).

The second structural loophole resides in the opacity and epistemic
asymmetry of medical documentation. While records function legally as
clinical evidence, they are selectively curated, inaccessible in
practice to those they affect, and resistant to amendment or correction.
Patients and families not in alliance with institutional narratives lack
any operative means of record rectification or evidence-based
counter-assertion (Rosenquist, Fowler, & Christakis, 2011). Legal
prerogatives grant near-total authority to center directors and
supervising clinicians to redact, deny, or withhold documentation,
including contested diagnostic labels, subjective impressions, and
fabricated behavioral histories. These practices produce cascading
epistemic distortions across the health-legal-administrative continuum.
They contribute to chronic medical neglect, increase the risk of
pharmacological overexposure, and institutionalize diagnostic
misattributions with transgenerational repercussions.

The evidentiary base of this thesis illustrates that suicidality,
behavioral dysregulation, and identity fragmentation are not isolated
mental states but systemic consequences of such intersecting
legal-medical violence. When individuals attempt to resist, protest, or
exit these circuits of control, their resistance is recoded as further
pathology, thus justifying additional containment. This recursive logic
is shielded by medical privilege and institutional self-referentiality.
Clinical epistemology, when not tempered by independent audit or
pluralistic verification, becomes a vehicle for harm. Psychiatric
practice ceases to be governed by the Hippocratic imperative to do no
harm and instead functions as an armature of biopolitical exclusion and
control (Priest, 2021).

The diagnostic, legal, and institutional structures governing mental
health in Spain, while ostensibly aligned with principles of care, have
evolved into mechanisms of legitimized harm, made possible by a series
of regulatory omissions and procedural loopholes that have become
structurally normalized. At the heart of this dysfunction is the
unqualified authority conferred to mental health professionals and
center administrators to enact and prolong coercive interventions based
on subjective interpretations of behavior, affect, and alleged risk,
absent rigorous standards of verification, trauma-informed assessment,
or adversarial review. The prevailing legislative framework delegates to
clinicians a form of legal-medical sovereignty that suspends
constitutional rights without need for immediate judicial authorization,
allowing for the enactment of involuntary treatment, forced
hospitalization, polypharmacy, and social sequestration based on opaque
thresholds of dangerousness or lack of insight. These interventions,
once deployed, often become indefinitely self-perpetuating, buttressed
by institutional inertia and the selective memorialization of patient
behavior through undocumented, uncorrected, or outright falsified
clinical records. Empirical data from this thesis confirm that patient
access to records is frequently denied or obstructed; that entries are
curated to fit a controlling narrative; and that redress or correction
is structurally impossible once a diagnostic pathway is
institutionalized (Paris, 2020).

In parallel, one of the most consequential but rarely examined legal
failures lies in the codified deference to family members as default
agents of psychiatric judgment and custodial authority. Guardianship
laws and involuntary admission statutes frequently empower family
members, often without any forensic or relational screening, to act as
proxies for the state and clinical system, transferring the locus of
control from the individual to those who may be socially or economically
incentivized to pathologize them. This dynamic creates a feedback loop
whereby psychiatric power becomes a tool of domestic control, enabled by
legal fictions of familial benevolence. Survey results and fieldwork
data presented in this dissertation detail numerous instances in which
individuals were forcibly institutionalized, overmedicated, or denied
access to their children based on unverified accusations or conflicts
with relatives, with no subsequent legal or clinical review. Once
embedded into the clinical file, these accusations become institutional
fact, resistant to contradiction, and shaping all subsequent engagements
across health, legal, and social service domains (Montero Carrera,
2020).

This delegation of authority to unvetted family members becomes
especially dangerous in situations of preexisting abuse, intimate
partner violence, or inherited patterns of intergenerational trauma.
However, the Spanish legal code remains silent on the obligation to
evaluate family dynamics prior to allowing custodial power or
influencing psychiatric decisions (Christakis & Fowler, 2009).
Protective protocols are absent or unenforced. Even when patients report
abuse or coercion by family members, these disclosures are often
reframed as symptoms of paranoia or noncompliance, and their credibility
is systemically discredited. The law thereby perpetuates a clinical
culture in which abusive family structures are legitimized, and the
person subjected to them is further pathologized for resisting or
seeking refuge.

Compounding this institutional failure is the lack of enforceable
procedures to ensure informed consent, the right to deprescribe, or
access to independent second opinions, particularly in cases where
adverse reactions to medications, cognitive decline, or somatic damage
are already evident. The biomedical architecture in which psychiatry
operates does not obligate the clinician to re-evaluate the necessity or
proportionality of pharmacological regimens unless prompted by
institutional protocols, which are often vague, outdated, or selectively
applied. There is no legal duty to initiate deprescription, even when
harm is demonstrable. In many psychiatric settings, the combination of
drugs with contraindicated substances, such as alcohol, or the
administration of medications under duress or without procedural clarity
remains common practice. These acts, despite their direct violation of
medical ethics and scientific guidelines, remain legally unchallenged
due to the clinician\'s procedural immunity and the broader systemic
reluctance to interrogate psychiatry\'s internal governance. When death
ensues, as often occurs through suicide, over-sedation, or progressive
iatrogenic disability, the event is typically reframed post hoc as a
natural progression of the supposed disorder, thereby exonerating the
system from scrutiny and attributing the outcome to intrinsic patient
pathology (Wyman, 2023).

This systemic insulation from liability reproduces cycles of structural
violence under the cover of medical legitimacy. It is further sustained
by the legal system's failure to provide mechanisms of real-time
accountability, particularly in cases of institutional misconduct, data
falsification, or documented epistemic abuse (Dayalu & Chou, 2008;
Degnin, 2009; Paris, 2024). The structural asymmetry in documentation
access, combined with the presumed infallibility of the medical
professional, allows for the widespread medical erasure of lived
experience and the historical rewriting of patient reality. Survey
respondents consistently reported this dynamic, being silenced,
misrepresented, or denied any narrative agency, as among the most
damaging aspects of their psychiatric experiences. The result is not
only a clinical breach, but a legal one, whereby fundamental rights such
as liberty, bodily integrity, informed consent, and redress are
suspended without adequate procedural safeguards (Oldani, 2014).

A truly preventive mental health system would require structural
realignment at every point of this clinical-legal architecture. This
includes the obligation to conduct independent trauma screening and
abuse risk assessment before any psychiatric measure is considered; the
establishment of automatic legal audits in cases of involuntary
admission or polypharmacy; the imposition of legal consequences for
unreported adverse effects or negligence in deprescription; and the
creation of patient-led oversight bodies with access to institutional
records and the authority to trigger independent forensic reviews.
Without these systemic correctives, the psychiatric system will remain a
site of selective justice, operating outside the bounds of scientific
integrity and constitutional protection. The very ethos of medicine, as
a restorative, accountable, and rights-respecting discipline, requires
that these reforms be implemented not as discretionary ideals, but as
enforced legal obligations, grounded in empirical data and bioethical
principle.

****

**6.1 National legal context: formal guarantees and operational gaps**

****The Spanish legal framework declares a comprehensive catalogue of
rights that include personal liberty, physical and mental integrity,
privacy, and health, as well as legal capacity and procedural safeguards
for individuals with disabilities. These guarantees are articulated in
the Spanish Constitution of 1978, specifically Articles 10, 15, 17, 18,
and 43, and elaborated in sectoral norms such as Ley 41/2002 de
Autonomía del Paciente, Ley General de Sanidad (14/1986), and Ley 8/2021
sobre derechos de las personas con discapacidad. Spain is bound by
international obligations such as the European Convention on Human
Rights and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities. However, the operational application of these protections
reveals a systematic disjunction between their declarative content and
institutional practice. The legacy of authoritarian medical paternalism
remains deeply embedded in mental health governance, where clinical
discretion continues to function as a mechanism of control. Psychiatry,
rather than adhering to dialogical or trauma-informed care standards,
remains empowered to enact restrictions on liberty and bodily autonomy
without transparent checks, multi-professional oversight, or narrative
accountability. This reflects not only a juridical limitation but a
broader epistemic paradigm wherein care is equated with domination and
safety with containment.****

****The most significant legal breach is observed in the expansive and
imprecise use of the subjective risk criterion to justify coercive
interventions. Article 763 of the Spanish Civil Procedure Act, Ley de
Enjuiciamiento Civil, authorizes involuntary admission and treatment on
the basis of a professional's assertion of danger to self or others,
often implemented by a single psychiatrist without corroborating
evaluation or context-specific reasoning. This clause, which legally
enables the deprivation of liberty and psychopharmacological imposition,
is frequently activated without any formal obligation to document
substantiated evidence of imminent or probable harm. There are no
uniform clinical thresholds, evidence standards, or time-sensitive
reassessment mechanisms. Judicial review, when it occurs, is typically
perfunctory and based exclusively on the initial medical report, which
itself is often constructed without structured risk assessment,
longitudinal data, or input from the individual affected. Regional
disparities in its application reveal profound structural arbitrariness.
In many ****instances, fieldwork confirms that this legal provision
operates not as a protective mechanism but as a gateway for the
unchecked exercise of coercion under the guise of medical necessity. The
affected subject is transformed into a legal object of management rather
than a biological and relational being endowed with agency and
rights.****

****Additional and compounding failures occur in the procedural aspects
surrounding psychiatric detention and treatment. Legal provisions
formally recognize the right to be informed of one\'s situation, to
access a second medical opinion, to obtain free legal counsel, and to
contest interventions judicially. However, empirical evidence from
professional and user surveys, combined with field testimonies,
indicates that these rights are systematically undermined. Individuals
rarely receive timely or comprehensible information about their legal
status or clinical options. The request for a second opinion is
obstructed by internal resistance, lack of institutional infrastructure,
and generalized fear of retaliation. Legal aid is often delayed,
under-resourced, or passive, and in many cases, representation is
assigned without adequate psychiatric knowledge or independent inquiry.
Judicial control mechanisms prescribed under Article 763 LEC are
procedurally weak, relying exclusively on the same medical accounts that
prompted the intervention, without reevaluation or verification. The
person's narrative, medical history, and consent are subsumed under
pathologizing assumptions that are neither questioned nor balanced by
counter-evidence. Anamnesis is rarely redone. The cycle of documentation
often replicates and consolidates previous diagnostic designations, even
if based on erroneous or outdated data. This produces a cascade effect,
whereby old entries anchor new decisions, and critical reassessment
becomes structurally impossible.****

****A further legal void, both ethically and practically significant,
arises from the obfuscation or inaccessibility of clinical records.
According to the Ley Orgánica 3/2018 de Protección de Datos Personales y
garantía de los derechos digitales, institutions may restrict access to
medical documentation if such access is considered harmful to the
patient. This provision allows clinicians and institutions to conceal
diagnoses, deny knowledge of interventions, or prevent verification of
coercive practices. Given that most psychiatric interventions are
justified by internal records rather than externally verifiable metrics,
this legal permissiveness enables a regime of archival impunity. It
permits practitioners to create and maintain clinical fictions that are
not subject to real-time correction, narrative challenge, or scientific
scrutiny. The person subjected to coercion is not only stripped of legal
defenses but also of the basic epistemic tools to trace, understand, and
respond to the chain of events that defined their trajectory. In the
absence of mandated version control, independent auditing, or obligation
to register refusals of consent, the clinical record becomes an
instrument of ontological erasure. Repeated findings from this thesis
confirm that access to these records is frequently denied or delayed,
especially when there are indicators of procedural irregularities or
familial collusion.****

****Coercion becomes routine not through open declarations but through
procedural habits and administrative automation. This normalized
suspension of rights is observed particularly in institutionalized
settings, where structural dependency, socioeconomic vulnerability, and
lack of external oversight converge. Within these environments, the
burden of proof is reversed: individuals are compelled to demonstrate
they are no longer dangerous rather than being presumed competent or
non-threatening. The possibility of contestation is foreclosed by the
same system that enforces and ****adjudicates coercion. This legal
circularity leaves no room for therapeutic innovation, reflection, or
person-centered evaluation. The ethical principles of beneficence,
justice, and respect for persons are thereby rendered nominal. Instead,
the scientific and moral foundation of care is replaced by a managerial
model of containment. This model is sustained by bureaucratic
imperatives and professional routines that obscure responsibility and
dilute accountability. In such a context, misdiagnosis, chemical
restraint, and the denial of personal testimony are not the exceptions
but the procedural core. This is a paradigm failure with far-reaching
biological, psychological, and social consequences (Chambers, 2019).****

****The structural constraints on ethical practice among professionals
further entrench this legal and institutional impasse. Data gathered
through mixed methods reveal that many psychiatrists, psychologists, and
nurses are aware of the moral ambiguity or clinical inadequacy of the
interventions they are instructed to perform. However, the prevailing
climate of fear, institutional conformity, and legal uncertainty
inhibits better action. Professionals report the absence of protocols
for refusal, lack of protection for dissent, and fear of professional
reprisal. Legal vagueness becomes a mechanism of both personal and
institutional immunity, disincentivizing innovation, preventing
whistleblowing, and fostering passive complicity. Ethical deliberation
is displaced by administrative compliance. What emerges is not an
environment of collective care or clinical progress but one of
system-wide obedience to authority, reinforced by ambiguous legal texts,
structural inertia, and a culture that confuses submission with safety.
In its most extreme expression, this culture normalizes social death
through a sequence of biomedical interventions that diminish autonomy,
decontextualize suffering, and produce lifelong dependency on systems
that neither protect nor repair. These findings call for immediate legal
and institutional transformation grounded in empirical observation,
interdisciplinary science, and the recognition of every person's
fundamental right to dignity, health, and justice (Farmer, 2004;
Bourdieu, 2001).****

****To address the systemic deficits outlined above, immediate
structural reform ought to be enacted across legislative, clinical, and
procedural domains. Legal norms cannot remain merely declarative while
clinical practice is governed by unwritten customs, discretionary acts,
and culturally tolerated violations of bodily integrity. A binding
mandate for real-time documentation, cross-check validation, and
independent ethical oversight ought to be enshrined in national
legislation. Clinical records ought to be subject to version control
protocols ensuring the traceability of every modification. An obligatory
inclusion of the patient's own account and informed disagreement ought
to be preserved in all documentation systems, with penalties for
omission or alteration. These protections are not auxiliary to medical
ethics but intrinsic to its core. Biological anthropology affirms that
health is not merely the absence of disease but the presence of systemic
integrity, dignity, and relational coherence. The absence of narrative
safeguarding mechanisms in psychiatry constitutes a violation of the
homeostatic equilibrium necessary for cognitive and affective recovery.
What cannot be said cannot be healed. Without epistemic integrity, no
biological model is sustainable, and no health outcome is reliable
(Levin & McDevitt, 2002).****

****Additionally, statutory reforms ought to explicitly preclude the use
of family testimony as sole clinical basis in cases of conflict,
coercion, or contested histories. This thesis, through its survey
findings, fieldwork, and case studies, has demonstrated a recurring
pattern in which family members with ****documented histories of
violence, coercion, or instrumental manipulation are permitted to
initiate or legitimize psychiatric detentions. This legal vacuum
operates as a secondary channel for familial abuse and institutional
complicity. Safeguards ought to be implemented to ensure that reports
from individuals with evident conflict of interest are not treated as
objective clinical data without formal verification. This entails
mandatory triangulation of information, engagement of external
mediators, and a default to protection rather than coercion when
familial abuse is even remotely suspected (Bourgois, 2001). Mental
health professionals ought to be legally obligated to consult
independent ethics committees prior to enforcing any measure based on
family testimony alone. Where risk exists, it ought to be scientifically
evidenced, not presumed; and where care is professed, it ought to be
structurally distinct from dominance (Gilligan, 1996).****

****Findings set clear that another critical reform ought to target the
opaque boundary between medical authority and judicial rubber-stamping.
Judges, though nominally responsible for reviewing involuntary
interventions, operate almost exclusively on the basis of clinical
reports, which are rarely challenged. The principles of fair trial,
non-maleficence, and proportionality are rendered inert when the
judiciary functions as an automated extension of the psychiatric report,
without hearing the subject's voice, assessing context, or scrutinizing
the plausibility of risk assumptions. To rectify this, mental health
hearings ought to become obligatory and adversarial, with independent
expert review, inclusion of a multidisciplinary assessment, and full
procedural transparency. Clinical recommendations ought to be examined
in light of recent jurisprudence and not accepted as self-validating.
Judicial practice cannot continue to outsource the ethical and
biological complexity of psychiatric cases to institutional inertia. A
true medico-legal interface requires rigorous evidentiary standards,
accountability for negligence, and responsibility for harm (Staub,
1989).****

****Structural protections ought to be embedded to prevent retaliatory
harm against individuals who challenge coercive interventions or seek
legal redress. Field data confirm that professionals and users alike
refrain from exercising their rights due to fear of material
retaliation, custody loss, or loss of housing. The consequences of
institutional dissent are not merely administrative but existential. For
those already marginalized, such consequences can escalate to
destitution, prolonged dependency, or death. The legal system ought to
therefore provide immediate access to protective legal representation,
whistleblower protections for professionals, and interim material
safeguards, such as housing guarantees and financial support, to prevent
reprisals from undermining resistance. This is not a matter of social
policy alone but of biological continuity, psychological stabilization,
and anthropological justice. Law ought to actively support the metabolic
and neurocognitive resilience of those who resist systemic harm
(Galtung, 1990).****

****The structural defects in current psychiatric practice in Spain are
not solely attributable to individual malice or ignorance but arise from
institutional logics that encode coercion as clinical safety and control
as care. These systems operate within a historical lineage where
psychiatric authority emerged in tandem with carceral and disciplinary
frameworks, legitimizing epistemic asymmetries and embedding submission
into therapeutic routines. The presumption of beneficence has become
immunized against empirical falsification, and the clinical apparatus
continues to function without mechanisms to detect or correct deviance
from minimally acceptable standards. This is not a failure of law in
theory but of its non-operationalization in the psychiatric domain. When
the right to liberty, ****bodily integrity, and informed refusal are
subordinated to the discretion of a single clinician acting without
procedural counterweights, the result is not care but sanctioned
dominance. The evidence shows this is not exceptional but routine
(Schreurs, Griffith, & Solomon, 1984).****

Findings show a key mechanism perpetuating this regime is professional
capture: the informal but systemic silencing of dissenting professionals
through bureaucratic obstruction, reputational retaliation, and
structural fear ****(Hysong, 2009)****. Practitioners who attempt to
implement dialogic, trauma-informed, or human rights-based practices
face institutional barriers that render such work unsustainable. In many
documented cases within this dissertation, professionals have reported
being forced to comply with dominant paradigms under threat of contract
termination, administrative scrutiny, or social exclusion within medical
teams. The lack of legal protection for clinical dissent and absence of
mandated ethical review structures reduces psychiatric institutions to
mono-disciplinary enclosures, incapable of reflexivity or reform.
Scientific progress, however, depends on iterative feedback, open
contestation, and methodological pluralism. Without safeguards for
intra-professional dialogue, psychiatry cannot evolve and instead
reproduces obsolete models of harm.

To reverse this condition, the law ought to enforce institutional
transparency, professional accountability, and multi-level audit. First,
there ought to be a national independent oversight body for psychiatric
care with legal authority to investigate, penalize, and correct
institutional malfeasance. This body ought to be composed of
interdisciplinary experts in law, neuroscience, public health, and
ethics, with representation from service users and independent
observers. It ought to have real-time access to anonymized case data,
compulsory reporting rights, and the ability to impose binding
recommendations. Second, every psychiatric facility ought to implement
internal ethical review committees, with obligatory referral for any
case involving involuntary treatment, high-dose medication, prolonged
hospitalization, or conflicting family involvement. These committees
ought to document justification, verify risk claims, and propose
least-restrictive better ways. Third, patient files ought to include a
section for independent narrative, written or verbal, updated regularly,
and auditable in court. Tampering with this narrative, or failure to
include it, ought to carry disciplinary and legal consequences. Fourth,
legislative reform ought to mandate full version control of all clinical
documentation and prohibit retroactive modifications without
traceability. Current systems allow annotations to be added, removed, or
rewritten without independent verification, which permits the
construction of fictive clinical histories that escape judicial
scrutiny. Where contradictions emerge between institutional narrative
and lived experience, the default ought to shift toward protective
inquiry, not bureaucratic denial. Each deletion or alteration of a
report ought to be timestamped, justified, and accessible to the patient
and legal representatives. This also requires robust digital
infrastructure and integration with national health record systems.
Legal codes ought to be reformed to allow immediate emergency
intervention by an independent ombudsman or legal defense office upon
user request, bypassing institutional gatekeeping. The judicial delays
built into current practice ensure that violations proceed unchecked
long enough to produce irreversible damage. These institutional repairs
are not merely legal or administrative: they are medical imperatives
grounded on biology, developmental, as lives are lost from early on, and
crimes affect the well-being of children once legality itself is also
destroyed.

Human neurobiology, particularly under conditions of trauma, depends on
predictability, coherence, and relational safety to restore functioning.
The current system, by contrast, undermines all three. It punishes
attempts at narrative correction to reality, bringing all onto the track
of crime and harming instrad of supporting the victims, delegitimizes
any complain and request, and medicalizes adaptive resistance. What
appears as symptomatic behavior in the clinical gaze may in fact be a
biologically regulated act of survival (Li et al., 2025). If the system
is incapable of distinguishing between pathology and protest, then it is
not diagnostic but punitive. The law ought to recognize this and
operationalize justice not only as legal restitution but as an
ecological precondition for repair. The stakes are not symbolic. They
are cellular, synaptic, and systemic. Law ought to ensure that
psychiatric care aligns with the biological foundations of health, not
against them.

The legal system ought to be designed not only to prosecute
retrospective harm but to anticipate and prevent violations at the
critical point where clinical, familial, and social power converge. This
point of convergence is the crisis encounter, the moment when a person,
under extreme distress, is subject to potentially irreversible clinical
decisions with minimal scrutiny or defense. Presently in Spain, the
emergency protocols governing mental health crises grant overwhelming
authority to clinicians, often acting on secondhand reports, under
poorly defined thresholds of danger to self or others. These thresholds
lack standardization, are not subject to transparent evidentiary
procedures, and are rarely re-examined once imposed. Yet, from a
neurobiological perspective, this moment is among the most vulnerable in
a person's lifespan. The amygdala-driven fear circuitry, the
dysregulation of affect, the loss of symbolic processing and trust,
these are compounded, not relieved, by coercive interventions
(Rodríguez-Cabrera et al., 2024).

The anthropological data collected for this thesis demonstrates that
individuals in such moments are overwhelmingly aware of what is at
stake: their credibility, their future, their relationships, their
children, their access to housing and employment. When professionals
impose interventions based on flawed assumptions, undocumented reports,
or family testimonies given undue weight, the result is not therapeutic,
it is epistemic and biological destabilization. These decisions fracture
the embodied sense of self, and they teach, especially to children
witnessing or undergoing them, that safety is not a right, that care is
indistinguishable from domination. This is not only unethical, it is
incompatible with healthy brain development and long-term recovery. Law,
to fulfill its protective role, ought to insert procedural safeguards
precisely at this junction. The right to have a designated trusted third
party, the immediate right to call for legal and psychosocial support,
and a written record of all risk claims and decision rationales ought to
be enforceable in real time. Professionals should not fear this; they
should welcome it, as it protects all parties and reinforces the
legitimacy of their clinical decisions ****(Rothschild, 2000)****.

Legal doctrine ought to also incorporate a scientifically grounded
understanding of structural risk. Structural risk is not merely the risk
a person poses to themselves or others, but the compounded vulnerability
they experience due to institutional neglect, social exclusion, economic
coercion, and previous trauma. Many of the most aggressive and damaging
psychiatric interventions are not applied to those with the most severe
symptoms, but to those with the fewest resources, weakest social
support, and most stigmatized profiles. Structural bias, racial,
gendered, class-based, and epistemic, permeates crisis response . The
law ought to counteract this by enforcing structural protection: the
right to equitable representation, to trauma-informed evaluation, and to
culturally competent care. Assessments ought to be conducted in the
language and idiom of the person affected, not the administrative
convenience of the institution. The failure to do so transforms the law
into a vector of harm rather than a shield. Trust, in this framework, is
not an abstract ethical principle but a neurodevelopmental substrate: a
condition for recovery, for repair, for reengagement with society.
Chronic institutional betrayal rewires the brain toward hypervigilance,
dissociation, and social withdrawal. These effects are not reversed by
medication alone, and are exacerbated when the legal system validates
the logic of control over care. To restore trust in psychiatric and
legal institutions, accountability ought to be visible, consistent, and
grounded in evidence-based relational practices. Institutional memory
ought to be built into the system: tracking prior violations, patterns
of negligence, and repeat institutional aggressors. Professionals who
repeatedly refuse to correct false information, who deny access to
records, who act without informed consent or judicial backing, ought to
be subject to disciplinary review, not to punish, but to correct course
and prevent harm. Such mechanisms would also protect professionals
working under duress, and reduce the likelihood of cascading
institutional failure (Tuncak, 2017; Pūras, 2017; Maté, 2021).

From a strictly medical-biological standpoint, the current legal
configuration governing mental health interventions in Spain fails to
meet the minimum thresholds required for ethical, developmentally sound,
and physiologically non-damaging care. The most egregious deficiency
lies in the unchecked discretionary authority granted to individual
clinicians or medical teams, without mandated second opinions, without
standardized evidence thresholds, and without real-time procedural
checks, to override fundamental rights ****(Epstein, 2013)****. This is
not a question of isolated malpractice but a systematic, legally
sanctioned breach of bodily sovereignty, narrative integrity, and
neurodevelopmental safety. These breaches directly contravene
constitutional protections under articles 15 (right to life and physical
integrity), 17 (right to liberty and security), and 18 (right to honor
and privacy) of the Spanish Constitution. The existing organic and civil
laws (notably Ley Orgánica 1/2004, Ley General de Sanidad, and article
763 of the Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil) provide a nominal legal scaffold
but lack operational protocols to prevent the institutionalization of
harm. A scientifically valid legal framework ought to explicitly
prohibit irreversible or high-risk interventions based on subjective or
uncorroborated declarations, especially when these originate from
parties with potential conflicts of interest, such as family members in
abusive or contentious relationships. The anthropological data and
survey responses reveal repeated patterns where psychiatric power was
wielded as a tool for domination, eviction, discrediting, or silencing.
These acts are not anecdotal but patterned, and they emerge precisely
because the law provides no effective mechanisms to question, counter,
or correct them in real time. There ought to be a legal mandate for full
version-controlled medical documentation, visible digital trails of all
record edits, and immediate access for the patient and their designated
legal or health proxy to all medical claims, diagnoses, risk appraisals,
and interventions. This is standard protocol in any other high-risk
clinical context; mental health cannot be excluded (Moyn, 2015).

The scientific basis for this reform lies in the principle of allostatic
load and neuroendocrine deregulation: coercion, uncertainty, and
betrayal by health institutions induce chronic stress responses that
have measurable and long-lasting effects on brain morphology, immune
functioning, endocrine rhythms, and psychiatric vulnerability. These are
not abstract notions. Peer-reviewed evidence confirms that patients
subjected to coercive psychiatry exhibit higher rates of cognitive
decline, social withdrawal, immune suppression, cardiovascular
deterioration, and suicidality. A law that permits interventions with
such risk profiles without parallel legal safeguards is, by definition,
a law in breach of the Hippocratic principle of non-maleficence. The
reform is not only moral or legal, it is required by scientific
consensus and basic clinical integrity.

Parliament ought to urgently enact a structured reform with the
following core measures:

-   ****Reform of Article 763 LEC**** to require not only judicial
    authorization within 24 hours, but interdisciplinary panel review
    with trauma-informed and rights-trained professionals, including
    lived-experience representatives, caring for the case as it unfolds,
    with the right of the victim to replace any and all members by
    trusted ones at all times.
-   ****Mandated version control and audit trails**** in all psychiatric
    records, accessible to the patient and their legal proxy, with
    independent oversight bodies receiving flagged cases of unexplained
    risk assessments or coercive measures. Open data made available on
    funding to practitioners, victims by center and professionals, on
    own medical history record in full.
-   ****Creation of an ombuds system for urgent psychiatric rights
    violations****, with autonomous investigative power and immediate
    suspension authority in cases of life-threatening or degrading
    practices. No compromises, the most strict legal and material
    protections.
-   ****Establishment of a national protocol for family conflict and
    mental health****, banning the use of psychiatric reporting from
    interested family parties without cross-verification and disallowing
    involuntary interventions in unresolved family abuse contexts unless
    forensic risk is formally established. All sources of suffering
    ought to be addresses, no assumptions made, specially not the taking
    for granted of anyone's account without double checking: this
    includes spiking, poisoning, other illness, abuses, lack of sleep
    due to those abuses or any other, crimes of any nature, ongoing
    normalization of violence; all, from earliest on.
-   ****Deployment of one health-compliant forensic care units****
    integrating medical, anthropological, psychological, and legal
    expertise, with compulsory recording and transparency of all crisis
    interactions involving loss of liberty or chemical restraint.
-   ****Criminal penalties for intentional misdiagnosis or obstruction
    of medical truth**** when used to restrict freedom, discredit, or
    financially or socially harm a person, including within family
    systems. Repayments, reparations, voluntary cognitive remediation,
    official apologies.

These reforms are direct responses to documented systemic failure,
grounded in robust empirical data, peer-reviewed scientific knowledge,
and the lived experience of both victims and ethical professionals
working under duress. Spain cannot claim constitutional fidelity or
medical advancement while upholding a psychiatric-legal architecture
that violates the very foundations of evidence, consent, and personhood.
Parliamentary resolution is not merely justified, it is scientifically
and ethically urgent.

Mid term achievable goal only if the will is present, are expert systems
deployed at full operational scale as foundational infrastructures for a
scientifically just, medically informed, surveillance safer and
constitutionally aligned society. The function of any and all
improvement in legilation and its enforcement is not auxiliary but
central to the protection of fundamental rights, the prevention of harm,
and the real-time monitoring of decisions that affect health, liberty,
and bodily integrity.

By integrating evidence-based logic, real-time data streams, and
ethically programmed thresholds, these systems establish continuous
accountability across clinical, judicial, educational, and domestic
domains. They ought to operate without interference from discretionary
authority, replacing subjectivity and power asymmetries with traceable,
reproducible, and medically coherent responses. Their embedded
algorithms ought to prioritize trauma-informed reasoning, relational
diagnostics, and ecological coherence, ensuring that no coercive
intervention proceeds without scientific indication, judicial oversight,
and continuous audit. These systems ought to reject every known pattern
of epistemic injustice, institutional silence, or algorithmic
obfuscation, and instead be programmed to escalate any deviation from
protective standards to a cross-disciplinary enforcement interface that
combines legal, clinical, and social action. The algorithmic law,
personalized, when it comes to aiding those who did not learn how to
take care of themselves and others, full coercing to a live of health
restored. These ought to not be conceptualized as optional digital tools
but as essential biomedical and ethical infrastructure ensuring
survival, dignity, and equity. Where professional failure, conflict of
interest, or subjective bias previously enabled structural harm, expert
systems now make it both detectable and prosecutable. Their role is to
uphold the core of medicine, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice, and
autonomy, by eliminating impunity, automating prevention, and securing a
living legal architecture where science, law, and human development
converge.

****

**6.2 International human rights law and mental health standards**

From the perspective of the person harmed, denied legal standing,
drugged without consent, and stripped of any avenue to report, appeal,
or stop the assault on their body, the gap between international rights
and their enforcement is not a matter of legal tension but a structure
of impunity. The person is rendered voiceless before the law and
meaningless to the institution. Spain has ratified the United Nations
Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the European
Convention on Human Rights, and the Convention Against Torture, and has
supported WHO QualityRights guidelines, yet these instruments are
functionally irrelevant in the life of the person subjected to coercive
psychiatry. The ratifications are not enforced. The rights are not
recognized. The protections are not applied. The mechanisms to activate
them are either inaccessible, nonexistent, or entirely captured by the
same professional bodies that commit the violations. This is not system
failure. It is design (Goodman et al., 2016).

Chemical restraint, euphemized as treatment, is carried out without
consent, often without a diagnosis grounded in current or complete
evaluation, and without real-time documentation of clinical reasoning or
better ways explored. Access to one\'s own clinical history is routinely
denied or delayed. Objections from the person affected are dismissed as
symptoms. The law is circumvented by the mere signature of a
practitioner, who faces no counterbalance, no oversight, no required
disclosure of side effects, and no version-controlled report subject to
external audit. These practices violate Articles 12, 14, 15, and 25 of
the UN CRPD, among others, but that violation is irrelevant to the
person drugged into submission without remedy. In Spain, neither
constitutional nor international guarantees are meaningfully actionable
once the psychiatric apparatus is activated.

The prohibition of torture and degrading treatment is not suspended by
clinical status. Yet, in practice, the assumption of dangerousness or
incapacity justifies prolonged and forced drugging that causes
cognitive, metabolic, and endocrine damage, often irreversibly. There is
no obligation to reverse, to reassess, to justify. The person affected
cannot file a police report while detained or medicated against their
will. Lawyers rarely intervene, and when they do, their capacity is
limited by the lack of access to contemporaneous clinical documentation
and the professional immunity embedded in medical institutions. No
forensic body exists to evaluate whether forced pharmacological
interventions are biologically warranted or legally defensible. The
entire system is closed, circular, and unaccountable. Under
international law, the right to refuse treatment, to be free from
torture, and to retain legal capacity is unconditional. In Spain, these
rights are conditional on institutional discretion and are denied
without procedural remedy. The obligation to prevent coercion is
binding. The duty to ensure consent is active. Yet, every provision is
bypassed in routine psychiatric practice through administrative
assumptions that remain unchecked. The law protects the system, not the
individual. The burden of proof remains on the victim, who often cannot
speak, write, or be heard. Structural impunity is disguised as care. A
system that allows this cannot be reformed with recommendations. It
ought to be dismantled where it violates life and rebuilt under
enforceable international norms, with independent oversight, forensic
accountability, real-time access to records, guaranteed external
reporting channels, and the automatic criminalization of forced drugging
without consent. Until then, international law remains an unfulfilled
promise, irrelevant to those most in need of its protection (Leys,
2018).

By the time a case reaches court, if it ever does, the harm has already
been inflicted, the body altered, the mind eroded, and the social
position dismantled. There is no legal avenue that retroactively
restores life capacity, familial bonds, dignity, or trust once
pharmacological violence and psychiatric sequestration have taken place
without consent. In practice, justice mechanisms activate only after
systemic betrayal has run its course. And when they do, they rarely
consider the biological and psychological consequences already encoded
in the body of the person harmed. No courtroom undoes neurochemical
disruption, metabolic collapse, or the social death that ensues from a
fabricated label institutionalized through professional complicity and
familial weaponization. The very idea of due process is a fiction when
the individual, from the first contact with psychiatric institutions, is
stripped of the capacity to refuse, to narrate, to access evidence, or
to demand time-sensitive protection (Kalisch et al., 2017). In many
cases, records are inaccessible or do not exist in retrievable form,
decisions are undocumented or vaguely noted, and witnesses are
professionals embedded in the same structure that authorized the abuse.
The person affected is presumed unreliable and discredited in advance,
denied procedural parity not only because of power asymmetry, but
because their very subjectivity has been preemptively invalidated by the
system. Legal guardianship, institutional confinement, and forced
pharmacology are implemented not as exceptional measures but as standard
procedures, justified by the preventive logic of risk, absent objective
criteria and absent any duty to reassess or consult external expertise.

Until then, children are removed to foster care or lost to crime,
growing in despair, homes are lost, health is deteriorated, and futures
are eradicated before any legal recognition of harm is even considered
(Solnit, 2009). The notion that rights can be vindicated post hoc
assumes a model of remedy that does not apply in the real conditions of
coercive psychiatry. There is no compensatory logic that equates to
years drugged against one\'s will, rendered infertile, neurologically
impaired, or stigmatized to the point of exclusion from education,
employment, and civic life. When the early signs of system involvement
emerge, typically through informal reports, family manipulation, or
school referrals, the machinery activates swiftly, and resistance is
framed as proof of pathology. Professionals wield the authority of
science without being required to validate their acts through replicable
standards or external review. Their interpretations become the legal
truth. Their omissions become institutional silence. Families that
initiate psychiatric proceedings in bad faith are rarely investigated or
held accountable, and the harm they enable or inflict is reframed as
concern. Structural violence is executed in the name of care, and those
subjected to it are forced to bear the cost not only biologically, but
legally, socially, and existentially (Hahn, 1995).

No court judgment restores a life fragmented in this way. Prevention is
the only ethical position. Law ought to act not after the fact, but as a
shield of dignity from the first moment of risk, not risk of violence
from the person, but risk of violence to the person. Legal safeguards
ought to be automated, obligatory, multidisciplinary, and available at
the moment coercion is considered, not once it has already succeeded.
Every hour under forced sedation, every day under control without due
process, is a biological, moral, and civic breach that cannot be
redressed retroactively. Once the damage is done, the person disappears
behind a clinical construction that society then accepts as reality. By
then, the injustice is normalized, the life disfigured, and the system
absolved. That is the pattern this dissertation reveals, and that is the
threshold upon which true reform ought to act.

This is the witnessing from within, not from a distance: the perspective
of one stripped of protection by those mandated to provide it, subjected
to coordinated institutional betrayal in spaces that claim legality but
operate on the currency of erasure. When violence is local, normalized,
and collectively denied, the law becomes theatre, its stage framed by
four walls that orient nowhere but further inward, enclosing lives until
what remains is only compliance or collapse. These four walls, symbolic
and real, become the cardinal structure of engineered despair: the
family complicit, the clinician unquestioned, the judge indifferent, the
state absent. In such a schema, no recourse exists. To push the victim
toward legal action becomes a new form of violence, delayed, procedural,
and fatal in consequence, suggesting that truth can survive where rights
were preemptively denied, and remedies exist in systems designed to
suppress dissent. International mechanisms, treaties, and conventions
are cited with solemnity while lives vanish long before their provisions
are triggered. Death here is not always biological, it is social, legal,
cognitive, and affective. It is the extinguishing of a future, the
preclusion of healing, the theft of voice through clinical inscription,
and the reformatting of subjectivity into a diagnosis that outlives the
person. This research acts as testimony and evidence. The researcher,
also victim, bears witness to a transnational architecture of cruelty
sustained by silence and procedural fictions. In doing so, it declares
the global imperative: to dismantle the regimes that enable such loss
and construct instead a planetary ethic grounded in factual protection,
immediate support, and the recognition that delay is complicity, and
proceduralism is often a final burial. That is the threshold this thesis
crosses, and that is where this chapter closes. All countries ratified
basic human rights, longest the ago; this reality accounted goes right
after the sanctity of life itself. Local hate bends reality as hell on
Earth (Lupton, 1997).

\
This is the witnessing of the researcher itself, on any law, at this
global scale the action-research is moving forward. Four walls, as
cardinal directions, and the unnumbered number of deadly and mortal sins
combining into burning pain, yet another set of lives destroyed; those
cells inside, and the loved ones left behind. Non apologetic addition
from the voice of a researcher who barely survived this research, and
never had a field day in Oviedo: that and all, laws can and do worsen,
once goodwill is lacking, the ill will prevailing instead (Kleinman,
1980).

The researcher, also victim, bears witness to a transnational
architecture of cruelty sustained not by ignorance, but by systematic
silence and the fictions of procedural order. In confronting this
reality, the thesis affirms a global imperative: to dismantle the
institutional configurations that permit such irreparable harm, and to
construct instead a planetary ethic of immediate protection, evidentiary
fidelity, and enforceable safeguards (Young, 1982). Delay is not a
neutral malfunction; it is complicity. Proceduralism, when abstracted
from lived suffering, becomes the final burial of justice. This is the
threshold this work crosses, where knowledge production and legal truth
ought to realign with the sanctity of life, not as a principle but as a
praxis. All nations have long ratified the core instruments of human
rights; the realities documented herein show that what is violated is
not interpretation, but the very basis of human protection. When this
failure becomes systemic, what is lost is not only rights but entire
trajectories of existence. The researcher speaks from within this
collapse: not as distant observer but as one enclosed within the four
walls that constitute the cardinal geometry of institutional betrayal.
In those walls, crimes go unacknowledged, abusers are protected, and
protective laws become ornamental. Local hatred, sanctioned by neglect,
transforms lived reality into something indistinguishable from hell on
Earth. This action-research is forged not only across geographic scales,
but across the raw topography of violated bodies, coerced silences, and
unrecorded loss. The unnumbered sins embedded in this architecture of
cruelty multiply within clinical cells and domestic spaces alike,
extinguishing lives and scarring those left behind. This closing is not
an apology but a direct statement: law, when unmoored from
accountability and decency, degenerates. Goodwill ought to be codified
and enforced; otherwise, law bends to ill will, and in places like
Oviedo, and many others, those most in need of justice become its first
casualties.

**6.3 Synthesis and proposals for systemic restoration**

The patterns revealed through this research demonstrate a persistent
breach of medical, ethical, and legal obligations in the management of
mental health care within institutional, domestic, and community
frameworks. These breaches are not isolated anomalies but constitute a
systemic configuration of harm, characterized by epistemic suppression,
misclassification of distress, abdication of protective duties, and both
formal and informal modalities of coercion. At their core, these
practices reflect a deviation from the principles of bioethical
medicine, non-maleficence, justice, autonomy, and clinical
proportionality, resulting in the reification of institutional power and
the objectification of persons in states of vulnerability (Foucault,
1973).

These findings emerge consistently across diverse forms of evidence:
long-term participant observation, structured surveys of professionals
and users, comparative legal analysis, and historical ethnographic
mapping. Medically and bio-culturally, this systemic deformation
generates pathophysiological consequences including chronic stress
states, medication-induced iatrogenesis, neuropsychiatric
destabilization, loss of therapeutic alliance, and disruption of
developmental and relational trajectories (Cohen, 2001). These outcomes
manifest not only as individual suffering but as epidemiologically
significant burdens of harm, institutionalized through bureaucratic
inertia, professional disempowerment, and judicial abstraction. The
biomedical framing of distress, when deployed without narrative
anchoring or contextualized interpretation, serves as a vector of
ontological reductionism, enabling the replacement of trauma histories
and social determinants with decontextualized labels. These labels, in
turn, facilitate mechanisms of exclusion, restraint, and silence under
the aegis of clinical management. From a structural standpoint, the
repetition of these patterns across institutions and jurisdictions
indicates a failure of internal feedback loops, ethical escalation
pathways, and external accountability mechanisms. Proposals for systemic
restoration ought to center not merely on regulatory revision but on the
reconstitution of clinical, legal, and organizational epistemologies.
These include: the creation of national registries of coercive
incidents, classified by type, context, and outcome, to allow
epidemiological visibility of harm; the establishment of independent,
intersectoral oversight bodies with legally binding authority to
intervene; and the implementation of open-source expert systems
calibrated for ethical clinical decision-making, ensuring that
diagnostics, prescriptions, and treatment planning are subject to
continuous evidentiary validation and rights-based review. Clinical
algorithmic aids ought to be built on transparency, data provenance, and
structural reflexivity, not proprietary secrecy.

In parallel, comprehensive educational reforms are essential. Curricula
at medical and allied health faculties ought to include structural
competency, forensic accountability, and lived-experience integration,
along with advanced modules on deprescription, harm reduction, and
trauma-informed care (Bandura, 1999). These proposals align with the
operational principles of EU BEACON One Health Education: shared
governance, democratic feedback, and the primacy of personhood as a core
epistemic and therapeutic value (Cianconi et al., 2020). Narrative
restoration, in this context, is not ancillary but foundational, an
essential vector of healing and systemic recalibration, necessary for
both individual recovery and institutional legitimacy. Crime and
corruption are not aberrations in this system but frequent outcomes of
its present configuration. The absence of binding ethical mandates, the
subjectivist loopholes in psychiatric authority, and the lack of
enforceable standards for documentation and redress have created
conditions under which abuse not only persists but becomes routinized
(Zola, 1972). This framework therefore cannot serve its own correction
without external input. It requires conscious political will,
intergovernmental collaboration, and scientifically anchored legal
reform. Though the action remains limited in size, its epistemological
and strategic foundations are solid. For these mechanisms to yield
enduring change, they ought to be endorsed and operationalized by
nations, judiciary systems, and transnational organizations acting with
clarity, integrity, and purpose. Mental health, when misused, becomes a
vector for structural dispossession; when scientifically and ethically
grounded, it becomes a cornerstone of human and planetary health (Frank,
1995). The shift ought to be enforced through rigorous design, not left
to good intentions (Good, 1994).
